title: The System Design Interview
objectives: A 45-minute collaborative conversation where you clarify, estimate, sketch, and defend trade-offs.

cards.title: What interviewers grade
cards.body: Interviewers grade how you think, not a single right diagram. They watch for: clarifying scope, sensible numbers, a clear API, a clean high-level design, a deep dive into one hard part, and honest trade-offs.

cards.title: Six stages on a 45-minute clock
cards.body: Every interview in this course uses the same six stages. API design is its own stage: agreeing the two or three key endpoints before drawing boxes fixes what the design has to serve. Interview mode and the Interview Playbook run this exact plan.
steps: Requirements · 0–5 min
Estimation · 5–10 min
API · 10–15 min
High-level design · 15–25 min
Deep dive · 25–40 min
Wrap-up · 40–45 min

cards.title: Misconception: there is one right answer
cards.body: Many candidates try to reach the 'correct' architecture. There isn't one. Two strong candidates can draw different designs for the same prompt and both pass, because the interviewer grades whether each choice follows from the stated requirements and numbers, and whether you can say what it costs.

cards.title: Trap: designing before scoping
cards.body: Jumping straight into Kafka and microservices before asking what the product does. Spend roughly the first five minutes on requirements; the interviewer may steer you sooner.

cards.title: Worked example: the first five minutes
cards.body: Interviewer: “Design a URL shortener.” Good clarifying questions: Who creates links, and roughly how many per day? Do links expire? Custom aliases? Is click analytics in scope? A strong opening answer: “I’ll assume 100M new links a month, about 100 reads per write, redirects under 50 ms, links never expire, analytics out of scope. Let me size that before drawing anything.”

questions.prompt: The interviewer says “Design a URL shortener.” What is the strongest first move?

choices.label: Propose Kafka and microservices up front so the design can scale later
Ask who creates links, roughly how many per day, and whether links expire
Estimate storage straight away using a guessed user count
Sketch the links table schema first so there is something concrete to discuss

questions.explanation: Scope first. The number of links, the read/write ratio and expiry change every later choice.

questions.prompt: Order the six stages of a 45-minute design interview.
questions.explanation: Requirements drive the numbers, the numbers and the API define what the design must serve, and the deep dive tests it. Wrap-up closes with trade-offs.

questions.prompt: What is the interviewer mainly grading?

choices.label: How many technologies you can name in 45 minutes
Whether your diagram matches the company’s real production architecture
How you scope the problem, reason with numbers and defend trade-offs
Whether each component is designed in full detail

questions.explanation: There is no single right diagram. Interviewers watch the reasoning.

questions.prompt: For a URL shortener, which clarifying question changes the design most?

choices.label: Should short codes use uppercase letters?
Which cloud provider does the team prefer?
Which programming language should the redirect service be written in?
How many new links a day, and roughly how many reads per write?

questions.explanation: Volume and read/write ratio decide caching, storage and ID generation. The others are details you can decide later.

questions.prompt: How should you spend the first five minutes of “Design WhatsApp”?

approaches.label: Ask every question you can think of
approaches.description: Cover each edge case before drawing

approaches.label: Ask 3–4 scoping questions, then state assumptions
approaches.description: Users, core features, scale, out of scope

approaches.label: Skip questions and start drawing

rationaleOptions.label: Scale and features drive every later choice
Interviewers expect every edge case settled before any design
Stating assumptions lets the interviewer correct you early

rationaleConflicts.r3: Time is limited. Ask what changes the design, then move on; edge cases come up in the deep dive.

questions.explanation: Short, targeted questions plus stated assumptions keep the rest of the interview grounded.

questions.prompt: You are 20 minutes into a 45-minute design interview and still listing requirements. What is the best move?

choices.label: Summarise the agreed requirements and move to a high-level design now
Keep asking until the edge cases are covered
Skip design and jump to a deep dive on the database
Ask the interviewer to extend the slot

questions.explanation: Requirements and scale should take roughly the first 10 minutes. At minute 20 you need a working design on the board, so summarise and move on.

flashcards.front: What is graded in a design round?
flashcards.back: Structured thinking, trade-offs, communication — not a single perfect diagram.
Clarify functional + non-functional requirements and scope.

flashcards.front: The six interview stages and their minutes?
flashcards.back: Requirements 0–5, estimation 5–10, API 10–15, high-level design 15–25, deep dive 25–40, wrap-up 40–45.

mechanism.title: A 45-minute interview runs in six stages. Knowing the clock keeps you from spending 30 minutes on boxes and 0 on depth.
steps: Requirements (minutes 0–5). Ask what the product does, who uses it, which features are in scope and which are out, plus the non-functional targets: daily users, read/write mix, latency, availability and retention. Write them where the interviewer can see them.
Estimation (minutes 5–10). Turn the scale into rough numbers: requests per second at peak, storage per year and bandwidth, and say which number drives the design.
API (minutes 10–15). Sketch the two or three key endpoints with inputs and outputs, and say how retries stay safe (idempotency keys on writes).
High-level design (minutes 15–25). Draw the request path end to end: client, load balancer, stateless services, cache, database, queue. Show one read and one write flowing through it.
Deep dive (minutes 25–40). Pick the hardest part (the hot key, the fan-out, the consistency rule) or let the interviewer pick, and go into data model, algorithms and failure handling.
Wrap-up (minutes 40–45). Name the bottlenecks, what breaks first at 10× scale, what you would monitor, and the trade-offs you made on purpose.

useWhen: Any open-ended prompt like 'design WhatsApp' or 'design a URL shortener': the phases give you a script so you never freeze.
When the interviewer is quiet: narrating which phase you are in and why invites them to steer you.
When you are unsure of scale: asking for numbers is itself a signal of seniority.
avoidWhen: Do not follow the script rigidly if the interviewer redirects you, for example 'skip the API, go straight to storage'. Follow them; they are telling you what they grade.
Do not spend the clarify phase asking about things that will not change the design, such as the logo, the programming language or the cloud vendor.

rows: Breadth first, then one deep dive
A complete working system plus evidence you can go deep
High: no end-to-end design, scope never agreed
Medium: reads as memorised, no judgement shown
High: runs out of time before any design

numbers.title: Budget the 45 minutes before you start
assumptions: Six stages of 5, 5, 5, 10, 15 and 5 minutes (the same plan as the Interview Playbook and Interview mode)
steps: Requirements, estimation and API: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 minutes, a third of the slot.
High-level design: 10 minutes, finishing at minute 25.
Deep dive: 15 minutes, the largest single block, finishing at minute 40.
Wrap-up: 5 minutes; 15 + 10 + 15 + 5 = 45.
numbers.result: A third on scoping, numbers and the API, a bit under a quarter on the first design, a third on depth, and five minutes to close. If you are still drawing the first box at minute 20, you are behind.

india.title: Clarifying an 'IRCTC Tatkal' prompt
india.label: Public facts, illustrative interview
india.body: Suppose the prompt is 'design train ticket booking'. The clarifying questions that change the design are Indian-specific. Tatkal booking opens a day before the journey, at 10:00 for AC classes and 11:00 for non-AC classes, so traffic is a cliff, not a curve: almost all demand lands in the first few minutes. Asking 'do we need to support Tatkal?' moves the design from an ordinary web app to one built around a waiting room, per-train seat inventory with strong consistency, and payment timeouts that release held seats. Asking about the logo or the front-end framework changes nothing. Those two kinds of question are exactly what interviewers are separating.

pitfalls.trap: Opening with 'we'll use Kafka, Kubernetes and microservices'.
pitfalls.say: 'Before picking components, can I confirm the core features and roughly how many users and requests we expect?'

pitfalls.trap: Treating the interviewer as an examiner and going silent while thinking.
pitfalls.say: Think aloud: 'I'm choosing between a cache-aside read path and precomputing results. Here's why I lean cache-aside...'

pitfalls.trap: Claiming the design has no weaknesses.
pitfalls.say: 'The weakest point is the single primary database for writes. If writes grow 10×, I would shard by user ID.'

deep.diagram:
[Requirements] -> [Estimation] -> [API] -> [High-level design] -> [Deep dive] -> [Wrap-up]
   0-5 min       5-10 min    10-15 min     15-25 min           25-40 min      40-45 min
takeaways: Interviewers grade reasoning: scoping, numbers, a working design, depth, and honest trade-offs.
Spend roughly the first 10 minutes on requirements and scale, not 0 and not 20.
Ask questions whose answers change the design; skip the ones that don't.
Always close by naming bottlenecks and what you would do at 10× scale.

interactive.title: What comes at minute 10?
interactive.prompt: You have agreed the requirements and done the estimates. Ten minutes have gone. What should you do next?

choices.label: Sketch the two or three key endpoints: the API stage
choices.feedback: Agreeing the endpoints fixes what the design has to serve before you draw boxes.

choices.label: Go straight into a deep dive on the database
choices.feedback: Too early: without an end-to-end design there is nothing to go deep on yet.

choices.label: Draw the full microservice architecture with every component
choices.feedback: Drawing everything at once skips the API and burns the time you need for depth.

interactive.reveal: The plan is six stages: requirements 0–5, estimation 5–10, API 10–15, high-level design 15–25, deep dive 25–40, wrap-up 40–45. API comes before the boxes because it tells you which reads and writes the design must handle.

title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
objectives: Turn users into QPS, storage and bandwidth with rounded math: 1 day ≈ 10⁵ seconds.

cards.title: The estimation formulas
cards.body: QPS = DAU × actions per user ÷ 86,400. Peak = average × a peak factor you assume and say out loud (for example 2–3× for a daily curve, 10×+ for event spikes). Storage = writes/day × object size × retention. Round aggressively; the order of magnitude matters.

cards.title: From users to peak QPS
cards.body: Multiply users by actions, divide by the seconds in a day, then multiply by the peak factor you assume for this product.
steps: DAU
× actions/user
= avg QPS
× peak factor

cards.title: Worked example: QPS, storage and bandwidth for a chat app
cards.body: Assume: 50 million DAU; 40 messages sent per user per day; 100 bytes per message body, 200 bytes with metadata; Messages kept for 1 year, stored 3× for replication; Peak factor 3× (an example assumption for a daily curve; event spikes could be higher).
steps: Messages per day = 50M × 40 = 2B (2 billion).
Average write QPS = 2B ÷ 86,400 ≈ 23,000 per second (with the 10⁵ shortcut: 20,000).
Peak write QPS ≈ 23,000 × 3 ≈ 70,000 per second, under the assumed 3× peak.
Storage per day = 2 billion messages × 200 bytes = 400 GB. Per year: 400 GB × 365 ≈ 146 TB, and with 3 replicas ≈ 440 TB.
Ingress at peak = 70,000 messages/s × 200 bytes = 14 MB/s ≈ 112 Mbit/s.
cards.note: About 23K average and 70K peak writes per second, and roughly 150 TB a year of raw messages (about 440 TB with replication). Raw message ingress is relatively modest under these assumptions; real network traffic is several times higher once fan-out to each recipient, replication, protocol overhead and media are added. Whether 70K writes/s fits on one database depends on the hardware (CPU, NVMe), the cost of each write (row size, number of indexes), durability settings (fsync per commit or group commit), batching, and the engine (B-tree or LSM). Distribute when measurements show one node lacks headroom at peak, when one machine cannot hold the data (hundreds of TB here does force splitting storage), or when you need to survive a node failure without losing write capacity.

cards.title: Trap: forgetting the peak
cards.body: Designing for the average. Traffic in India is spiky around cricket finals, Big Billion Days and Tatkal at 10 AM, so state a peak factor for the workload and ask whether events push it higher.

questions.prompt: 10M daily users each make 10 requests a day. Roughly what is the average QPS?
A chat app has 50M daily users sending 40 messages a day each. Estimate average messages per second (in thousands).
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 23K/s is roughly ten times what one well-tuned app server handles for simple writes, so even the average needs a small fleet, and the peak you assume sets the real size.

questions.prompt: A photo app stores 2M new photos a day at 500 KB each. How much storage is added per year, in TB?
questions.workedAnswer: 2M × 500 KB = 1 TB a day; 1 TB × 365 = 365 TB a year.
questions.explanation: Design implication: 365 TB a year, before replicas and thumbnails, rules out keeping photos on app servers or in the database. Store the bytes in object storage and keep only metadata in the database.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site averages 2,000 QPS, but sales open at 10 AM. What should you design for?

choices.label: A stated peak several times the average, e.g. 10–20K QPS
2,000 × 86,400, the daily total
2,000 QPS, since the average already includes the 10 AM spike
2× the average, the standard peak factor for web systems

questions.explanation: Averages hide spikes. A peak factor is a workload assumption you state and confirm: about 2–3× for a smooth daily curve, 10× or more when sales open.

questions.prompt: Order the steps from daily users to the number you design for.
questions.explanation: Users × actions gives daily volume; divide by seconds per day; then multiply for peak.

questions.prompt: 50M users each send 40 messages a day at 200 bytes each. About how much raw message data is written per day?

choices.label: About 400 GB
Roughly 40 GB
About 4 TB
About 4 GB

questions.explanation: 50M × 40 = 2B messages a day. 2 billion messages × 200 bytes each is 400 billion bytes, which is 400 GB per day.

flashcards.front: How do you pick a peak factor?
flashcards.back: It is an assumption you state, not a constant: for example 2–3× for a daily curve, 10× or more for events. Ask the interviewer.

mechanism.title: Every estimate is a chain of multiplications. Write the chain down, round each factor, then multiply.
steps: Start from users: daily active users (DAU), and how many times each one does the action per day.
Average QPS = DAU × actions per user per day ÷ 86,400 seconds. Round 86,400 to 10⁵: it makes mental maths easy and errs slightly low, so note that.

Peak QPS = average × a peak factor. The factor is an example assumption to state and confirm, not a rule: a smooth daily curve might give about 2–3×, while event-driven traffic (a sale opening, a match final, Tatkal) can be 10× or far more.
Storage per year = new objects per day × average size × 365 (× replication factor, usually 3).
Bandwidth = QPS × bytes per request. Do it separately for ingress (writes) and egress (reads); egress is usually far larger.
Sanity-check the answer against something you know, for example one well-tuned server handling a few thousand simple requests per second.

useWhen: To decide whether you need sharding, caching or a CDN at all: one well-tuned machine is often enough for a few thousand simple requests per second, depending on how much work each request does.
To size storage tiers: hot data in memory, warm on SSD, cold in object storage.
To justify a design choice out loud: 'At about 70,000 peak writes per second I'd check whether one primary keeps up, given row size, indexes and commit durability, before deciding to partition.'
avoidWhen: Do not chase precision: 3.7 TB versus 4 TB never changes the design. Keep one significant figure.
Do not estimate things that do not drive a decision, such as the size of an error log line in a payments design.

rows: Order of magnitude is unchanged; QPS comes out ~14% low, so lean on the peak factor
Rounds storage up, a safe direction
State it as an assumption and ask; events often dominate

Raw message ingress is relatively modest under these assumptions; real network traffic is several times higher once fan-out to each recipient, replication, protocol overhead and media are added. Whether 70K writes/s fits on one database depends on the hardware (CPU, NVMe), the cost of each write (row size, number of indexes), durability settings (fsync per commit or group commit), batching, and the engine (B-tree or LSM). india.title: Why UPI peaks matter more than averages
india.label: Publicly reported (NPCI), rounded
india.body: NPCI publishes UPI volumes every month. In 2025 UPI crossed roughly 20 billion transactions a month. Spread evenly, 20 × 10⁹ ÷ (30 × 86,400 s) ≈ 7,700 transactions per second. But payments are not spread evenly: they cluster around meal times, evenings, salary days and festival sales, so a system sized for 7,700 TPS would fail at the moments that matter most. A design discussion should size for a peak several times the average (for example 3–5×, so roughly 25,000–40,000 TPS) and say clearly that the multiplier is an assumption to confirm. The method is the point: average from the public monthly figure, then an explicit, labelled peak factor.

pitfalls.trap: Giving the average QPS as the design target.
pitfalls.say: 'Average is about 23K; assuming a 3× daily peak I'd design for about 70K, and I'd ask whether launches or events spike higher.'

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting replication and indexes when sizing storage.
pitfalls.say: 'Raw data is about 150 TB a year; with 3× replication and indexes I'd budget roughly half a petabyte.'

pitfalls.trap: Doing silent arithmetic and announcing a number.
pitfalls.say: Write the chain on the board: 50M × 40 ÷ 10⁵ = 20K. The interviewer can follow and correct an assumption instead of your maths.

deep.diagram:
DAU 50M  x 40 msgs/day  = 2 billion/day
2 billion / 86,400 s    ~ 23K/s avg
23K x 3 (assumed peak)  ~ 70K/s
2 billion x 200 bytes   = 400 GB/day -> ~146 TB/yr (x3 = ~440 TB)
takeaways: Average QPS = DAU × actions ÷ 86,400; treat 86,400 as 10⁵ for speed.
Design for the peak, not the average. Peak factors are assumptions you state, for example 2–3× for a daily curve and 10×+ for events.
Storage = objects per day × size × retention × replication.
Keep one significant figure and say your assumptions out loud.

interactive.title: Find the peak your fleet can take
interactive.prompt: A chat app has 50M daily users sending 40 messages each. Your fleet handles 100K writes per second. Raise the peak factor: where does the fleet run out?
interactive.takeaway: The average stays near 23K/s whatever you assume; the peak factor decides the capacity. Above about 4.3× the 100K/s fleet runs out, so state the factor you are assuming and ask whether events spike higher.

title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal + Load Balancers
objectives: Scale up with a bigger box or scale out with more boxes behind a load balancer.

cards.title: Scale up or scale out
cards.body: Vertical scaling is simple but hits a ceiling and is a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling needs stateless services, a load balancer and partitioned data. It adds capacity, and it only adds availability if the copies fail independently and traffic is routed away from dead ones (health checks, no shared single database). Gains are rarely linear: shared state, coordination and hot keys eat into them.

cards.title: Growing from one server to many
cards.body: Scale up first because it is simple; before scaling out, move state off the servers so any instance can serve any request.
steps: One server
Bigger server (vertical)
Make stateless
Add LB
N servers (horizontal)

cards.title: Worked example: how many app servers for a peak?
cards.body: Assume: Peak 60,000 requests per second; One app server handles about 2,000 requests per second at a safe 60–70% CPU (measure this in a load test); Each server is 99.9% available on its own.
steps: Servers needed for load = 60,000 ÷ 2,000 = 30.
Add headroom to survive losing one availability zone of three: 30 ÷ (2/3) = 45 servers.
Availability of one server = 99.9%: about 8.8 hours of downtime a year (0.001 × 8,760 h).

With two independent servers behind a load balancer, both are down at once with probability 0.001² = 10^-6, so the app tier is about 99.9999% available, ignoring the load balancer and correlated failures.
cards.note: About 30 servers for raw load and about 45 to stay up through a zone failure. Redundancy, not size, is what moves availability from 'three nines' towards 'six nines'; correlated failures and shared dependencies stop you getting the full benefit.

cards.title: Trap: in-memory sessions
cards.body: Saying "just add servers" while keeping session state in server memory. Stateless first, then scale out.

questions.prompt: What must be true before app servers can scale horizontally easily?

choices.label: Sticky sessions pin each user to one server for good
Session state lives outside the app servers (Redis or signed tokens)
Each server keeps its own full copy of the database
All servers run on identical hardware and OS versions

questions.explanation: If any server can handle any request, the balancer can spread load and servers can come and go.

questions.prompt: What is the main limit of vertical scaling?

choices.label: It adds CPU cores, but memory and disk cannot grow
Load balancers cannot route traffic to a bigger server
A hardware ceiling, and the one machine is still a single point of failure
It forces you to rewrite the app to be fully stateless

questions.explanation: A bigger box is simple but finite, and it is still one box.

questions.prompt: Four app servers sit behind a load balancer, all using one primary database. Has availability improved?

choices.label: No: more app servers change only speed, not availability
Yes: four app servers make the system four times as available
Yes, fully, as long as the balancer uses round robin across all four
Partly: an app server can fail safely, but the single database is still a single point of failure

questions.explanation: Copies only raise availability where failures are independent and traffic is routed away from the dead one.

questions.prompt: Order the usual path from one server to many.
questions.explanation: Scale up while it is cheap; move state out before scaling out.

questions.prompt: A shop runs on one large server at 80% CPU. A sale in three weeks is expected to bring 5× traffic.
constraints: The next instance size is only 2× bigger
Sessions live in server memory today

approaches.label: Upgrade to the largest instance
Shard the database now
Move sessions to Redis, then run several servers behind a load balancer

rationaleOptions.label: The biggest box gives 2×, short of the 5× needed
Moving sessions out first lets any server take any request
Adding app servers also makes the database faster

rationaleConflicts.r3: The database is shared; more app servers add load to it rather than speeding it up.

questions.explanation: The bottleneck is app CPU, so scale the app tier out once it is stateless.

questions.prompt: Peak load is 60,000 requests/s and one server safely handles 2,000/s. You run in 3 zones and must survive losing one. How many servers?

choices.label: About 45
About 30
About 90
About 20

questions.explanation: 60,000 ÷ 2,000 = 30 for load. To survive losing one of three zones, the remaining two-thirds must carry it: 30 ÷ (2/3) = 45.

flashcards.back: Hardware ceiling and single point of failure.
Stateless services (externalise sessions).

mechanism.title: Going from one server to many, step by step
steps: Start with one server running the app and the database. It is simple, and the whole site goes down if that server does.

Scale vertically: move to a bigger machine with more CPU, RAM and faster disks. No code changes, but there is a hardware ceiling, cost grows faster than capacity at the top end, and it is still a single point of failure.
Split the database onto its own machine so the app tier and the data tier can scale independently.
Make the app tier stateless: move sessions, uploads and caches out of local memory and disk into shared stores (Redis, object storage, the database).
Put a load balancer in front and run N identical app servers. The load balancer health-checks them and stops sending traffic to failed ones.
Scale the data tier last and most carefully: read replicas for reads, then sharding for writes.

useWhen: Vertical: early on, or for a stateful component that is hard to split (a primary database). A larger instance buys time cheaply.

Horizontal: when you need fault tolerance (no single point of failure), when load exceeds the biggest affordable machine, or when traffic is spiky and you want to add and remove capacity automatically.
avoidWhen: Do not scale out a stateful app server: if sessions live in memory, users get logged out whenever the load balancer sends them to another box.
Do not shard the database before you need to: replicas, caching and a bigger primary usually come first because sharding makes joins, transactions and resharding hard.

rows: Top-end machines cost more per unit of capacity

numbers.title: How many app servers for a peak?
assumptions: One app server handles about 2,000 requests per second at a safe 60–70% CPU (measure this in a load test)
Each server is 99.9% available on its own
steps: Servers needed for load = 60,000 ÷ 2,000 = 30.
Add headroom to survive losing one availability zone of three: 30 ÷ (2/3) = 45 servers.
Availability of one server = 99.9%: about 8.8 hours of downtime a year (0.001 × 8,760 h).

With two independent servers behind a load balancer, both are down at once with probability 0.001² = 10^-6, so the app tier is about 99.9999% available, ignoring the load balancer and correlated failures.
numbers.result: About 30 servers for raw load and about 45 to stay up through a zone failure. Redundancy, not size, is what moves availability from 'three nines' towards 'six nines'; correlated failures and shared dependencies stop you getting the full benefit.

india.title: Flipkart Big Billion Days: why scale-out wins
india.label: Illustrative estimate; public event facts
india.body: Flipkart's Big Billion Days sale opens at a fixed time, often with early access for some members, so traffic jumps within minutes rather than ramping over hours. A single huge server cannot absorb that kind of jump, and it would be a single point of failure at the worst moment. The workable pattern is a stateless storefront and API tier behind load balancers, scaled out ahead of the announced start time (pre-warming, because autoscaling reacts in minutes), with sessions and carts in shared stores so any server can take any user. If, purely as an illustration, peak browse traffic were 20× a normal evening, a tier that normally runs 50 servers would need around 1,000 at the same per-server load. That is only practical when every server is identical and disposable.

pitfalls.trap: 'Just add more servers' while sessions live in server memory.
pitfalls.say: 'First I'd make the service stateless by moving sessions to Redis, then scale out behind a load balancer.'

pitfalls.trap: Assuming horizontal scaling also scales the database.
pitfalls.say: 'The app tier scales out easily. The primary database becomes the bottleneck next, so I'd add read replicas and caching, and shard writes only if needed.'

pitfalls.trap: Multiplying nines as if failures were independent when everything shares one zone or one database.
pitfalls.say: 'Redundancy helps only for independent failures, so I'd spread nodes across zones and avoid a shared single point of failure.'

deep.diagram:
+-> [app 1] -+
[clients] -> [LB] -> [app 2] -+-> [Redis sessions]
           +-> [app N] -+-> [DB primary] -> [read replicas]
takeaways: Vertical scaling is quick but has a ceiling and stays a single point of failure.
Horizontal scaling needs stateless services and a load balancer with health checks.
Size servers from measured per-node throughput plus headroom for losing a zone.
Scale the app tier first; the database is the hard part and comes last.

interactive.title: How much peak can 40 servers take?
interactive.prompt: One stateless app server safely handles 2,000 requests per second. You can run 40 servers and want 30% headroom plus one spare. Find the highest peak you can serve.
interactive.takeaway: About 60,000 requests per second fits: 30 servers of raw capacity, 39 with headroom, 40 with the spare. Scaling out is this linear only when servers are stateless and the database behind them keeps up.

title: OSI & TCP/IP
objectives: Place HTTP, TLS, TCP/UDP and IP in the right layer
Explain what a TCP handshake costs a request
Choose TCP or UDP for a given workload

cards.title: Why layers matter
cards.body: Interviewers rarely ask for all seven OSI layers. They ask which layer a component works at: an L4 load balancer sees IPs and ports, an L7 one sees HTTP paths and headers. Knowing the layer tells you what a box can and cannot do.

cards.title: The four layers you actually use
cards.body: Application (HTTP, gRPC, DNS) → Transport (TCP, UDP) → Internet (IP) → Link (Ethernet, Wi-Fi). TCP gives ordered, reliable byte streams with retransmits; UDP gives fire-and-forget datagrams with no ordering.

cards.title: A new HTTPS connection
cards.body: Before the first byte, a cold HTTPS request pays for a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake, each costing round trips.
steps: DNS lookup
TCP handshake (1 RTT)
TLS handshake (1 RTT on TLS 1.3)
HTTP request
Response

cards.title: Trap: ignoring round trips
cards.body: Ignoring round trips. From Mumbai to a us-east server one RTT is roughly 200 ms, so a cold HTTPS connection spends about 400 ms before the first byte. Keep-alive, connection pooling and edge termination exist to avoid paying that on every request.

questions.prompt: A multiplayer game sends each player’s position 20 times a second; a lost update does not matter because the next one replaces it. Which transport fits best?

choices.label: UDP (or a UDP-based protocol such as QUIC)
TCP, so each stale update is retransmitted in order
A new TCP connection for each update

questions.explanation: Retransmitting stale data only adds delay. TCP works, but it is not the best fit. (A browser score widget is different: it usually uses SSE or WebSockets over HTTP, as lesson 10 shows.)

questions.prompt: An L4 load balancer can route on which of these?

choices.label: The Authorization header
The URL path, such as /api
Destination IP and port
A cookie set by the app

questions.explanation: L4 sees transport information only. Paths, headers and cookies are HTTP, which is L7.

questions.prompt: Where does TLS sit in a typical HTTPS request?

choices.label: Below IP, so routers cannot see addresses
Above HTTP, inside the JSON body
Between TCP and HTTP: it encrypts the byte stream TCP carries
Inside DNS, during name resolution

questions.explanation: TLS runs on TCP and under HTTP. QUIC (HTTP/3) folds transport and TLS together over UDP.

questions.prompt: Order what happens before a brand-new HTTPS request can be sent.
questions.explanation: Resolve the name, open the connection, encrypt it, then send.

questions.prompt: Mumbai to us-east is about 200 ms round trip. With DNS cached, how many ms do the TCP and TLS 1.3 handshakes take before the request can be sent?
questions.workedAnswer: TCP 1 RTT + TLS 1.3 1 RTT = 2 × 200 ms = 400 ms.
questions.explanation: Design implication: 400 ms of handshakes before the first byte is why you terminate TLS close to users (a CDN or edge PoP) and reuse connections instead of opening a new one per request.

questions.prompt: RTT from Mumbai to a US server is about 200 ms. With TLS 1.3 and no reused connection, roughly how long before the first response byte (ignoring server time and DNS)?

choices.label: About 600 ms
About 200 ms
About 400 ms
About 1,200 ms

questions.explanation: One round trip each for the TCP handshake, the TLS 1.3 handshake and the HTTP request: 3 × 200 ms ≈ 600 ms.

flashcards.front: Which transport gives ordered, reliable delivery?
flashcards.back: TCP. UDP gives unordered datagrams with no retransmits.

flashcards.front: What does an L4 load balancer see?
flashcards.back: IP addresses and ports, not HTTP paths or headers.
Each new HTTPS connection pays TCP + TLS round trips before the first byte.

mechanism.title: What actually happens, layer by layer, when your browser fetches https://example.in/menu
steps: Application layer: the browser builds an HTTP request (method, path, headers). Before it can send anything it needs an IP address, so it asks DNS, which is itself an application-layer protocol, usually over UDP port 53.

Transport layer: TCP opens a connection to port 443 with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). That costs one round trip before any application data moves. TCP then numbers bytes, acknowledges them and retransmits losses, so the app sees an ordered, reliable stream.
Security: TLS runs on top of TCP. TLS 1.3 needs one more round trip to agree keys and verify the server certificate (TLS 1.2 needed two).
Internet layer: each TCP segment is wrapped in an IP packet with source and destination addresses. Routers forward packets hop by hop using only the IP header; they do not look at TCP or HTTP.
Link layer: on each hop the packet is framed for the physical medium (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 4G/5G radio) using MAC or radio addressing, then the frame is discarded and rebuilt at the next hop.
Back up the stack: the server's network card hands frames to IP, IP to TCP, TCP reassembles the byte stream, TLS decrypts it, and the web server finally parses the HTTP request.

useWhen: Placing components: an L4 load balancer works with IPs and ports (fast, protocol-agnostic); an L7 load balancer or API gateway reads HTTP paths, headers and cookies.
Explaining latency: count round trips per layer (DNS, TCP, TLS, request) to see where the time goes.
Debugging: 'can I reach the IP?' (L3), 'is the port open?' (L4), 'what status code?' (L7) separates network faults from application faults.
avoidWhen: Do not recite all seven OSI layers in a design interview; the four-layer TCP/IP model is what systems actually use.
Do not put application logic at L4: an L4 balancer cannot route by URL path or inspect cookies.

columns: What a device there can see
rows: API gateway, L7 load balancer, WAF
MAC addresses on one network segment

numbers.title: Why a cold HTTPS request from Mumbai to the US feels slow
assumptions: Round trip time (RTT) Mumbai ↔ US East coast ≈ 200 ms (typical public measurements are roughly 180–230 ms)
steps: TCP handshake: 1 RTT = 200 ms.
TLS 1.3 handshake: 1 RTT = 200 ms.
HTTP request and first byte of the response: 1 RTT = 200 ms, plus server time.
Total before the first byte ≈ 3 × 200 = 600 ms, before the server does any work.
Same request to a Mumbai region with RTT ≈ 5 ms: 3 × 5 = 15 ms.
numbers.result: About 600 ms versus about 15 ms for the same request: distance and round trips dominate. That is why we reuse connections (keep-alive, HTTP/2), terminate TLS at a nearby edge, and serve Indian users from Indian regions.

india.title: Why Indian apps terminate connections in India
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Most large Indian consumer apps (food delivery, payments, streaming) serve users from cloud regions in Mumbai or Hyderabad and from CDN points of presence inside India. Using the numbers above, a cold HTTPS request to a US origin spends roughly 600 ms just on round trips, while one to a Mumbai edge spends tens of milliseconds even from a city a few hundred kilometres away. On a mobile network, where each round trip is already slower, those extra US round trips are visible as a sluggish first screen. So the TCP and TLS handshakes are terminated as close to the user as possible, and the edge keeps warm, long-lived connections back to the origin.

pitfalls.trap: Saying 'the load balancer reads the URL' without saying which layer it works at.
pitfalls.say: 'For path-based routing I need an L7 balancer; an L4 balancer only sees IPs and ports.'

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring round trips when explaining latency.
pitfalls.say: 'A cold HTTPS request is about three round trips before the first byte, so I'd reuse connections and terminate TLS near the user.'

deep.diagram:
Browser                                Server
 HTTP  (L7)  GET /menu                  HTTP
 TLS         encrypt                    TLS
 TCP   (L4)  port 443, seq/ack          TCP
 IP    (L3)  src/dst IP  --routers-->   IP
 Link  (L2)  Wi-Fi / 4G  frames         Ethernet
takeaways: Use the four-layer TCP/IP model: application, transport, internet, link.
L4 devices see IPs and ports; L7 devices see HTTP paths, headers and cookies.
A cold HTTPS request costs about 3 round trips (TCP, TLS 1.3, request) before the first byte.
Latency is mostly distance × round trips, so serve users from nearby regions and reuse connections.

interactive.title: How far away can the server be?
interactive.prompt: A cold HTTPS request needs about three round trips before the first byte: TCP, the TLS 1.3 handshake, then the request itself. Keep that under 300 ms. Move the round-trip time.
interactive.takeaway: At 200 ms (roughly Mumbai to the US east coast) the user waits about 600 ms before any data arrives. At 100 ms or less you are inside the budget. Distance, not bandwidth, sets this, which is why edges and connection reuse matter.

title: TCP vs UDP
objectives: Explain what TCP guarantees and what UDP leaves to the app
Recognise head-of-line blocking
Choose a transport for a real workload

cards.title: What each gives you
cards.body: TCP is a connection: a three-way handshake, then an ordered, reliable byte stream with retransmits and congestion control. UDP sends independent datagrams: no handshake, no ordering, no retransmits. The app decides what to do about loss.

cards.title: Head-of-line blocking
cards.body: TCP delivers bytes in order, so one lost packet stalls everything behind it until it is resent. For live video or game state a late packet is worthless, and UDP lets the app skip it. HTTP/3 runs QUIC over UDP so a loss only stalls its own stream.

cards.title: Opening a TCP connection
cards.body: TCP's three-way handshake opens the connection; sequence numbers then let the receiver spot gaps and the sender retransmit lost segments.
steps: Client sends SYN
Server replies SYN-ACK
Client sends ACK: connection open
Data flows with sequence numbers
Lost segment is retransmitted

cards.title: Choosing
cards.body: TCP for anything that must arrive complete: APIs, payments, file transfer, chat history. UDP (often through QUIC or WebRTC) for real-time voice, video and game state, and for small DNS queries, where speed beats completeness.

cards.title: Trap: 'UDP is faster'
cards.body: Saying UDP is “faster” and stopping there. It skips handshakes and waiting on retransmits, but if you need reliability you must rebuild it in the app, which is exactly what QUIC does.

questions.prompt: Which workload fits UDP better than TCP?

choices.label: Submitting a UPI payment
Loading chat history when the app opens
Uploading a 2 GB file to object storage
Voice on a video call, where a late packet is useless

questions.explanation: Real-time media prefers dropping late packets over waiting for them.

questions.prompt: Why does one lost packet hurt a TCP stream carrying many requests?

choices.label: The client must redo the three-way handshake
Everything behind it waits until it is retransmitted (head-of-line blocking)
TCP closes the connection whenever a packet is lost
The receiver discards all later packets permanently

questions.explanation: In-order delivery means later bytes cannot be handed to the app until the gap is filled.

questions.prompt: Order the start of a TCP connection.
questions.explanation: The handshake costs one round trip before any data.

questions.prompt: Why does HTTP/3 run on QUIC over UDP?

choices.label: So it can skip encryption and save a round trip
Because TCP cannot carry compressed HTTP headers
So a loss on one stream does not stall the others, with TLS built in
Because UDP itself provides delivery and ordering

questions.explanation: QUIC adds reliability per stream on top of UDP, avoiding TCP-level head-of-line blocking.

questions.prompt: Pick transports for a multiplayer racing game.
constraints: Position updates 20 times a second per player
The game also has chat and in-app purchases

approaches.label: UDP for everything, including purchases
UDP for positions, TCP (HTTPS) for chat and purchases
approaches.description: Match each message type to its needs

approaches.label: TCP for everything

rationaleOptions.label: UDP keeps position updates in order
Purchases must arrive complete and in order
Stale position updates are not worth retransmitting

rationaleConflicts.r3: UDP has no ordering; the game must number updates and drop old ones itself.

questions.explanation: Use each transport where its guarantees match the data.

questions.prompt: A live stream at 4 Mbit/s over TCP loses one packet and it takes about 200 ms to recover. Roughly how much data waits behind it?

choices.label: About 100 KB
About 10 KB
About 1 MB
Nothing; TCP delivers the rest immediately

questions.explanation: 4 Mbit/s × 0.2 s = 0.8 Mbit = 100 KB, all held back because TCP delivers in order.

flashcards.front: Which workload fits UDP better than TCP?
flashcards.back: Voice on a video call, where a late packet is useless. Real-time media prefers dropping late packets over waiting for them.

flashcards.front: Why does one lost packet hurt a TCP stream carrying many requests?
flashcards.back: Everything behind it waits until it is retransmitted (head-of-line blocking). In-order delivery means later bytes cannot be handed to the app until the gap is filled.

flashcards.front: Why does HTTP/3 run on QUIC over UDP?
flashcards.back: So a loss on one stream does not stall the others, with TLS built in. QUIC adds reliability per stream on top of UDP, avoiding TCP-level head-of-line blocking.

mechanism.title: How each protocol moves your data
steps: TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), costing one round trip before data flows.
TCP numbers every byte. The receiver acknowledges what arrived; anything not acknowledged within the retransmission timeout, or flagged by duplicate ACKs, is sent again.
TCP delivers bytes strictly in order. If packet 5 is lost, packets 6–20 wait in the receiver's buffer until 5 is retransmitted: this is head-of-line blocking.

TCP's congestion control (slow start, then additive increase) grows the sending window gradually and shrinks it on loss (Reno halves it; CUBIC, the Linux default, cuts it to about 0.7×), sharing bandwidth fairly but ramping up slowly on new connections.

UDP just sends datagrams: no handshake, no ordering, no retransmission and no congestion control. Each datagram may arrive late, duplicated, out of order or not at all, and the app decides what to do.

QUIC (the transport under HTTP/3) runs over UDP and rebuilds reliability per stream in user space, so a loss on one stream does not stall the others, and it merges the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes into one round trip.

useWhen: TCP: APIs, payments, file transfer, database connections, chat history: anything that must arrive complete and in order.
UDP: live voice and video, game state, DNS lookups, telemetry where the newest value beats a retransmitted old one.
QUIC/HTTP/3: mobile clients on lossy networks that make many parallel requests, and that switch between Wi-Fi and cellular (QUIC connections can survive an IP change).
avoidWhen: Do not pick raw UDP for anything that needs every byte; you would end up re-implementing TCP badly.
Do not pick TCP for real-time media where a 300 ms retransmit makes the data useless; a dropped frame is better than a frozen call.

numbers.title: How much a single lost packet costs a live stream over TCP
assumptions: RTT 100 ms on a mobile network
One packet lost; the sender notices through duplicate ACKs after about one RTT and resends it
steps: Time until the lost packet is resent and received ≈ 1 RTT to detect + 1 RTT to deliver ≈ 2 × 100 = 200 ms.
Data stuck behind it in that time = 4 Mbit/s × 0.2 s = 0.8 Mbit = 100 KB.
If the loss is only caught by the retransmission timeout instead (at least 200 ms in Linux, often more on mobile), the stall is longer still.
Over UDP or QUIC streams, the player skips or conceals the missing piece and keeps playing the 100 KB that already arrived.
numbers.result: One lost packet can stall about 200 ms of video (roughly 100 KB) behind it on TCP. For live media, dropping data beats waiting for it.

india.title: Video calls and live cricket on Indian mobile networks
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: On crowded 4G cells in Indian cities, packet loss of a few percent is common at busy hours. A video call app that sends media over TCP would freeze every time a packet is lost, because everything behind it waits for the retransmit. That is why calling apps use WebRTC media over UDP (lost frames are concealed, not waited for), and why large streaming services have adopted HTTP/3 over QUIC for their apps: loss on one stream no longer blocks the others, and a QUIC connection can survive the phone moving from home Wi-Fi to mobile data. The control plane (login, payments, chat history) stays on reliable TCP or QUIC streams.

pitfalls.trap: 'UDP is faster, so use UDP.'
pitfalls.say: 'UDP avoids handshakes and retransmit stalls, which helps real-time media. For anything that must arrive complete I'd use TCP or QUIC rather than rebuild reliability.'

pitfalls.trap: Thinking HTTP/2 solved head-of-line blocking.
pitfalls.say: 'HTTP/2 removed it at the HTTP layer, but it still runs on one TCP connection, so one lost packet stalls every stream. HTTP/3 on QUIC fixes it at the transport layer.'

deep.diagram:
TCP:  [1][2][ ][4][5][6]  -> app waits for 3, then gets 3,4,5,6
QUIC: stream A [1][ ][3]  -> waits for A2
      stream B [1][2][3]  -> delivered now
UDP:  [1][2][ ][4][5]     -> app gets 1,2,4,5; decides about 3
takeaways: TCP: ordered, reliable, congestion-controlled, but one loss stalls everything behind it.
UDP: no guarantees; ideal when late data is useless (voice, video, games, DNS).
QUIC gives TCP-like reliability per stream over UDP with a 1-RTT handshake that includes TLS.
Choose by what late or lost data means for the user, not by 'speed'.

interactive.title: A lost packet on a live score feed
interactive.prompt: Live cricket scores stream to a phone over TCP. Update #41 is lost in the network; update #42 has already arrived. What does the app see?

choices.label: Nothing new until #41 is retransmitted, then both arrive in order
choices.feedback: Right: TCP hands bytes to the app strictly in order, so #42 waits behind the gap.

choices.label: #42 straight away; #41 is quietly dropped
choices.feedback: That is what a UDP-based design could choose to do, not TCP.

choices.label: The connection resets and reconnects
choices.feedback: A single loss triggers a retransmission, not a reset.

interactive.reveal: This is head-of-line blocking. For data where only the newest value matters, UDP (or separate QUIC streams) lets the app show #42 and skip #41, at the cost of handling loss yourself.

title: DNS
objectives: DNS maps names to IPs through a cached hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.

cards.title: How a name becomes an IP
cards.body: Browsers ask a recursive resolver, which walks root → .in/.com TLD → authoritative server and caches by TTL. Low TTLs allow fast failover; high TTLs reduce lookups.

cards.title: One DNS lookup, hop by hop
cards.body: A cache miss walks from the recursive resolver to the root, the TLD and the authoritative server; every answer is cached for its TTL.
steps: Browser cache
Recursive resolver
Root server
TLD (.in)
Authoritative
IP

cards.title: Worked example: how long does a TTL keep users on a dead region?
cards.body: Assume: A record TTL = 300 s (5 min); The region fails at 10:00:00; Resolver caches filled at random times before the failure.
steps: A resolver that cached the record just before 10:00 keeps serving it until about 10:05.
On average a cached entry has half its TTL left: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 s, so the typical user is stuck for about 2.5 minutes.
Worst case is the full 300 s, plus any client or resolver that ignores the TTL.
With a 24-hour TTL (86,400 s), the average stuck time would be 43,200 s = 12 hours.
cards.note: A 5-minute TTL means roughly 2.5 minutes of average impact and up to 5 minutes (plus stragglers); a 24-hour TTL means up to a day. Choose the TTL from how fast you must move traffic.

cards.title: Trap: long TTLs slow failover
cards.body: Forgetting that DNS caching delays failover. A 24 h TTL means some users hit the dead region for a day.

questions.prompt: Why lower a DNS TTL a day before moving to a new server?

choices.label: So resolvers stop caching the old IP for long and switch quickly
Lower TTLs make each lookup resolve faster
It is required to issue a new TLS certificate
It makes browsers skip the recursive resolver

questions.explanation: Caches keep a record until its TTL expires. A short TTL bounds how long clients use the old address.

questions.prompt: Order a cold DNS lookup.
questions.explanation: The resolver walks the hierarchy and caches each answer.

questions.prompt: On a cold lookup, who walks from the root down to the authoritative server?

choices.label: The root server forwards the query down the chain
The browser contacts each server itself
The authoritative server pushes records to browsers
The recursive resolver (your ISP’s or a public one)

questions.explanation: Browsers ask one resolver; it does the walking and caches the results.

questions.prompt: A record with a 24-hour TTL points at a region that just died. What happens?

choices.label: Browsers fail over to the next region on their own
DNS detects the failure and refreshes caches within seconds
Some users keep reaching the dead region until their cached record expires, up to a day
The authoritative server pushes the new IP to all resolvers

questions.explanation: DNS is pull-based. Caches keep the old answer until the TTL runs out.

questions.prompt: Pick a TTL for api.example.in.
constraints: Regional failover must take minutes, not hours
Millions of clients, so lookup volume matters

approaches.label: 60–300 seconds
24 hours
0 seconds

rationaleOptions.label: A few minutes still lets resolvers absorb most lookups
A long TTL is fine because DNS failover is instant
A short TTL bounds how long clients hold a dead IP

rationaleConflicts.r3: Cached records keep sending users to the dead region until the TTL expires.

questions.explanation: Minutes-long TTLs balance failover speed against lookup load.

questions.prompt: A region fails and its A record has a 300-second TTL. Roughly how long are typical users stuck before their resolver re-asks?

choices.label: About 2.5 minutes on average, up to 5 minutes
Zero: resolvers switch at once
300 milliseconds for each user
About 24 hours, whatever the TTL

questions.explanation: Cached entries have on average half the TTL left: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 s. The worst case is the full 300 s.

flashcards.front: What does TTL control in DNS?
flashcards.back: How long resolvers cache the record.
Return different IPs based on user location.

mechanism.title: Resolving api.example.in from a cold cache
steps: The app asks the operating system's stub resolver, which checks its own cache and then forwards the query to a recursive resolver (your ISP's, or a public one such as 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1).
The recursive resolver, if it has nothing cached, asks a root server. The root does not know the answer but replies with the name servers for the .in top-level domain.
The resolver asks a .in TLD server, which replies with the authoritative name servers for example.in.
The resolver asks the authoritative server, which returns the record (for example an A record with an IPv4 address) and a TTL in seconds.
The resolver caches the answer for the TTL and returns it. The next user of the same resolver gets it from cache in about a millisecond.
Managed DNS can return different answers to different resolvers (by location, health or weight), which is how DNS-based global load balancing and failover work.

useWhen: Low TTLs (30–60 s) on records you may need to fail over or shift traffic quickly, such as the entry point of a multi-region service.
High TTLs (hours) on records that rarely change, to cut lookup latency and resolver load.
Geo or latency-based DNS to send users to the nearest region or CDN point of presence.
avoidWhen: Do not rely on DNS alone for instant failover: some resolvers and clients cache longer than the TTL, so traffic drains over minutes, not seconds.
Do not set a very low TTL everywhere: every lookup that misses cache adds a round trip to the authoritative server, and query bills grow.

rows: Slow: up to a day for some users

numbers.title: How long does a TTL keep users on a dead region?
assumptions: Resolver caches filled at random times before the failure
steps: A resolver that cached the record just before 10:00 keeps serving it until about 10:05.
On average a cached entry has half its TTL left: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 s, so the typical user is stuck for about 2.5 minutes.
Worst case is the full 300 s, plus any client or resolver that ignores the TTL.
With a 24-hour TTL (86,400 s), the average stuck time would be 43,200 s = 12 hours.
numbers.result: A 5-minute TTL means roughly 2.5 minutes of average impact and up to 5 minutes (plus stragglers); a 24-hour TTL means up to a day. Choose the TTL from how fast you must move traffic.

india.title: Shifting traffic between Mumbai and Hyderabad regions
india.label: Illustrative design
india.body: Many Indian services now run in two Indian cloud regions, commonly Mumbai and Hyderabad, partly for resilience and partly to keep data in India. A common pattern is a global DNS name with a 60-second TTL whose answers point at the healthy region. If health checks on Mumbai fail, the DNS provider stops returning Mumbai's address, and within roughly a minute most new connections go to Hyderabad. Existing long-lived connections (WebSockets, HTTP/2) do not move until they reconnect, so clients need retry and reconnect logic. For very fast failover, anycast IPs or a global load balancer in front of both regions can react in seconds, with DNS as the slower backstop.

pitfalls.trap: 'We'll fail over with DNS instantly.'
pitfalls.say: 'DNS failover is bounded by the TTL and by resolvers that over-cache, so I'd use a 60 s TTL plus client retries, or anycast for faster switching.'

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting that DNS is a dependency that can fail.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd use a managed DNS provider with anycast name servers and keep a reasonable TTL so cached answers ride out a short outage.'

deep.diagram:
app -> stub -> recursive resolver
                 |-> root:        'ask .in servers'
                 |-> .in TLD:     'ask ns1.example.in'
                 |-> authoritative: A 203.0.113.10, TTL 60
                 '-> cache for 60 s
takeaways: Resolution walks root → TLD → authoritative, then caches by TTL.
TTL trades failover speed against lookup latency and load.
Average stuck time after a failure is about half the TTL; the worst case is the full TTL plus stragglers.
DNS can route by geography and health, but it is a slow lever; pair it with retries or anycast.

interactive.title: Pick a TTL for failover
interactive.prompt: Health checks take about 60 s to notice a dead region; then DNS points to the healthy one. You want everyone moved within 5 minutes. Find the longest TTL you can afford.
interactive.takeaway: A TTL of up to about 240 s meets a 5-minute target in the worst case. Shorter TTLs fail over faster but send more queries to resolvers, and some resolvers and clients hold records longer than the TTL, so do not rely on DNS alone for sub-minute failover.

title: HTTP/HTTPS/TLS
objectives: Describe what TLS adds to HTTP
Count the round trips for a new HTTPS connection
Decide where to terminate TLS

cards.title: HTTPS in one sentence
cards.body: HTTPS is HTTP sent over a TLS-encrypted connection. TLS gives confidentiality (nobody can read it), integrity (nobody can change it unnoticed) and server authentication via a certificate chain.

cards.title: The handshake
cards.body: In TLS 1.3 the client and server exchange key shares in one round trip, the client checks the certificate chain, and both sides derive the session keys.
steps: Client hello (supported ciphers, key share)
Server hello + certificate
Client verifies certificate chain
Both derive session keys
Encrypted HTTP flows

cards.title: Where to terminate TLS
cards.body: Usually at the edge: a CDN or L7 load balancer decrypts, routes on the path, and talks to services over a private network (optionally re-encrypted with mTLS). Terminating close to the user cuts handshake latency.

cards.title: Trap: 'HTTPS makes it secure'
cards.body: Saying HTTPS makes an API secure. It protects data in transit only. You still need authentication, authorization, input validation and rate limiting.

questions.prompt: Your L7 load balancer must route /payments and /catalog to different services. Where should TLS terminate?

choices.label: At the load balancer (or edge), so it can read the HTTP path
Nowhere: plain HTTP is fine inside a data centre, so clients can skip TLS too
At the database, the last hop
Only at each backend, so the balancer sees no plaintext

questions.explanation: An L7 balancer can only route on paths it can read. Re-encrypt to services with mTLS if needed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about HTTPS is accurate?

choices.label: It proves which user is making each request, so no login is needed
It protects data in transit; you still need authentication and authorization
It also encrypts the data at rest inside the database and all of its backups
It blocks SQL injection because the request body is encrypted

questions.explanation: TLS secures the connection, not the application.

questions.prompt: Order the TLS 1.3 handshake.

items.label: Server sends certificate; client verifies chain and CertificateVerify
Finished; switch to application keys for HTTP

questions.explanation: In TLS 1.3 both sides derive handshake keys right after the hellos; the certificate then travels encrypted, the client verifies it, and Finished switches to application keys.

questions.prompt: A user in Chennai reaches an origin in Singapore at 60 ms RTT. On a fresh TLS 1.3 connection, roughly how many ms until the first byte of the response (ignore DNS and server time)?
assumptions: TCP and TLS 1.3 each take one round trip
The request itself takes one more
questions.explanation: Sanity check: three round trips, each one 60 ms. TLS 1.3 resumption (0-RTT) or a nearer edge removes most of that cost on repeat visits.

questions.prompt: What does the server’s certificate chain prove to the browser?

choices.label: That the server is really the owner of the domain you asked for
That the connection will be faster
That the server’s code has no vulnerabilities
That the user is logged in

questions.explanation: Authentication of the server is one of TLS’s three guarantees, with confidentiality and integrity.

questions.prompt: Why should a payment request never be sent as TLS 0-RTT early data?

choices.label: Early data can be replayed by an attacker
0-RTT data is not encrypted
0-RTT only works over UDP
0-RTT skips all of the certificate checks

questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 0-RTT data is encrypted but has no replay protection by itself, so only idempotent requests should use it.

flashcards.front: What three things does TLS provide?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality, integrity and server authentication.

flashcards.front: Why terminate TLS at the edge?
flashcards.back: Shorter handshakes for users, and the L7 balancer can route on HTTP paths.
No. It protects data in transit; you still need AuthN and AuthZ.

mechanism.title: A TLS 1.3 handshake and what each step buys you
steps: Client hello: the client sends the cipher suites it supports and a key share (an ephemeral Diffie–Hellman public key), guessing the group the server will choose.

Server hello: the server picks a cipher, sends its own key share, and both sides now derive the same session keys without ever sending them. Because the keys are ephemeral, recording traffic and stealing the server's private key later still cannot decrypt it (forward secrecy).

Certificate and proof: the server sends its certificate chain and signs the handshake with its private key. The client checks the chain up to a trusted certificate authority, the hostname, and the expiry.
Finished: both sides confirm the handshake was not tampered with. All of this costs one round trip in TLS 1.3 (two in TLS 1.2).

Data: HTTP requests and responses flow encrypted and integrity-protected. A resumed session can send data with the first flight (0-RTT), but that early data can be replayed, so only safe, idempotent requests should use it.
mTLS: for service-to-service traffic, the client also presents a certificate, so each side authenticates the other.

useWhen: Always, for anything on the public internet: login pages, APIs, static assets (mixed content breaks pages).
Terminate TLS at the edge (CDN or L7 load balancer) to route on paths and reuse warm connections to the origin.
mTLS between internal services in zero-trust networks or service meshes.
avoidWhen: Do not treat HTTPS as 'the API is secure': it protects data in transit, not authorization, input validation or abuse.
Do not send non-idempotent requests (payments, orders) as TLS 0-RTT early data; it can be replayed.

rows: Fast handshakes near users; caching; DDoS absorption
The edge sees plaintext; re-encrypt to origin for sensitive data
Path routing, header inspection, central certificates
Traffic inside the VPC is plaintext unless re-encrypted
End to end at each service (mTLS)
Certificate rotation and CPU cost; needs automation such as a mesh

numbers.title: What resumption and keep-alive save
assumptions: RTT 50 ms between a Delhi user and a Mumbai edge
steps: New TCP + TLS 1.3 connection = 2 RTT = 100 ms before the first request.
If each of 20 requests opened its own connection sequentially: 20 × 100 = 2,000 ms of handshakes.
With one kept-alive HTTP/2 connection: one handshake of 100 ms, then requests are multiplexed.
With TLS 1.2 instead of 1.3, each new connection would cost 3 RTT = 150 ms.
numbers.result: Reusing one connection saves about 1.9 seconds of handshakes on this page. Connection reuse and TLS 1.3 matter more than raw cipher speed.

india.title: UPI apps: TLS is necessary but not sufficient
india.label: Public scheme rules, simplified
india.body: Every UPI app talks to its bank or payment service provider over TLS, but nobody treats that as the whole security story. UPI registration binds the app to the phone's SIM by sending an SMS from the device, so a stolen password alone is not enough. Each payment is approved with the user's UPI PIN, which is captured in a secure component and encrypted for the issuing bank, so the app never sees it in plain text. Payment requests are signed, and banks apply limits and fraud checks. TLS keeps the traffic private and untampered on the wire; device binding, the PIN and server-side checks decide whether the payment is allowed.

pitfalls.trap: 'We use HTTPS, so the API is secure.'
pitfalls.say: 'HTTPS covers transit. I'd still add authentication, per-resource authorization, input validation and rate limiting.'

pitfalls.trap: Not saying where TLS terminates.
pitfalls.say: 'TLS terminates at the L7 load balancer; inside the VPC services use mTLS so traffic stays encrypted and authenticated.'

deep.diagram:
Client                         Server
 ClientHello + key share  --->
                          <---  ServerHello + key share
                          <---  Certificate, signature, Finished
 Finished + GET /         --->            (1 RTT total in TLS 1.3)
                          <---  200 OK (encrypted)
takeaways: TLS gives confidentiality, integrity and server authentication; mTLS adds client authentication.
TLS 1.3 needs one round trip; reuse connections to avoid paying it again.
0-RTT data can be replayed, so only idempotent requests should use it.
Decide and say where TLS terminates; HTTPS alone does not authorise anything.

interactive.title: First byte from Chennai
interactive.prompt: A user in Chennai reaches a Singapore origin over a fresh TLS 1.3 connection: one round trip for TCP, one for TLS, one for the request. Keep the first byte under 200 ms.
interactive.takeaway: At 60 ms the first byte arrives after about 180 ms. TLS 1.3 needs one handshake round trip (TLS 1.2 needed two); terminating TLS at a nearby edge shortens every round trip, and session resumption saves work on repeat visits.

title: REST API Design
objectives: Resources as nouns, HTTP verbs as actions, proper status codes, pagination and idempotency.

cards.title: Resources, verbs and status codes
cards.body: GET /orders/42, POST /orders, PATCH /orders/42. Use 2xx/4xx/5xx correctly, cursor pagination for large lists, and versioning (/v1). PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not by default.

cards.title: Creating an order over REST
cards.body: A POST is validated, creates the resource, and answers 201 with a Location header pointing at the new order.
steps: Client
POST /v1/orders
Validate
Create resource
201 Created + Location

cards.title: Worked example: why offset pagination hurts on a large table
cards.body: Assume: Orders table with an index on created_at; Page size 20; User scrolls to page 5,000.
steps: Offset query: OFFSET 99,980 LIMIT 20, because 4,999 pages × 20 = 99,980 rows to skip.
The database walks about 100,000 index entries and discards all but 20.
Cursor query: WHERE created_at < :last_seen ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 seeks straight to the position and reads about 20 entries.
Work ratio ≈ 100,000 ÷ 20 = 5,000 times more rows touched for the offset version on that page.
cards.note: At deep pages offset pagination does thousands of times more work than a cursor, and it gets worse as users scroll. Use cursors for feeds and long lists.

cards.title: Trap: verbs in URLs, 200 for errors
cards.body: Using verbs in URLs (/getOrder) and returning 200 with an error body. Status codes are part of the contract.

POST /orders

GET /v1/orders/42

Offset-based: ?page=2500&size=20
Cursor-based: ?after=<last seen id>
Return the newest 20 only, with no way to go further

mechanism.title: Designing one resource well: orders
steps: Name resources as plural nouns and nest only for ownership: /v1/orders, /v1/orders/{id}, /v1/users/{id}/orders.
Map actions to methods: GET reads (safe, cacheable), POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates part, DELETE removes. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST is not.
Make POST safe to retry with an Idempotency-Key header: the server stores the key with the first result and returns the same result for any retry with that key.

Return precise status codes: 201 Created with a Location header, 200 OK, 204 No Content, 400 for invalid input, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 validation failure, 429 rate limited, 5xx for server faults.
Paginate lists with a cursor (the last seen sort key, encoded) and a limit, not page numbers, so results stay stable while rows are inserted.
Version the contract (/v1 in the path or a header) and only make additive changes within a version.

useWhen: Public and partner APIs, where predictability, caching (GET) and broad tooling matter.
CRUD-shaped domains: orders, users, restaurants, tickets.
Anywhere HTTP caching and CDNs can help: GET responses with Cache-Control and ETags.
avoidWhen: Very chatty internal service calls with tight latency budgets, where gRPC's binary encoding and streaming fit better.
Clients that need many differently shaped views of a graph of data in one round trip; GraphQL may fit better.

rows: Skip offset rows, return the next page
Deep pages are slow (the DB still reads skipped rows); inserts cause duplicates or gaps
WHERE sort_key > last_seen ORDER BY sort_key LIMIT 20
Fast at any depth via an index; stable under inserts

assumptions: Orders table with an index on created_at
steps: Offset query: OFFSET 99,980 LIMIT 20, because 4,999 pages × 20 = 99,980 rows to skip.
The database walks about 100,000 index entries and discards all but 20.
Cursor query: WHERE created_at < :last_seen ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 seeks straight to the position and reads about 20 entries.

india.title: Placing a food order without charging twice
india.label: Illustrative design
india.body: Picture a food delivery app in India on a patchy 4G connection. The user taps Place order, the request reaches the server and the payment is captured, but the response is lost when the phone changes towers. The app retries. If POST /v1/orders is not idempotent, the user gets two orders and two charges. The fix is an Idempotency-Key generated on the phone when the checkout screen opens, sent with every retry. The server stores the key with the created order ID in a table with a unique constraint; a retry finds the key and returns the original 201 response instead of creating a second order. This is the same idea payment providers document for their order and payment APIs.

pitfalls.trap: Verbs in URLs (/createOrder) and 200 OK with an error in the body.
pitfalls.say: 'POST /v1/orders returns 201 with a Location header; validation errors return 422 with a structured error body.'

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring retries on create endpoints.
pitfalls.say: 'POST isn't idempotent, so clients send an Idempotency-Key and the server dedupes on it.'

deep.diagram:
POST /v1/orders  Idempotency-Key: k-81f
  -> new key?   create order 42, store (k-81f -> 42)  -> 201, Location: /v1/orders/42
  -> seen key?  look up 42                           -> same 201 response
takeaways: Nouns for resources, HTTP methods for actions, precise status codes.
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; make POST retry-safe with an idempotency key.
Prefer cursor pagination for large or changing lists.
Version the API and keep changes additive within a version.

interactive.title: A retried payment
interactive.prompt: A POST /v1/payments call times out on a phone, and the app retries. Which design stops a double charge?

choices.label: The client sends an Idempotency-Key; the server stores it with the result and returns the stored result on a retry
choices.feedback: Right: the retry is recognised and answered from the stored result.

choices.label: Switch the call to PUT, because PUT is idempotent
choices.feedback: PUT is idempotent only when the client names the resource and the server enforces it; changing the verb alone stops nothing.

choices.label: Tell the client never to retry
choices.feedback: Timeouts are ambiguous: the first call may or may not have worked, so the user is left guessing.

interactive.reveal: A timeout does not tell the client whether the charge happened. Idempotency keys make the retry safe: the server records the key and the outcome atomically and replays the outcome for repeats.

title: gRPC & GraphQL
objectives: GraphQL lets clients pick fields; gRPC gives fast typed RPC over HTTP/2 with protobuf.

cards.title: GraphQL for clients, gRPC between services
cards.body: GraphQL fits varied frontends that need different shapes from one endpoint. gRPC fits service-to-service calls: binary, schema-first, streaming, low latency.

cards.title: One GraphQL query fanning out to gRPC
cards.body: The gateway parses the query, resolvers call services over gRPC, and the response is shaped to exactly the fields asked for.
steps: Client query
GraphQL gateway
Resolvers
gRPC to services
Shaped response

cards.title: Worked example: the cost of N+1 on a home screen
cards.body: Assume: Home screen shows 50 orders, each with its restaurant; Each database round trip takes 2 ms inside the data centre; Resolvers run one after another.
steps: Naive: 1 query for orders + 50 queries for restaurants = 51 round trips.
Time ≈ 51 × 2 ms = 102 ms of database waiting per request.
Batched with a DataLoader: 1 query for orders + 1 IN query for 50 restaurants = 2 round trips ≈ 4 ms.
At 1,000 requests/s, naive = 51,000 queries/s versus 2,000 queries/s batched.
cards.note: Batching cuts this screen from 51 queries to 2 and the database load by about 25×. Always mention DataLoader-style batching when you propose GraphQL.

cards.title: Trap: unbounded nested queries
cards.body: Using GraphQL without query cost limits — one nested query can fan out into thousands of DB calls (N+1).

questions.prompt: Best fit for low-latency calls between internal services?

choices.label: gRPC with protobuf over HTTP/2
Server-sent events
GraphQL, so each service picks its fields
REST with JSON over a new connection per call

questions.explanation: Binary, schema-first, multiplexed calls suit service-to-service traffic.

questions.prompt: A mobile app and a web dashboard need different fields from the same data. What fits?

choices.label: A separate database for each client
GraphQL, so each client asks for exactly the fields it needs
One REST endpoint returning all fields to both
gRPC streaming straight to the browser

questions.explanation: GraphQL lets varied frontends shape their own responses from one endpoint.

choices.label: A cache stampede: add TTL jitter to the author cache entries
Normal load for 100 posts: add read replicas
Head-of-line blocking: switch the API to HTTP/3
The N+1 problem: batch the author lookups and cap query cost

questions.explanation: Resolvers that fetch per item multiply calls; batching (a DataLoader) and cost limits contain it.

questions.prompt: Order a request through a GraphQL gateway in front of gRPC services.
questions.explanation: The gateway shapes the response; services stay fast and typed behind it.

questions.prompt: What does “schema-first” mean for gRPC?

choices.label: Clients and servers share a .proto contract and generate code from it
JSON keys are only checked at runtime
The database schema must be designed before the API
Clients send their own schema with each request

questions.explanation: The contract is defined once and both sides are generated from it.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL query lists 50 orders and naively resolves each order's restaurant separately. How many database round trips is that?
questions.explanation: One query for the list plus one per order: 1 + 50 = 51. Batching brings it down to 2.

flashcards.back: N+1 queries and expensive nested queries.
Protocol Buffers.

mechanism.title: How each one works on the wire
steps: gRPC: you define services and messages in a .proto file. Code generators create typed client and server stubs in each language, so a call looks like a local function call.
gRPC sends protobuf, a compact binary encoding, over HTTP/2. One connection carries many concurrent calls (multiplexing), and calls can stream in either direction or both.
GraphQL: the server publishes a schema of types and fields. The client sends one query naming exactly the fields it wants, usually as a POST to a single /graphql endpoint.
The GraphQL server runs a resolver per field. A naive resolver for 'each order's restaurant' makes one database call per order: one query for the list plus N for the children, the N+1 problem.
Fix N+1 with batching (a DataLoader collects all restaurant IDs in one tick and fetches them with a single IN query) and per-request caching.
Protect GraphQL with query depth and cost limits, persisted queries, and timeouts, because a client controls how much work one request does.

useWhen: gRPC: service-to-service calls inside your platform, polyglot microservices, streaming (live location updates, log tailing), latency-sensitive internal paths.
GraphQL: one backend serving several frontends (Android, iOS, web) that need different shapes of the same data, or a gateway that aggregates many services into one round trip for mobile.
avoidWhen: gRPC directly from browsers needs gRPC-Web and a proxy; for public APIs, REST/JSON is easier for partners to adopt.
GraphQL for simple CRUD with one client adds a schema, resolvers, cost limiting and harder HTTP caching for little gain.
