title: URL Shortener
objectives: Scope URL Shortener: create short link from long url, redirect short link to original
Size it: 100M redirects/day, about 5,800/s at peak
Defend the design: generate ids with a counter/snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5t ids)

cards.title: What URL Shortener must do
cards.body: URL Shortener: A short-link service for SMS links sent by Indian banks and shopping apps, where a 160-character SMS cannot fit a long tracking URL. In scope: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry.

cards.title: URL Shortener: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Redirect p99 < 50 ms. 100:1 read/write. Links never collide. Out of scope: Link-in-bio pages and QR design; Full marketing analytics dashboards.

cards.title: One reference path for URL Shortener
cards.body: Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 chars ≈ 3.5T ids). → Store id → URL in a key-value store; cache hot links in Redis; 301/302 redirect. → Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links.

cards.title: Where URL Shortener breaks first
cards.body: Id generation: Hashing the long URL and truncating causes collisions that need retries; a counter or Snowflake id encoded in base62 never collides. 301 versus 302: 301 is cached by browsers, which cuts load but hides repeat clicks from analytics and makes link edits sticky; 302 keeps every click visible.

cards.title: Closing URL Shortener in one minute
cards.body: Summarise in four points: the peak you designed for (about 5,800 redirects per second under the brief's assumptions), the main path (load balancer, stateless services, cache, NoSQL store, CDN), the riskiest part (id generation) and the one mitigation you would build first.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in the first version of URL Shortener?

choices.label: Link-in-bio landing pages
Create short link from long URL
Branded custom domains per customer
Per-link QR code designer

questions.explanation: In scope: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry. Out of scope for this interview: Link-in-bio pages and QR design; Full marketing analytics dashboards; Per-link QR code designer; Link-in-bio landing pages.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-functional requirement for URL Shortener?

choices.label: Redirect short link to original
Optional custom alias & expiry
Redirect p99 < 50 ms
Video upload

questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, durability and availability: Redirect p99 < 50 ms; 100:1 read/write; Links never collide. The others are features (functional) or out of scope.

questions.prompt: URL Shortener: assume 50M daily users each doing about 2 redirects a day, with traffic peaking at 5× the daily average. Estimate peak redirects per second.
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the peak is 5× the average of about 1,200/s, so capacity sized for the average would run short at the busy hour. What it means for the design: the problem is read latency and caching, not storage.

questions.prompt: The create-link call (POST /v1/links) times out on a phone and the app retries. How do you avoid making two short links?

choices.label: Send an Idempotency-Key; retries get the stored result
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate request
Generate the short code on the client from the current time
Raise the client timeout so the app need not retry

questions.explanation: The first request may have succeeded before the timeout. An idempotency key lets the server recognise the retry and return the same short link; TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart.

questions.prompt: A link goes viral and redirects jump 10× with no cache in front of the store. What saturates first?

diagramNodes.label: KV store partition for that code

questions.explanation: Every redirect for one code hits the same key, so one partition of the store takes the whole spike. Stateless redirect servers scale out; caching the hot code in Redis or at the edge absorbs it.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism guarantees two new links never get the same short code?

choices.label: Let each server count from one on its own
Pick a random code and hope collisions stay rare
Pre-allocated counter ranges per server, encoded in base62
Hash the long URL and keep just the first seven characters

objectives: Scope Rate Limiter: limit requests per user/ip/key, return 429 with retry hint

cards.title: What Rate Limiter must do
cards.body: Rate Limiter: Protect the OTP and login APIs of a fintech from abuse, shared across every API server. In scope: Limit requests per user/IP/key; Return 429 with retry hint; Configurable rules.

cards.title: Rate Limiter: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Adds < 5 ms latency. Highly available. Shared across instances. Out of scope: Billing and quota invoicing; Bot detection with ML.

cards.title: One reference path for Rate Limiter
cards.body: Gateway calls a rate limiter backed by Redis token buckets (Lua for atomicity). → Rules stored in SQL and cached locally. → Fail-open for non-critical APIs, fail-closed for OTP.

cards.title: Where Rate Limiter breaks first
cards.body: Fail open or fail closed?: Failing closed during a Redis outage blocks every login; failing open lets attackers through. Nothing; silently drop the connection to save work

choices.label: A SQL row lock taken on every single request
The client counts its own requests and reports them
An atomic token-bucket update in Redis via a Lua script

questions.explanation: A Lua script runs the read-check-decrement atomically in Redis, so concurrent gateways cannot both spend the last token. Local-only counters let a user exceed the limit N times over.

Switch all limits off globally until an engineer is paged and responds

questions.explanation: For security-sensitive endpoints, failing closed (or falling back to a strict local limit) is safer; for ordinary reads, failing open keeps the product up.

An atomic token-bucket update in Redis via a Lua script
Each gateway keeps its own local counter, unshared

questions.explanation: A Lua script runs the read-check-decrement atomically in Redis, so concurrent gateways cannot both spend the last token. Local-only counters let a user exceed the limit N times over.

questions.prompt: Redis, which holds the rate-limit counters, goes down. For a login endpoint under attack, what is the safer default?

choices.label: Restart every gateway until Redis comes back
Fail open for login, so legitimate users are never blocked
Fail closed for login, so attackers cannot brute-force freely
Switch all limits off globally until an engineer is paged and responds

questions.explanation: For security-sensitive endpoints, failing closed (or falling back to a strict local limit) is safer; for ordinary reads, failing open keeps the product up.

bossDeep.pitch: Protect the OTP and login APIs of a fintech from abuse, shared across every API server.

assumptions: 20 million daily users, about 20 API calls each per day
Each check is one Redis round trip of about 0.5 ms in-zone
One Redis shard handles about 100,000 simple operations per second (illustrative)

Redis shards needed at peak = 23,000 ÷ 100,000, well under 1, so one primary with a replica works, and 3 shards give headroom and isolation.
Added latency per request ≈ 0.5 ms network plus script time, inside the 5 ms budget.
Rule config (limits per endpoint and tier) is small and cached in each gateway instance, refreshed every few seconds.

steps: The API gateway calls the limiter before routing each request, with keys such as user id, phone number, API key and IP range.

Rules are stored in a config service and pushed to gateways; changes take effect without deploys.
If Redis is unavailable, the gateway falls back to a conservative local in-memory limit per instance (fail open with a cap) for most APIs, and fails closed for OTP sends.

client -> gateway -> limiter (Lua token bucket in Redis, keyed by user/phone/IP)

cards.title: What Unique ID Generator must do
cards.body: Unique ID Generator: Generate unique, roughly time-sortable 64-bit ids for orders, messages and payments across data centres. In scope: Generate unique 64-bit IDs on demand; IDs roughly sortable by time; Work across many data centres.

cards.title: Unique ID Generator: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Under 1 ms per ID. No duplicates, ever. No single point of failure. Out of scope: Human-readable vanity IDs; Cryptographic secrecy of IDs.

cards.title: One reference path for Unique ID Generator
cards.body: Each generator node has a unique worker ID (Snowflake: timestamp + worker + sequence). → Clock moving backwards is detected and the node waits or refuses. → No central counter on the hot path.

cards.title: Where Unique ID Generator breaks first
cards.body: Clock skew: NTP corrections can move clocks backwards; issuing ids then could repeat a timestamp with a reused sequence. questions.prompt: A put(key, value) times out and the client retries. How does the store avoid a lost or doubled update?

choices.label: Append both values so no write is lost
Ignore the retry because a timeout means failure
Send the version context so the retry overwrites it
Lock the key across all replicas before each write

diagramNodes.label: The three replicas that own that key

questions.prompt: A replica is down during a write with W=2. Which mechanism keeps the write and repairs the replica later?

choices.label: Reject writes until all three replicas are back
Hinted handoff to another node, replayed when the replica returns
Ask the client to resend once the replica recovers
Write to one node only and skip the others

questions.explanation: Another node stores the write with a hint and hands it over on recovery; read repair and Merkle anti-entropy fix anything left.

questions.prompt: Carts must never lose an item, even if two devices update at once. Which conflict policy fits?

choices.label: Last write wins using each server's wall clock
Keep siblings with version vectors and merge them on read
Pick whichever replica answered first and drop all the others
Reject the second write with an error to the user

questions.explanation: Last-write-wins silently drops one device's item. Keeping both versions and merging (union of items) matches the cart's needs.

steps: Peak ≈ 5,790 × 3 ≈ 17,000 operations per second (the quiz target is about 17,000).

steps: Partition keys with consistent hashing and virtual nodes; each key lives on the next N = 3 distinct nodes on the ring.
Any node can coordinate a request: writes go to all 3 replicas and succeed after W acknowledgements; reads ask R replicas (QUORUM: R = 2, W = 2).
Each node stores data in an LSM tree (commit log, memtable, SSTables) for fast writes.
Conflicts are detected with version vectors or resolved with last-writer-wins timestamps, chosen per use case.
Repair with hinted handoff for briefly down nodes, read repair on reads, and Merkle-tree anti-entropy in the background; gossip spreads membership.

cards.title: What Distributed Cache must do
cards.body: Distributed Cache: Build a Redis- or Memcached-like distributed cache cluster that application servers share. In scope: get/set with TTL; Eviction; Scale nodes.

cards.title: Distributed Cache: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Sub-ms latency. Survive node loss. Even load. Out of scope: Durable storage of record (the database stays the source of truth); Cross-key transactions.

cards.title: One reference path for Distributed Cache
cards.body: Consistent hashing with vnodes for key placement. → Primary-replica per shard with failover. → LRU eviction; hot key replication.

cards.title: Where Distributed Cache breaks first
cards.body: Eviction policy: LRU suits recency-driven access such as sessions; LFU protects steadily popular items from being pushed out by one-off scans. Node loss: Losing a primary without a replica sends its share of keys to the database at once; replicas, request coalescing and circuit breakers keep the database safe.

steps: Clients hash each key onto a consistent-hashing ring with virtual nodes (or Redis Cluster's 16,384 hash slots) to find the owning node.
Each node stores keys in memory with a TTL and evicts with approximate LRU or LFU when memory is full.
Each primary has a replica; on primary failure, the replica is promoted by the cluster or a sentinel quorum.
Hot keys are replicated to several nodes or cached briefly in the application process to spread load.
Adding a node moves only its share of keys; warming is gradual, and TTL jitter prevents mass expiry.

cards.title: What Notification System must do

bossDeep.pitch: Instagram: upload photos, follow users and view a feed of images.

assumptions: 100 million daily users, about 15 photo views each per day
Uploads: 10,000,000 photos per day at 2 MB original, plus 3 resized versions adding about 1 MB
Average photo view served at about 200 KB
steps: Peak ≈ 17,400 × 3 ≈ 52,000 photo views per second (the quiz target is about 52,000).
Storage per day = 10,000,000 × 3 MB = 30,000,000 MB, about 30 TB, roughly 11 PB per year.
Peak egress = 52,000 views per second × 200 KB = 10,400,000 KB per second, about 10.4 GB per second, around 83 Gbit per second, which must come from a CDN.
Metadata (who posted, captions, likes) is small and lives in a sharded database.
capacity.result: About 52,000 photo views per second and 30 TB of new media a day: object storage plus CDN for bytes, a feed cache for ids.

steps: Upload: the client gets a presigned URL and uploads the original straight to object storage; a metadata row is created as pending.
Workers create resized versions and thumbnails, strip location metadata if needed and mark the photo ready.
Feed: follower feeds are precomputed with hybrid fan-out of photo ids.
Display: the app requests the feed page (ids and metadata) and loads images from CDN URLs at the right size for the screen.
Likes and comments use sharded counters and a separate comments store.

app --presigned PUT--> object storage --event--> resize workers -> CDN
app -> feed svc -> feed cache (ids) -> metadata DB

bossDeep.pitch: Dropbox or Google Drive: upload, sync across devices and share files with permissions.

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 10 file ops each per day
Average file 1 MB split into 4 MB chunks (most files are one chunk)
About 30% of uploaded chunks already exist (dedup)
steps: Peak ≈ 5,790 × 3 ≈ 17,000 file ops per second (the quiz target is about 17,000).

capacity.result: About 17,000 file operations per second and tens of TB per day: chunking, dedup and a consistent metadata service.

steps: The client splits files into chunks and hashes each one (SHA-256).
It asks the metadata service which chunk hashes are missing, then uploads only those via presigned URLs to object storage (resumable).
Once chunks are stored, the client commits a new file version: the list of chunk hashes, in a transactional metadata database.
The metadata service publishes a change event; other devices, connected by long-polling or WebSocket, fetch the changed file list and download only missing chunks.
Sharing writes permission entries (user or link, role) checked on every access; conflicting edits from two devices create a 'conflicted copy'.

client: chunk + hash -> metadata svc: which missing? -> upload missing chunks -> object storage
commit version (SQL) -> change event -> other devices sync -> download missing chunks

deepDives.title: Conflicts
deepDives.body: If two devices edit the same version offline, the second commit fails the version check and is saved as a conflicted copy instead of overwriting.

rubric: Chunks and hashes files for resumable, deduplicated uploads.
Keeps metadata transactional and separate from blobs.
Notifies devices of changes and syncs only deltas.
Handles permissions and edit conflicts explicitly.

cards.body: Payment System UPI-style: Pay to a VPA, collect requests and history. In scope: Send money via VPA; Collect requests; Transaction history.

cards.title: Payment System UPI-style: targets and exclusions

cards.title: One reference path for Payment System UPI-style
cards.body: Idempotent transaction service with unique txn ref; ledger in SQL. → Async calls to NPCI with timeouts, circuit breakers per bank. → Reconciliation workers; notifications via queue.

cards.body: Exactly-once debit: The unique transaction reference is enforced at the PSP and checked by the banks, so a retried request can never trigger a second debit. bossDeep.pitch: A UPI-style payment app (PSP) on top of NPCI: pay to a VPA, collect requests and history.

assumptions: 150 million daily users, about 3 transactions each per day
Each transaction writes about 5 ledger and state rows of 500 bytes
Peak days such as festivals add more; UPI volumes are publicly reported by NPCI monthly
steps: Peak ≈ 5,210 × 5 ≈ 26,000 transactions per second (the quiz target is about 26,000).
Daily transactions = 450,000,000; storage ≈ 450,000,000 × 2,500 bytes = 1,125,000,000,000 bytes, about 1.1 TB per day.

Peak of about 26,000 transactions per second, each writing several indexed rows with synchronous durability, is likely beyond a comfortable margin for one primary, so plan to partition the transaction store (for example by payer id) and confirm with a load test.
Every transaction involves calls to NPCI and banks, so most latency is external; the app must handle timeouts and pending states.
capacity.result: About 26,000 transactions per second with external dependencies: idempotency, a clear state machine and reconciliation matter more than raw speed.

steps: The app creates a transaction with a unique transaction reference (idempotency key) and status INITIATED in a SQL ledger sharded by user.
The PSP sends the request to NPCI, which routes the debit to the payer's bank and the credit to the payee's bank.
Responses move the state machine (INITIATED → PENDING → SUCCESS or FAILED); retries reuse the same reference, so no double debit.
Timeouts leave the transaction PENDING; a status-check job queries NPCI and a reconciliation job compares daily settlement files.
History is served from a read model; every state change is written to an append-only audit log.
architecture.diagram:
app -> PSP txn svc (unique txn ref, SQL ledger) -> NPCI -> payer bank (debit) / payee bank (credit)
responses -> state machine | timeouts -> status check | daily recon files

deepDives.title: Pending states
deepDives.body: Network timeouts are common; showing 'pending, we will update you' and resolving via status checks is safer than guessing success or failure.

rubric: Uses a unique transaction reference end to end.
Models an explicit state machine including PENDING.
Reconciles with settlement files.
Keeps an append-only audit trail.

steps: Window = 60 seconds.
Peak = 1,000,000 ÷ 60 ≈ 16,700 booking attempts per second (the quiz target).
Spread over a whole day the same attempts would average about 12 per second, which is why daily averages mislead here.
Seats per popular train-class are a few hundred, so most attempts must fail fast and fairly.

steps: Pre-scale web, search and booking tiers before 09:55, and serve static content from a CDN.

Only Aadhaar-authenticated users can book Tatkal online (from 1 July 2025), with Aadhaar OTP (from 15 July 2025, rolled out train by train); authorised agents are blocked for the first 30 minutes (10:00–10:30 AC, 11:00–11:30 non-AC). Source: Railway Board order of 10 Jun 2025, PIB 11 Jun 2025.
A waiting room issues queue tokens and admits users to the booking flow at a rate the payment and reservation systems can handle; availability is shown from a cache that may lag by seconds.
The user pays first (or authorises an iPay Autopay mandate, which is debited only when the PNR is generated). No berth is held while the user pays, so availability can change in the meantime.

After payment, the reservation system (PRS) allocates with a conditional decrement per (train, date, class, quota). Success generates the PNR; if no berth is left, the payment is refunded or the mandate released. Bots are limited with CAPTCHAs and per-account limits.
architecture.diagram:
users -> CDN -> waiting room (tokens, Aadhaar OTP) -> booking svc -> payment / Autopay lien -> PRS allocation (conditional decrement per train/class/quota) -> PNR
no berth -> refund / release lien | availability from cache

deepDives.title: Fairness
deepDives.body: A queue with tokens admits users in arrival order and rate, instead of rewarding whoever retries fastest. The 2025 rules add identity checks (Aadhaar OTP) and keep agents out of the first 30 minutes, so bulk and bot bookings cannot take the opening burst (PIB, 11 Jun 2025).

deepDives.title: Pay, then allocate
deepDives.body: IRCTC takes payment (or an Autopay lien) before the reservation system allocates a berth and generates the PNR. That avoids holding scarce berths for users who never pay, at the cost of refunds when allocation fails. A hold-then-pay design, as used for cinema seats, is the alternative trade-off.

deepDives.title: Graceful degradation
deepDives.body: Under overload, turn off non-essential features (detailed history, recommendations) and keep search and booking alive.

rubric: Quantifies the opening-minute burst.
Uses a waiting room, rate limiting and authenticated users.
Takes payment, then allocates atomically and issues the PNR.
Refunds or releases the lien when allocation fails, and blocks bots.

bossDeep.pitch: A Kafka-like distributed message log: produce, consume with offsets, retain for days.

outOfScope: Exactly-once end to end across external systems

steps: Peak ≈ 116,000 × 2 ≈ 230,000 messages per second (the quiz target is about 230,000).
Daily data = 10,000,000,000 × 1 KB = 10,000,000,000 KB, about 10 TB; with 3 replicas, 30 TB per day.
7 days of retention needs about 210 TB of disk across brokers.
Peak of about 230,000 messages per second, about 230 MB per second in, must be spread over many partitions and brokers.
capacity.result: About 230,000 messages per second and about 210 TB of retained replicated data: partitioned, replicated append-only logs.

steps: Topics are split into partitions; each partition is an append-only log of segment files on a broker's disk, with an offset index.
Each partition has a leader and followers; producers write to the leader, followers fetch and stay in the in-sync replica set.
With acks=all, a write is acknowledged once all in-sync replicas have it; leader election on failure picks an in-sync follower.
Consumers in a group are assigned partitions and commit offsets; they can rewind to replay.
Retention deletes whole old segments by time or size; compacted topics keep only the latest value per key.
architecture.diagram:
producer -> partition leader (append segment) -> followers (ISR)
consumer group -> assigned partitions -> read from offset -> commit offset
retention: delete old segments | metadata: controller (Raft)

title: Distributed Job Scheduler
objectives: Scope Distributed Job Scheduler: schedule recurring/one-off jobs, execute on workers
Size it: 10M job runs/day, about 350/s at peak
Defend the design: jobs stored in sql indexed by next_run_time

cards.title: What Distributed Job Scheduler must do
cards.body: Distributed Job Scheduler: A distributed job scheduler for cron-like and one-off jobs across many services. In scope: Schedule recurring/one-off jobs; Execute on workers; Retries & history.

cards.title: Distributed Job Scheduler: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: No missed jobs. At-least-once. Scale to millions. Out of scope: Workflow DAG authoring UI; Running arbitrary user containers.

cards.title: One reference path for Distributed Job Scheduler
cards.body: Jobs stored in SQL indexed by next_run_time. → Leader-elected scheduler enqueues due jobs. → Workers execute idempotently, retry, DLQ.

cards.title: Where Distributed Job Scheduler breaks first
cards.body: At-least-once: Workers may crash after running a job but before reporting; jobs must be idempotent or check a run id. Thundering herd at :00: Thousands of jobs scheduled at the top of the hour arrive together; adding a small random offset spreads load.

cards.title: Closing Distributed Job Scheduler in one minute

bossDeep.pitch: A distributed job scheduler for cron-like and one-off jobs across many services.

assumptions: 1 million daily users, about 10 job runs each per day
10,000,000 job runs per day; each run record about 1 KB
steps: Average = 10,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 116 per second.
Peak ≈ 116 × 3 ≈ 350 job runs per second (the quiz target is about 350).
Run history = 10,000,000 × 1 KB = 10,000,000 KB per day, about 10 GB.
Peak of about 350 runs per second; many cron jobs cluster at the top of the hour, so add jitter or spread start times.
Polling for due jobs every second with an index on next_run_time is cheap at this rate.
capacity.result: About 350 job runs per second: modest load, so correctness (no missed or double runs) dominates.

steps: Jobs are stored in SQL with schedule, next_run_time, owner and retry policy, indexed by next_run_time.
Scheduler instances poll for due jobs and claim them with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or a conditional status update, so each run is claimed once.
Claimed runs are pushed to a queue; workers execute them and report success or failure.
Failures retry with backoff up to a limit; runs that exceed a timeout are marked failed and retried; history is kept per run.
next_run_time is computed after claiming, so a crashed scheduler does not skip the next occurrence.
architecture.diagram:
jobs (SQL, idx next_run_time) <- schedulers poll + claim (SKIP LOCKED) -> queue -> workers
workers -> result -> run history | failure -> retry with backoff

title: Proximity Service Yelp
objectives: Scope Proximity Service Yelp: search places nearby, view details
Size it: 250M nearby searches/day, about 12,000/s at peak
Defend the design: geohash/quadtree index cached in memory

cards.title: What Proximity Service Yelp must do
cards.body: Proximity Service Yelp: Find nearby restaurants or shops, view details, add or update places. In scope: Search places nearby; View details; Add/update places.

cards.title: Proximity Service Yelp: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Read-heavy. Results < 200 ms. Updates within hours. Out of scope: Reviews and ratings system; Turn-by-turn navigation.

cards.title: One reference path for Proximity Service Yelp
cards.body: Geohash/quadtree index cached in memory. → Places in SQL with read replicas. → Batch rebuild of geo index.

cards.title: Where Proximity Service Yelp breaks first
cards.body: Geohash or quadtree: Geohash is simple and works in any key-value store; a quadtree adapts cell size to density, which helps in crowded city centres. Update freshness: Places change rarely, so rebuilding or patching the index every few minutes is enough; real-time updates are not required.

Place details for the result page come from a cache in front of the database.

assumptions: About 10 million users each make about 3 buy attempts in the first 5 minutes (illustrative)
10,000 units of a phone on sale
steps: Window = 5 × 60 = 300 seconds.
Peak = 30,000,000 ÷ 300 = 100,000 buy attempts per second (the quiz target).

steps: Sale pages and assets are static and served by a CDN; the countdown uses client time synced to the server.

A reservation creates an order with a short payment window; unpaid reservations expire and return stock.
Once stock reaches zero, the sale page flips to sold out at the edge, so later requests never reach the backend.

users -> CDN (static) -> waiting room (tokens, rate limit) -> reserve: atomic decrement (stock buckets) -> order -> pay

steps: Average = 80,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 926 per second.

steps: Property details and location live in a search index (Elasticsearch) for filters such as city, price and amenities.
Availability per (property, room type, date) lives in SQL, cached for search; the cache may be slightly stale.

Payment follows with a hold window; supplier hotels connected through channel managers are confirmed through their APIs, with retries.
Confirmation and cancellation emit events for emails, invoices and supplier sync.

book -> SQL txn: decrement each night WHERE available > 0 -> hold -> pay -> confirm (supplier API)
events -> email, invoice, sync

steps: Peak ≈ 11,600 × 3 ≈ 35,000 click events per second (the quiz target is about 35,000).
Daily click events = 1,000,000,000; raw data = 1,000,000,000 × 200 bytes = 200,000,000,000 bytes, about 200 GB per day.
Peak of about 35,000 events per second fits a modest Kafka cluster and Flink job.
Aggregates per ad per minute are tiny compared with raw events and go to an OLAP store.
capacity.result: About 35,000 clicks per second and 200 GB of raw events a day: stream aggregation with exactly-once effects, plus raw storage for reconciliation.

steps: Click servers validate and log each click with a unique click id, then publish to Kafka keyed by ad_id.
A Flink job deduplicates by click id within a window, aggregates per ad per minute using event time and watermarks, and writes results transactionally.
Aggregates land in an OLAP store (ClickHouse, Druid or Pinot) for reports and billing queries.
Raw events are also archived to object storage; a daily batch job recomputes counts to reconcile with the stream results.
Fraud filters (bots, repeated clicks) run in the stream and mark clicks as invalid before billing.
architecture.diagram:
click servers (click id) -> Kafka (key ad_id) -> Flink: dedup, window per minute (event time) -> OLAP store
raw -> object storage -> daily batch recompute -> reconcile

deepDives.title: Exactly-once counts
deepDives.body: Unique click ids, deduplication in the stream and transactional or idempotent sinks give exactly-once effects; the batch recompute is the safety net.

deepDives.title: Late events
deepDives.body: Mobile clicks can arrive minutes late; watermarks with allowed lateness update the right minute, and anything later is fixed by the daily reconciliation.

rubric: Keys the stream by ad and windows by event time.

bossDeep.pitch: A stock-exchange matching engine: accept orders, match by price-time priority, publish trades.

functional: Match buy and sell orders by price-time priority
Publish trades and order book updates
nonFunctional: Matching latency in microseconds to low milliseconds

assumptions: Market hours 9:15 to 15:30, 6 hours 15 minutes (as on NSE, publicly documented)
About 5,000 listed symbols, with trading concentrated in a few hundred
steps: Session = 6.25 × 3,600 = 22,500 seconds.
Average = 500,000,000 ÷ 22,500 ≈ 22,200 orders per second.
Peak ≈ 22,200 × 10 ≈ 222,000 orders per second (the quiz target).
Using 86,400 seconds would understate the load almost 4×, because no orders arrive outside market hours.

The busiest symbol may take a large share, and one single-threaded matching engine handles hundreds of thousands of simple operations per second in memory, so one engine per symbol (or per group) fits.
capacity.result: About 222,000 orders per second at peak: deterministic in-memory matching per symbol, with a durable sequenced log for recovery and audit.

steps: Orders arrive through gateways that validate them and run risk checks (margin, limits).
A sequencer assigns a global sequence number and writes each order to a replicated log before matching.
A single-threaded matching engine per symbol keeps the order book in memory: buy and sell sides sorted by price, then time; incoming orders match against the best opposite prices.
Trades and book updates are published to market-data feeds and to clearing; every event is in the log.
Hot standby engines replay the same log; on failure, a standby with the same state takes over deterministically.
architecture.diagram:
traders -> gateways (validate, risk) -> sequencer (seq no, replicated log) -> matching engine per symbol (in-memory book)
 -> trades -> clearing | book updates -> market data | standby replays log

deepDives.title: Latency

rubric: Uses price-time priority in an in-memory order book.
Sequences and persists orders before matching.
Keeps matching single-threaded per symbol for determinism.
Fails over by replaying the log on a standby.

steps: Average = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231 per second.
Peak ≈ 231 × 4 ≈ 930 joins per second (the quiz target is about 930).

steps: Clients join via a signalling service over WebSocket, which authenticates them and assigns a room to a nearby regional SFU.

Each client sends simulcast layers (for example 180p, 360p and 720p); the SFU forwards to each receiver the layer that fits its bandwidth and window size.
Screen share is another stream, prioritised for clarity over frame rate.
Large webinars switch to a broadcast model where a few speakers are forwarded to many viewers, possibly via a CDN with HLS for very large audiences.

assumptions: 2 million daily users, about 10 submissions each per day

steps: Average = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231 per second.

steps: The API stores the submission and puts a job on a queue (separate queues per contest for fairness).

Tests run against hidden inputs; outputs are compared and a verdict (accepted, wrong answer, time limit) is produced.
Verdicts are written back and pushed to the user; contest leaderboards update from verdict events.
Workers autoscale on queue depth before and during contests.

functional: PUT and GET objects by bucket and key

assumptions: About 2 billion object requests per day

steps: Peak ≈ 23,100 × 3 ≈ 69,000 object requests per second (the quiz target is about 69,000).

steps: A front-end tier authenticates requests (signed URLs, access keys) and routes them.

GET: fetch 8 of 12 -> verify -> stream | scrubbers repair

title: Distributed Counter

cards.title: What Distributed Counter must do
cards.body: Distributed Counter: A distributed counter for likes and views that handles very hot counters. In scope: Increment a counter (likes, views); Read the current count; Handle very hot counters.

cards.title: Distributed Counter: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Increments under 10 ms. Counts may lag by a few seconds. No lost increments. Out of scope: Per-user like history UI; Fraud detection.

cards.title: One reference path for Distributed Counter
cards.body: Hot counters sharded into N sub-counters summed on read. → Increments batched by workers before hitting storage. → Consumers idempotent per event ID.

cards.title: Where Distributed Counter breaks first
cards.body: No lost increments: Redis alone can lose recent writes on failover; the Kafka log or periodic durable snapshots allow counts to be rebuilt exactly. Lag versus cost: Summing 32 keys on every read is cheap with a short cache; allowing counts to lag a few seconds is what makes the design scale.

steps: Increments go to a counter service, which writes to Redis with INCR on the counter key, or on one of N sub-keys chosen at random for hot counters.

Increments are also written to a log (Kafka) so counts can be rebuilt and persisted to a durable store periodically.
Counters become hot automatically: when a key's rate passes a threshold, the service starts spreading it over more sub-keys.

title: Clarifying Requirements
objectives: Separate functional from non-functional requirements
Ask the questions that change the design
State assumptions when answers are vague

cards.title: Functional first
cards.body: Ask what users do: the three or four core actions, such as post, follow and view the feed. Say out loud what is out of scope.

cards.title: Non-functional next
cards.body: Scale (users, QPS, data), latency targets, availability, consistency needs and the read/write ratio. These shape the architecture more than features do.

cards.title: Five clarifying minutes

steps: Who are the users and what do they do?

mechanism.title: The first five minutes, step by step
steps: Restate the problem in one sentence to confirm scope: 'A service where riders request autos and nearby drivers accept, in one country, mobile apps only.'
Functional requirements: list 3–5 core user actions and agree which are in scope (request ride, match driver, track trip, pay) and which are out (ratings, scheduled rides, chat).
Non-functional requirements: ask for scale (daily active users, peak factor), latency targets, availability, consistency needs per feature, durability, and regional or regulatory constraints.
Write explicit assumptions where the interviewer has no preference: '10 million DAU, peak 3× average, 99.9% availability, match within 5 seconds at p99.'
Turn assumptions into anchor numbers you will reuse: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth. Do the arithmetic aloud and round sensibly.
Confirm priorities: 'I'll focus on matching and location updates, and treat payments as a black box unless you want me to go there.'

useWhen: Always, in the first few minutes, before drawing any boxes.
Again whenever the interviewer adds a twist ('now make it work offline'): restate the changed requirement before redesigning.
avoidWhen: Do not spend more than about 5 minutes of a 45-minute interview on requirements; move on with stated assumptions.
Do not ask questions you will not use; every number you gather should change a design decision.

rows: How many daily users? Peak factor?
How fast must a match feel?
Can two drivers accept one ride?
Conditional writes or locks on the ride

numbers.title: Turning assumptions into anchor numbers
assumptions: 10 million DAU; each user makes 2 ride requests per day
steps: Average per second = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231.
Peak per second = 231 × 3 = 693, call it about 700.
Driver location pings: 500,000 online drivers every 4 seconds gives 500,000 ÷ 4 = 125,000 writes per second, far larger than ride requests, so location ingestion is the scaling hot spot.
numbers.result: Anchor numbers show that location pings, not ride requests, dominate load, which tells you where to spend the deep dive.

india.title: Clarifying a 'design an IRCTC-like booking system' prompt
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: If asked to design a train-booking system for India, strong candidates first separate normal booking from the Tatkal window, when demand spikes sharply at the opening minute. They ask whether the focus is search, seat inventory or payments, whether waitlist and RAC (reservation against cancellation) rules are in scope, and what consistency is required: a berth must never be sold twice, so seat allocation is strongly consistent while availability displays can be slightly stale. Stating 'I'll assume a burst of a few lakh booking attempts in the first minute, an illustrative estimate' lets them size queues and inventory locks instead of guessing later.

pitfalls.trap: Jumping straight to drawing a load balancer and a database.
pitfalls.say: 'Before designing, let me confirm the core features and the scale, so I size the right parts.'

pitfalls.trap: Collecting numbers and never using them.
pitfalls.say: 'At about 700 peak ride requests per second but 125,000 location writes per second, I'll focus the design on location ingestion.'

takeaways: Clarify scope before drawing anything.
Ask only questions that change design decisions.
Write assumptions down and turn them into anchor numbers.
Use the numbers to choose where to deep-dive.

restate -> functional (in/out) -> non-functional (scale, latency, consistency, availability)

title: Deep Dives & Trade-off Language
objectives: Choose the part of the design worth a deep dive

cards.title: Choosing the deep dive
cards.body: Pick the part most likely to break at your numbers: the hot key, the write path, the fan-out. Or ask which part the interviewer wants. Go deep on one, not shallow on five.

cards.title: Trade-off sentences
cards.body: Use: “A or B. I choose A because requirement X; the cost is Y; I’ll mitigate with Z.” It shows judgement instead of memorised answers.

cards.title: A deep dive
cards.body: A strong deep dive puts a number on the risk, shows how the design fails, compares two fixes and names the cost of the one you pick.

Show how the design fails

Pick one and name its cost
Say how you would monitor it

cards.title: Soften absolutes
cards.body: Avoid “always” and “never”. Say “for this read-heavy feed I’d cache with a short TTL”, not “caching is always right”.

cards.title: Trap: an option with no downside

mechanism.title: Running a deep dive
steps: Pick the component where the requirements are hardest: the hot path at peak, the strongest consistency need, or the biggest data volume. Say why you picked it.
State the problem precisely: 'Two drivers can accept the same ride within milliseconds; we must allow exactly one.'
Offer two or three options, each in one sentence.
Compare with the trade-off template: 'Option A gives X at the cost of Y; option B gives Y but costs Z. Given our requirement W, I choose A.'
Go one level deeper on the chosen option: data model, the exact query or write, failure cases, and the numbers it must handle.
Close the loop: name what would make you switch options later (for example, 'if accepts exceed 10,000 per second on one city partition, I'd split by zone').

useWhen: Whenever you choose a technology or pattern, and whenever the interviewer asks 'why not X?'.
On the one or two components that carry the most risk; depth beats breadth.
avoidWhen: Do not deep-dive into something generic, like the load balancer algorithm, while the hard problem (matching, consistency) stays vague.
Do not use absolutes such as 'always use Kafka' or 'NoSQL is faster'; tie every claim to a requirement.

rows: 'X fits because we need ...; the cost is ...'
'It scales to about N per second per node; we need M, so about M ÷ N nodes'
'Cache menus for 5 minutes, invalidate on edit; prices at checkout from the database'
'Strong for ride acceptance, eventual for driver locations shown on the map'

numbers.title: Comparing two options with numbers
assumptions: Ride accept rate at peak 700 per second across a city
Option A: conditional update on the ride row in Postgres, about 2 ms each
Option B: a Redis lock per ride, about 0.5 ms each plus lock expiry handling
steps: Option A load: 700 writes per second, each touching one row, which one Postgres primary handles comfortably.
Total busy time for option A = 700 × 2 ms = 1,400 ms of work per second, spread over many connections and cores.
Option B is faster per call but adds a second system whose failover can drop locks, plus a lease to manage.
Since option A meets the load with the source of truth, choose A and mention B only if accepts grow 10× or more.
numbers.result: Use numbers to show the simpler option is enough, and name the threshold at which you would switch.

india.title: Deep dive on Tatkal seat allocation
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: In a train-booking interview, the right deep dive is seat allocation during the Tatkal opening, not the search page. A good answer compares a queue in front of the inventory service (fair and smooth, but adds waiting time), conditional decrements per train-class-date row (simple and strongly consistent, but one hot row per popular train), and pre-splitting a train's quota into several counters (more parallelism, slightly more complex rebalancing). The candidate then picks, for example, a queue plus conditional decrements, explains the failure cases (payment fails, hold expires and the seat returns), and states the illustrative load the design must take.

pitfalls.trap: 'Cassandra is better than Postgres.'
pitfalls.say: 'For ride acceptance we need a conditional write on one row; Postgres does that at 700 per second easily, so I'd keep it there.'

pitfalls.trap: Diving into a generic component.
pitfalls.say: 'The hard part here is double acceptance, so I'll go deep on that rather than load-balancer algorithms.'

takeaways: Deep-dive where the requirements are hardest.
Use 'X gives A at the cost of B; given W, I choose X'.
Replace absolutes with numbers and requirements.
Say what would make you change your mind.
deep.diagram: pick hardest part -> state problem -> 2-3 options -> trade-off template -> deeper on choice -> 'switch if ...'

choices.feedback: An absolute with no cost named invites pushback.

choices.label: 'We'll use Kafka because it scales.'
choices.feedback: A tool name is not a trade-off; what does it cost, and why here?

interactive.reveal: Name the option, what it buys, what it costs, and why the cost is acceptable for this requirement. Interviewers push until you do; doing it first earns the point.

title: Common Mistakes
objectives: Recognise the most common design-interview mistakes
Keep designs proportional to the numbers
Recover when you get stuck

cards.title: Designing before scoping
cards.body: Drawing boxes before knowing scale or features. Everything after rests on guesses.

cards.title: Over-engineering
cards.body: Kafka, microservices and sharding for 1,000 users. Start simple and add components when a number forces you.

cards.title: Unused numbers
cards.body: Estimating, then never using the estimate. If you computed 50K QPS, say what it means for caching and the database.

cards.title: Recovering from a stall
cards.body: When you stall, say so, go back to the requirements, pick the simple option and park the hard question for the deep dive.
steps: Notice you are stuck
Say what you are weighing
Go back to the requirements
Pick a simple option and move on
Note it for a later deep dive

cards.title: Silent thinking
cards.body: Long silences leave the interviewer guessing. Think aloud, check in (“should I go deeper here?”) and accept hints.

questions.prompt: At 1,000 daily users, which design is reasonable?

choices.label: Sharded Cassandra across three regions
Kubernetes with a service mesh
Kafka plus twelve microservices
One app server and one managed database, with backups

questions.explanation: Proportional to the load.

choices.label: Use it: say a cache is needed and roughly how many app servers
Move on: estimation is just a phase to get through
Re-estimate it more precisely with exact figures
Ask whether 50K is right and stop there

choices.label: Stay silent until you are completely sure of the right answer
Think aloud about the options and check in with the interviewer
Switch to talking about the frontend to fill the time
Pick one quickly without explaining to them why you chose it

questions.explanation: Reasoning out loud earns credit even when unsure.

items.label: Note it for a deep dive

Halfway through, you learn the system only needs 10 writes a day

questions.explanation: The design was built on guesses.

choices.label: It is over-engineered; a database table or simple managed queue is enough at this rate
It is required for any event-driven system, whatever the rate
It should use five brokers instead, to leave room for growth
It is fine because Kafka is popular and widely understood

questions.explanation: Components should match the anchor numbers; at about 1 event per second Kafka adds cost without benefit.
