mechanism.title: How common mistakes unfold, and how to catch them
steps: No scope: the candidate starts drawing before agreeing on features and scale, then designs the wrong thing for 20 minutes.
Over-engineering: Kafka, microservices, multi-region active-active and a service mesh for a system with 50 requests per second.
Unused numbers: the estimate says 2 TB per year, then the design ignores it (or contradicts it by sharding across 100 nodes).
Silence: long stretches of thinking without speaking, so the interviewer cannot follow or help.
Ignoring hints: the interviewer asks 'what if two users book the same seat?' and the candidate moves on.

Recovery: when you notice any of these, say so plainly ('I over-built this; at 50 requests per second one service and Postgres are enough'), simplify and continue. Correcting yourself is a positive signal.

useWhen: Use this list as a self-check every ten minutes: scope agreed? numbers used? speaking aloud? following hints?
Use the recovery script whenever you realise you are off track.
avoidWhen: Do not hide a mistake and hope the interviewer misses it; they almost never do.
Do not overcorrect into designing nothing; keep a working end-to-end design on the board.

rows: Restate and agree core features first
Tie each component to a number
Narrate the options you are weighing
Treat a repeated question as the priority

numbers.title: Is Kafka justified here?
assumptions: Internal tool: 5,000 users, each creating 20 events per day
Kafka cluster minimum: 3 brokers, plus operations effort
steps: Events per day = 5,000 × 20 = 100,000.
Average per second = 100,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1.2.
Even at a 10× peak that is about 12 events per second, which a Postgres table or a simple managed queue handles easily.
A three-broker Kafka cluster adds cost and on-call load for no benefit at this scale.
numbers.result: About 1 event per second does not need Kafka; matching tools to numbers is the cure for over-engineering.

india.title: Over-building a college fest ticketing app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A candidate asked to design ticketing for a college fest in Kolkata, about 20,000 tickets sold over two weeks, proposes Kubernetes, Kafka, Cassandra and multi-region failover. The interviewer asks for the numbers: 20,000 tickets over 14 days is about 1,430 a day, and even if a quarter sell in the first hour, that is about 5,000 in an hour, around 1.4 per second. The strong recovery is: 'I over-built this. A single web app with Postgres, a unique constraint on seat ids, a payment gateway webhook and a CDN for the poster is enough; I'd add a queue only if launch traffic proves bursty.'

pitfalls.trap: Defending an over-built design when challenged.
pitfalls.say: 'You're right, at about 1.4 tickets per second this is over-built; let me simplify to one service and Postgres.'

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring a repeated question from the interviewer.
pitfalls.say: 'You've asked about double booking twice, so let me address it now: a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) makes the second booking fail cleanly.'

pitfalls.trap: Long silent thinking.
pitfalls.say: 'I'm weighing a queue against direct writes; the queue smooths bursts but adds latency. Given our numbers, direct writes are fine.'

takeaways: Agree scope before designing.
Match every component to a number.
Think aloud; silence hides good reasoning.
Recover openly; self-correction is a strength.
deep.diagram:
every ~10 min: scope agreed? -> numbers used? -> talking aloud? -> hints followed?
 off track -> name it -> simplify -> continue

interactive.title: Your design ignores your own number
interactive.prompt: Mid-design, you notice your architecture ignores the 10× spike you estimated earlier. What is the best move?

choices.label: Say so, and add what the number calls for, such as an admission queue or pre-scaling
choices.feedback: Right: using your numbers is exactly what is being graded.

choices.label: Keep going and hope the interviewer doesn't notice
choices.feedback: Unused numbers are a classic mistake; noticing it yourself is a strength.

choices.label: Start over from scratch
choices.feedback: Adjust the design; a restart wastes the time you have.

interactive.reveal: Estimates exist to drive decisions. Tie each major component back to a number ('the 10× spike is why the queue is here').

title: Communication in the Interview
objectives: Narrate decisions with their reasons
Grow a design step by step from the numbers
Work with the interviewer’s hints

cards.title: Narrate the design
cards.body: Say what you are drawing and why: “Reads dominate, so I’m putting a cache here.” The interviewer grades reasoning they can hear.

cards.title: Evolve, don’t jump
cards.body: Start with the simplest design that works, then add a component each time a number forces you: one server, then a load balancer, cache, replicas, shards.

cards.title: Growing a design aloud
cards.body: Grow the design one bottleneck at a time and say which number forces each step, instead of drawing the final architecture first.
steps: One server
Add a load balancer and stateless apps
Add a cache and CDN
Add read replicas
Add shards and regions

cards.title: Work with the interviewer
cards.body: Check in at transitions (“requirements look settled; shall I estimate?”). Treat hints as help, and if you do not know a tool, describe the property you need.

cards.title: Trap: bluffing
cards.body: Arguing with a hint or bluffing about a technology. Say “I haven’t used X, but I need a store with property Y” instead.

questions.prompt: Which is good narration?

choices.label: This is how Netflix does it, so we will copy that design
Now I’ll add a box here, and then another box over here
Reads are 100× writes, so I’ll put a cache in front of the database
I’ll add Redis here because Redis is what everyone uses

questions.explanation: Decision plus reason.

questions.prompt: You do not know a database the interviewer mentions. Best move?

choices.label: Refuse to use it and insist on your own
Change the subject to a database you know
Say so, and describe the properties you need from it
Pretend you know it and keep talking

questions.explanation: Honesty plus reasoning beats bluffing.

questions.prompt: At 1K users, what should your first diagram be?

choices.label: The final multi-region design
Microservices with Kafka
A sharded cluster
One server and a database

questions.explanation: Start simple, then grow.

questions.prompt: Order the growth of a design.
questions.explanation: Each step answers a specific bottleneck.

questions.prompt: When is a good time to check in with the interviewer?

choices.label: At transitions, such as after requirements and before the deep dive
After every sentence, to be sure they agree
Only at the very end, once the design is done
Never: checking in makes you look unsure

questions.explanation: Natural break points.

questions.prompt: Why present a simple working design before adding caches, shards and queues?

choices.label: Each addition can then be justified by a requirement or number
Interviewers prefer small diagrams that fit on one screen
Complex designs are always wrong in an interview setting, by rule
It avoids having to discuss any of the trade-offs at all

questions.explanation: Evolving step by step shows why each component exists rather than presenting an unexplained final picture.

flashcards.back: Reads are 100× writes, so I’ll put a cache in front of the database. Decision plus reason.

flashcards.front: You do not know a database the interviewer mentions. Best move?
flashcards.back: Say so, and describe the properties you need from it. Honesty plus reasoning beats bluffing.

flashcards.front: At 1K users, what should your first diagram be?
flashcards.back: One server and a database. Start simple, then grow.

flashcards.front: When is a good time to check in with the interviewer?
flashcards.back: At transitions, such as after requirements and before the deep dive. Natural break points.

mechanism.title: A communication rhythm for a 45-minute design interview
steps: Minutes 0–5: requirements and assumptions, spoken and written down.
Minutes 5–10: estimates, said out loud with the assumptions behind them.
Minutes 10–15: the API: key endpoints with request and response shapes.
Minutes 15–25: a simple end-to-end design that works for the core flow, narrating each box: what it does and why it exists.

Minutes 25–40: deep dive and evolution: add caching, sharding, queues or replicas one at a time, each tied to a number, and cover failure modes; check in with the interviewer about which area to go deep on.
Minutes 40–45: summarise the design, the main trade-offs, what you would monitor and what you would do next with more time.

useWhen: Narrate continuously: options, the choice, and the reason.
Collaborate: ask 'shall I go deeper on matching or on payments?' at natural checkpoints, and use the interviewer's hints.
avoidWhen: Do not monologue for 15 minutes without checking in.
Do not present a final complex design in one go; evolve from simple to scaled so each addition is justified.

rows: Restates the problem, asks scoped questions
Simple first, then scaled step by step

numbers.title: Budgeting the 45 minutes
assumptions: The same six-stage plan used in Lesson 1, the Interview Playbook and Interview mode: 5, 5, 5, 10, 15, 5 minutes
steps: Requirements: 5 minutes, about 11% of 45.
Estimates and API: 5 + 5 = 10 minutes.
Simple design: 10 minutes; deep dive and failures: 15 minutes.
numbers.result: The deep dive gets the largest single block, 15 minutes; protect it by keeping requirements to about 5. If you reach minute 25 without a complete request path on the board, say so and simplify.

india.title: A food-delivery design interview, narrated
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Asked to design a Zomato- or Swiggy-style ordering flow, a strong candidate says: 'I'll start with one order service and Postgres so the core flow works: browse menu, place order, pay, track. At about 1,000 orders per second at dinner peak, an illustrative estimate, Postgres handles writes, so first I'll cache menus, since they are read about a hundred times per order. Shall I go deeper on rider assignment or on payment consistency?' The interviewer picks rider assignment, and the candidate evolves the design there, keeping the rest simple. Each step is spoken, justified and checked.

pitfalls.trap: Silent drawing for several minutes.
pitfalls.say: 'I'm adding a cache in front of menus because they're read about a hundred times per order and change rarely.'

pitfalls.trap: Running out of time before failures and a summary.
pitfalls.say: 'We have about eight minutes left, so let me cover what breaks and how we detect it, then summarise the trade-offs.'

pitfalls.trap: Using jargon without explaining the choice.
pitfalls.say: 'I'll use an outbox here, which means the order and its event commit in one transaction, so no event is lost if we crash.'

pitfalls.trap: Arguing with a hint.
pitfalls.say: 'Good point about duplicate payments; I'll add an idempotency key on the payment request.'

takeaways: Think aloud: options, choice, reason.
Check in at natural points and use hints.
Start simple, then evolve under the numbers.
Keep time for failures and a summary.
deep.diagram: 0-5 reqs | 5-10 estimates | 10-15 API | 15-25 simple design | 25-40 deep dive + failures | 40-45 summary

interactive.title: A question you hadn't considered
interactive.prompt: The interviewer asks, 'What if the cache cluster dies?' You hadn't thought about it. Best response?

choices.label: Think aloud: what breaks, how the database is protected, how the cache refills
choices.feedback: Right: reasoning in the open is the signal.

choices.label: 'It won't die; it's replicated.'
choices.feedback: Dismissing the scenario misses the point of the question.

choices.label: Think silently for two minutes, then answer
choices.feedback: Silence hides your reasoning, which is what is graded.

interactive.reveal: Narrate: 'Without the cache, reads hit the database at about 10×. I'd rate-limit, serve stale data where allowed, and warm hot keys first.' Collaboration beats a perfect answer.

title: Numbers & Latency Cheat Sheet
objectives: Recall the latency ladder by order of magnitude
Convert daily volumes to per-second rates
Size a server fleet from peak QPS

cards.title: Latency ladder
cards.body: Memory read: about 100 ns. SSD random read: about 100 µs. Same-datacentre round trip: about 0.5 ms. Disk seek: about 10 ms. Mumbai to Singapore: about 60 ms. India to US East: about 200 ms.

cards.title: Throughput anchors
cards.body: A tuned app server handles roughly 1–10K simple requests/s; a single Postgres primary a few thousand writes/s; Redis around 100K operations/s per node. Rough, but enough to size a fleet.

cards.title: Powers of ten
cards.body: A day is 86,400 s, about 10⁵. A million a day is about 12 a second; a billion a day is about 12K a second. A million 1 KB records is about 1 GB; a million 1 MB files is about 1 TB.

cards.title: Sizing a fleet
cards.body: Divide peak QPS by what one server handles, round up, add headroom for spikes and one spare server for failures.
steps: Peak QPS from the estimate
Per-server capacity from the anchors
Divide and round up
Add about 30% headroom
Add N+1 for failures

cards.title: Trap: false precision
cards.body: Quoting numbers to three significant figures. Interviewers want orders of magnitude and stated assumptions, not false precision.

questions.prompt: Which is fastest?

choices.label: A disk seek
A same-datacentre round trip
Reading from memory
An SSD random read

questions.explanation: 100 ns versus 0.5 ms, 100 µs and 10 ms.

questions.prompt: Peak is 60K QPS and each server handles 5K. With 30% headroom, how many servers (before N+1)?
questions.explanation: Design implication: the 30% headroom absorbs bursts and slow requests. After that, add at least one more server (N+1) so losing one server does not push the rest past their safe load.

questions.prompt: A billion requests a day is roughly how many per second?
Order the fleet-sizing steps.
questions.explanation: Headroom and spare capacity come last.

questions.prompt: A round trip from India to US East is about:

choices.label: About 200 ms
2 ms
2 s
20 ms (illustrative)

questions.explanation: Distance sets a floor that caching cannot remove.

questions.prompt: About how many requests per second is 1 billion requests per day on average?

choices.label: About 11,600
About 1,160
About 116,000
About 86,400

questions.explanation: 1,000,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11,574, roughly 11,600 per second before any peak factor.

flashcards.back: Reading from memory: about 100 ns, versus about 100 µs for an SSD read, 0.5 ms for a same-datacentre round trip and 10 ms for a disk seek.

flashcards.front: A billion requests a day is roughly how many per second?
A round trip from India to US East is about:
flashcards.back: 200 ms. Distance sets a floor that caching cannot remove.

mechanism.title: Estimating with the cheat sheet, step by step
steps: Memorise rough latency orders: L1 cache about 1 ns; main memory about 100 ns; SSD random read about 100 µs; same-zone network round trip about 0.5 ms; disk seek about 10 ms; cross-continent round trip about 150 ms. These are order-of-magnitude figures, not exact.
Memorise powers of two and ten: 2 to the power 10 ≈ 1 thousand, 2 to the power 20 ≈ 1 million, 2 to the power 30 ≈ 1 billion, 2 to the power 40 ≈ 1 trillion.
Memorise the day: 86,400 seconds, so 1 million requests per day is about 12 per second, and 1 billion per day is about 11,600 per second.
Estimate requests per second: daily actions ÷ 86,400, then multiply by a peak factor (2–5×).
Estimate storage: items per day × bytes per item × retention days × replication factor.
Estimate servers: peak requests per second ÷ requests one server handles (measure or assume, for example 1,000–5,000 simple requests per second), plus headroom for failures.

useWhen: Any time a design choice depends on scale: caching, sharding, number of servers, bandwidth, storage tier.
Sanity checks: if an estimate says one server handles everything, do not shard; if it says petabytes, do not use one database.
avoidWhen: Do not chase precision; one significant figure is enough.
Do not quote latency figures as exact facts about specific hardware; say 'roughly' and use them for orders of magnitude.

numbers.title: Sizing photo storage for a social app
assumptions: Average 500 KB after compression; keep 3 sizes adding 50% more
Replication or erasure-coding overhead 1.5×; keep 5 years
steps: Bytes per photo with sizes = 500 KB × 1.5 = 750 KB.
Per day = 5,000,000 × 750 KB = 3,750,000,000 KB, which is about 3.75 TB.
Per year = 3.75 TB × 365 ≈ 1,369 TB, about 1.4 PB.
Five years with 1.5× storage overhead = 1.4 PB × 5 × 1.5 ≈ 10.5 PB, which points to object storage rather than any database.
numbers.result: About 10 PB over five years: the estimate itself decides the storage tier.

india.title: Latency from Indian users to servers
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A user in Chennai calling an API hosted in a US region pays a round trip of roughly 200–250 ms before any server work, and a page needing four sequential calls pays that four times, about a second. Hosting in an Indian cloud region (Mumbai, Hyderabad or Chennai offerings exist from major providers) cuts round trips to tens of milliseconds for most Indian users. That is why Indian consumer apps keep latency-sensitive APIs in India and push static assets to CDN edges in many Indian cities. These latency numbers are typical orders of magnitude, not measurements of a specific network.

pitfalls.trap: Spending minutes on exact arithmetic.
pitfalls.say: 'Roughly 20 million a day is about 230 per second; with 3× peak, about 700.'

pitfalls.trap: Never using the cheat sheet in decisions.
pitfalls.say: 'A same-zone round trip is about 0.5 ms, so five sequential service calls add only a few milliseconds; cross-region calls would add hundreds.'

takeaways: Know latency orders of magnitude from nanoseconds to hundreds of milliseconds.
Divide daily counts by 86,400, then apply a peak factor.
Storage = items × size × retention × replication.
Round to one significant figure and let the result pick the architecture.
deep.diagram:
ns: L1 (1) -> RAM (100)
µs: SSD read (100)
ms: zone RTT (0.5) -> disk seek (10) -> India-US RTT (~200+)
 day = 86,400 s | 1M/day ≈ 12/s | 1B/day ≈ 11,600/s

interactive.title: Size the fleet
interactive.prompt: Each server handles 5,000 requests per second. You have a budget of 20 servers and want 30% headroom plus one spare. Find the highest peak you can cover.
interactive.takeaway: About 70,000 requests per second: 14 servers of raw capacity, 19 with headroom, 20 with the spare. Per-server capacity is an assumption to confirm with a load test, not a constant.

title: Pattern-to-Use-Case Map
objectives: Map workload shapes to standard patterns
Pick patterns for read-heavy, write-heavy, real-time and correctness-first features
Link each pattern back to its lesson

cards.title: Read-heavy
cards.body: Cache-aside, a CDN for static files and media, read replicas. Examples: product pages, news feeds, URL redirects.

cards.title: Write-heavy and spiky
cards.body: Queues to absorb bursts, batching, LSM or wide-column stores, sharding by a high-cardinality key. Examples: logging, IoT, clickstreams.

cards.title: Real-time
cards.body: WebSockets or SSE through gateways, pub/sub to route messages, presence in Redis. Examples: chat, live scores, ride tracking.

cards.title: Correctness first
cards.body: Transactions, idempotency keys, sagas, strong consistency on the hot rows. Examples: payments, bookings, inventory.

cards.title: Search and nearby
cards.body: An inverted index for text, geohash or a quadtree for location, both fed from the primary database by CDC. Examples: product search, restaurants near me.

questions.prompt: A live cricket score goes to 20M phones. Which patterns?

choices.label: SSE or WebSockets through gateways, with pub/sub fan-out
Every phone polling the database each second
A strongly consistent transaction per update
A nightly batch export

questions.explanation: Push through gateways.

questions.prompt: Ticket booking for a concert. Which pattern matters most?

choices.label: Transactions and idempotency on seat holds
Caching seat availability at the CDN for an hour
Fan-out on write
Eventual consistency on seat counts

questions.explanation: Double-selling a seat is the failure to avoid.

questions.prompt: IoT sensors write 1M points a second. Which patterns?

choices.label: A queue to absorb bursts, then a write-optimised store sharded by device
One Postgres primary with many indexes on the readings table
Strongly consistent writes replicated synchronously across several regions
An inverted index over the sensor readings, like a search engine uses

questions.explanation: Absorb, then spread writes.

questions.prompt: Restaurants within 2 km. Which pattern?

choices.label: An LRU cache alone
A full-text inverted index on names
Kafka partitions by city
A geohash or quadtree index

questions.explanation: Spatial queries need spatial indexes.

questions.prompt: URL redirects at 100K per second.

approaches.label: Strong consistency on every read
Cache-aside plus CDN or edge caching
approaches.description: Serve hot links from memory near users

approaches.label: Write-behind caching

rationaleOptions.label: Edge caching cuts latency for distant users
Reads dwarf writes and links rarely change
Write-behind speeds up redirects

rationaleConflicts.r3: Redirects are reads; write-behind only changes how writes are stored.

questions.explanation: Read-heavy, rarely changing: cache close to users.

questions.prompt: A product page gets 50,000 reads/s and 50 writes/s. Which pattern fits first?

choices.label: Cache-aside plus CDN: reads are 1,000× writes
Kafka in front of every read request
Two-phase commit across all of the database replicas
A write-optimised LSM store for the page

questions.explanation: A 1,000 to 1 read-to-write ratio is the classic case for caching.

flashcards.front: A live cricket score goes to 20M phones. Which patterns?
flashcards.back: SSE or WebSockets through gateways, with pub/sub fan-out. Push through gateways.

flashcards.front: Ticket booking for a concert. Which pattern matters most?
flashcards.back: Transactions and idempotency on seat holds. Double-selling a seat is the failure to avoid.

flashcards.front: IoT sensors write 1M points a second. Which patterns?
flashcards.back: A queue to absorb bursts, then a write-optimised store sharded by device. Absorb, then spread writes.
A geohash or quadtree index. Spatial queries need spatial indexes.

mechanism.title: Mapping a requirement to a pattern
steps: Read-heavy (reads much greater than writes): cache-aside with Redis, a CDN for static and cacheable responses, read replicas, and denormalised read models.
Write-heavy (high ingest): append-only logs (Kafka), LSM-based stores (Cassandra), batching, partitioning by a high-cardinality key, and asynchronous processing.
Real-time updates to clients: WebSockets or server-sent events for push, pub/sub to fan out, presence in memory with TTLs.
Correctness under concurrency (money, inventory, bookings): ACID transactions, conditional writes, unique constraints, idempotency keys, outbox for events, sagas across services.
Search and location: inverted index (Elasticsearch) for text, geohash or H3 cells for nearby queries, kept in sync from the source of truth by CDC.
Analytics: CDC into a warehouse or lake with columnar storage; stream processing for second-level dashboards.

useWhen: Use the map to propose a first design quickly once requirements are clear.
Combine patterns per feature: one product can be read-heavy in the catalogue and correctness-critical at checkout.
avoidWhen: Do not apply a pattern just because the system 'sounds like' one category; check the numbers.
Do not use one pattern for every feature; the cache that helps the catalogue would harm the wallet balance.

numbers.title: Classifying a feature by its numbers
assumptions: Product page: 50,000 reads per second, 50 writes per second
Rider location: 125,000 writes per second, 10,000 reads per second
steps: Product page read-to-write ratio = 50,000 ÷ 50 = 1,000 to 1, so it is read-heavy: cache plus CDN.
Rider location write-to-read ratio = 125,000 ÷ 10,000 = 12.5 to 1, so it is write-heavy: in-memory geo store, partitioned by city, with short TTLs.
The two features in the same app need opposite patterns.
Checkout, at a few hundred writes per second, is correctness-first: transactions and idempotency keys rather than caches.
numbers.result: Ratios, not product names, decide patterns: 1,000 to 1 reads means cache; 12.5 to 1 writes means an ingest-optimised store.

india.title: One quick-commerce app, four patterns
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A 10-minute grocery app in India shows all four families at once. The catalogue is read-heavy, served from a cache and CDN images. Rider and order-tracking updates are real-time, pushed to the customer's phone over a persistent connection. Stock reservation at each dark store is correctness-critical, using conditional decrements and idempotent order creation so that the last packet of milk is not sold twice. Product search uses an inverted index with Hinglish synonyms, filtered by the customer's nearest dark store using geo cells. Naming the requirement first, then the pattern, then the component, is what interviewers want to hear.

pitfalls.trap: Putting a cache on everything.
pitfalls.say: 'The catalogue is read-heavy, so it's cached; stock reservation must be exact, so it goes to the database with a conditional write.'

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting that one product mixes patterns.
pitfalls.say: 'The same app is read-heavy in the catalogue and correctness-critical at checkout, so I design those two paths differently.'

pitfalls.trap: Naming tools without the requirement.
pitfalls.say: 'Because location updates are write-heavy at about 125,000 per second, I'd use a partitioned in-memory geo store rather than a relational table.'

takeaways: Name the requirement, then the pattern, then the component.
Read-to-write ratios decide caching versus ingest designs.
Different features of one product need different patterns.
Correctness-critical paths never rely on caches.
deep.diagram:
requirement -> pattern -> component
read-heavy -> cache/CDN -> Redis
write-heavy -> log/LSM -> Kafka/Cassandra
correctness -> txn/idempotency -> Postgres
real-time -> push -> WebSockets
search/geo -> index/cells -> Elasticsearch/H3

interactive.title: First pattern for product pages
interactive.prompt: Product pages: 100 reads for every write, and a few seconds of staleness is fine. What do you reach for first?

choices.label: A cache (plus a CDN for images) and read replicas
choices.feedback: Right: the classic read-heavy pattern.

choices.label: Sharding the write path
choices.feedback: Writes are the small part of this load.

choices.label: Two-phase commit across services
choices.feedback: Nothing here needs cross-service atomic writes.

interactive.reveal: Map the shape of the load to a pattern: read-heavy → caches and replicas; write-heavy and spiky → queues and partitioning; real-time → push channels; correctness-first → transactions and idempotency.

title: How Browsers Render a Page
objectives: Trace HTML and CSS into the DOM, the CSSOM and the render tree
Tell layout, paint and composite apart
Predict which change triggers which stage

cards.title: From bytes to pixels, stage by stage
cards.body: The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree of visible boxes, works out each box’s size and position (layout), fills in pixels (paint), then stacks painted layers on screen (composite).

cards.title: Misconception: the DOM is what you see
cards.body: The DOM holds every element, including ones with display: none, the head and script tags. Only the render tree decides what is drawn, so an element can be in the DOM and take no space on screen.

cards.title: One frame through the pipeline
cards.body: A style change runs only the stages after the one it touches. Changing width forces layout, paint and composite; changing colour skips layout; changing transform or opacity on its own layer can skip straight to composite.
steps: Style: match CSS rules to elements
Layout: compute size and position of each box
Paint: record drawing commands per layer
Composite: combine layers on the GPU into the frame

cards.title: Layers and the compositor thread
cards.body: Some elements are promoted to their own layer, for example while transform or opacity animates. The compositor can move such a layer without re-running layout or paint, which is why those animations stay smooth when the main thread is busy.

cards.title: Trap: reading layout in a write loop
cards.body: Changing a style and then reading an element’s size forces the browser to run layout immediately so it can answer. Doing that inside a loop forces layout once per iteration. Group the reads first, then the writes.

cards.title: Edge case: skipping work for off-screen sections
cards.body: content-visibility: auto lets the browser skip style, layout and paint for a section until it nears the viewport, which can cut the first render of long pages sharply. Pair it with contain-intrinsic-size so the skipped section keeps an estimated height; otherwise the scrollbar jumps as sections render.

questions.prompt: An element has display: none. Where does it appear?

choices.label: Nowhere: the parser drops it
In the DOM but not in the render tree
In the CSSOM only
In the render tree with zero size

questions.explanation: display: none removes the box from the render tree; the element is still in the DOM for scripts.

questions.prompt: You change an element’s background colour. Which stages must run again?

choices.label: Layout, paint and composite
Paint and composite
DOM and CSSOM construction
Composite only

questions.explanation: Colour does not change geometry, so layout is skipped; the pixels still change.

questions.prompt: Which property change can usually be handled by the compositor alone?

choices.label: font-size of a heading
top on an absolutely positioned element
transform on a promoted layer
width of a flex item

questions.explanation: transform and opacity are the usual compositor-only properties; the others change layout.

questions.prompt: A loop sets each card’s height, then reads the next card’s rendered height. What is the cost?

choices.label: A repaint but never a layout
No layout until the next frame
One layout at the end of the loop
A forced layout on every iteration

questions.explanation: Reading geometry after a write forces synchronous layout; batch reads before writes.

questions.prompt: Put the rendering stages in order for a first page load.
questions.explanation: DOM and CSSOM feed the render tree; geometry comes before pixels, and layers are combined last.

questions.prompt: Animate a side panel sliding in on mid-range phones.
constraints: Must stay smooth while the main thread parses data

approaches.label: Animate transform: translateX
Animate width from 0 to 300px
Animate left from -300px to 0

rationaleOptions.label: Animating width is cheaper because the box is small
It keeps running even when the main thread is busy
The compositor can move the layer without layout or paint

rationaleConflicts.r3: Width changes geometry, so layout and paint run every frame regardless of size.

questions.explanation: transform keeps the work on the compositor; left and width re-run layout on the main thread each frame.

flashcards.front: What does the render tree contain?
flashcards.back: Only the visible boxes: DOM nodes matched with their computed styles, minus things like display: none and <head>.

flashcards.front: Which stage computes size and position?
flashcards.back: Layout (also called reflow).

flashcards.front: Two properties that usually animate on the compositor?
flashcards.back: transform and opacity.

sources.title: web.dev: Avoid large, complex layouts and layout thrashing

mechanism.title: What the browser does between receiving HTML and showing pixels
steps: Parsing: HTML is tokenised and built into the DOM tree incrementally, so the browser can start work before the whole file arrives. A preload scanner looks ahead for images, styles and scripts to fetch early.

Styles: CSS from link tags, style tags and inline styles is parsed into the CSSOM. CSS is render-blocking: the browser will not paint content until the stylesheets it already knows about have loaded, because painting with the wrong styles would cause a flash of unstyled content.

Render tree and style calculation: every visible DOM node gets its computed style. Nodes that are not rendered, such as head, script and anything with display: none, are left out. visibility: hidden stays in because it still takes space.

Layout: the browser walks the render tree and computes each box’s exact size and position from the viewport width down. A change high in the tree, such as the width of the body, can force layout for everything beneath it.
Paint: the browser records drawing commands (backgrounds, borders, text, shadows) for each layer and rasterises them into pixels, often in tiles.

Composite: layers are combined in the right order on screen, usually on the GPU and on a separate compositor thread. Scrolling and transform or opacity animations on promoted layers can update here without the main thread.

useWhen: Use transform and opacity for movement and fades so the compositor can do the work.
Batch DOM reads before writes when you must measure and then change many elements.
avoidWhen: Avoid promoting many elements to layers “just in case”: each layer costs memory and compositing time.
Avoid animating layout properties (width, height, top, left, margin) on large or complex pages.

numbers.title: The frame budget for a smooth animation
assumptions: The display refreshes 60 times per second (many phones and laptops; some screens are faster)
The browser needs part of each frame for its own housekeeping
steps: One frame lasts 1000 ms ÷ 60 ≈ 16.7 ms.
web.dev’s rendering guidance suggests aiming for roughly 10 ms of your own work per frame, leaving the rest for the browser.
A layout of a large page that takes 20 ms on a mid-range phone already overruns the frame, so the animation drops frames every time it runs.
Moving the same element with transform skips layout and paint, leaving only compositing, which fits easily.
numbers.result: At 60 Hz there is about 16.7 ms per frame; work that re-runs layout every frame is the usual reason an animation stutters.

india.title: Chrome DevTools Performance panel
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Browser developer tools show this pipeline directly. In a Performance recording, each frame is broken into purple “Layout” and “Recalculate Style” blocks, green “Paint” blocks and a “Composite Layers” step, and a warning flags forced reflows with the line of script that caused them. Recording a janky animation and seeing a tall purple Layout block in every frame is the most reliable way to confirm the cause before changing code.

pitfalls.trap: “The DOM is the page on screen.”
pitfalls.say: “The DOM is the document model; the render tree is what gets laid out and painted, and display: none nodes are not in it.”

pitfalls.trap: “Animations are slow because JavaScript is slow.”
pitfalls.say: “Most jank comes from re-running layout or paint each frame; I’d animate transform or opacity and check the Performance panel.”

takeaways: HTML becomes the DOM, CSS the CSSOM; together they form the render tree.
Layout computes geometry, paint draws pixels, composite stacks layers.
A change re-runs only the stages after the one it affects.
transform and opacity can animate on the compositor without layout or paint.

interactive.title: Fit the work in one frame
interactive.prompt: Your script, style and layout work takes 12 ms per frame. Change the screen’s refresh rate and see whether that work still fits in one frame.
interactive.takeaway: At 60 Hz a frame lasts about 16.7 ms, so 12 ms of work fits. At 90 Hz the frame is about 11.1 ms and the same work overruns it. Faster screens leave less time, so cutting layout and paint out of each frame matters more.

seeAlso.why: How CDNs deliver the HTML and CSS this pipeline starts from
How the cascade, specificity and layers decide which rule wins

title: The Critical Rendering Path
objectives: Find the resources that block the first paint
Choose between blocking, defer and async scripts
Shorten the path to first content

cards.title: What blocks the first paint
cards.body: Stylesheets in the head are render-blocking: nothing paints until they load. A classic script tag is parser-blocking: HTML parsing stops while the script downloads and runs, because the script might change the document.

cards.title: Worked example: three requests before anything shows
cards.body: Each blocking resource the browser discovers late adds at least one round trip to the first paint.
steps: Assume: 100 ms round trip, HTML references one CSS file, the CSS imports a font stylesheet
Round trip 1: fetch the HTML
Round trip 2: the parser finds the CSS link and fetches it
Round trip 3: the CSS imports another stylesheet, fetched only now
cards.note: Result. About 300 ms of round trips before the first paint, plus connection setup and download time. Inlining critical CSS or linking both stylesheets from the HTML removes one round trip.

cards.title: How the three script modes load
cards.body: A classic script blocks the parser; defer downloads in parallel and runs in document order after parsing; async downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it arrives, in any order.
steps: Classic: stop parsing, download, run, resume
defer: download alongside parsing, run in order after the document is parsed
async: download alongside parsing, run immediately when ready
type=module: deferred by default

cards.title: Shortening the path
cards.body: Three levers: fewer critical resources (inline the small CSS needed above the fold, defer the rest), fewer bytes (minify, compress), and fewer round trips (reference critical files directly from the HTML so the preload scanner finds them early).

cards.title: Trap: async for scripts that depend on each other
cards.body: async scripts run in whatever order they finish downloading. If one script needs another, async can run them in the wrong order on a fast network one day and work the next. Use defer to keep document order.

cards.title: Edge case: an inline script waits for the stylesheet above it
cards.body: Because a script might read computed styles, browsers do not run any classic script while a stylesheet earlier in the document is still loading, whatever that script actually does. An inline script placed after a slow stylesheet therefore blocks the parser until that CSS arrives: the CSS has become parser-blocking too. Put such scripts before the stylesheet link, or defer them.

questions.prompt: Why does the browser wait for stylesheets before the first paint?

choices.label: The DOM cannot be built without CSS
CSS must run before JavaScript is downloaded
Otherwise unstyled content would flash, then jump
The GPU needs all the styles uploaded before drawing

questions.explanation: CSS is render-blocking to avoid a flash of unstyled content; DOM construction itself continues.

questions.prompt: Two scripts must run in order after the HTML is parsed, without blocking the parser. Which attribute?

choices.label: async on the first, defer on the second
No attribute, scripts at the top of head
defer
async

questions.explanation: defer preserves document order and waits until parsing ends.

questions.prompt: An analytics script is independent of everything else on the page. Which loading mode fits?

choices.label: Inline it in the body before the content
defer with a dependency on the app bundle
async
A classic blocking script in head

questions.explanation: Independent scripts can run whenever they arrive; async avoids blocking the parser.

questions.prompt: Which change removes a round trip from the critical path?

choices.label: Serving the CSS from a different domain without preconnect
Moving the stylesheet link to the end of the body element
Adding a second, empty stylesheet to the head of the page
Linking the stylesheet from the HTML, not via @import

questions.explanation: An imported stylesheet is only discovered after its parent arrives; linking it from HTML lets the browser fetch both together.

questions.prompt: Order the work before the first paint of a page with one stylesheet.

items.label: Build the render tree and lay out
Parse HTML and discover the stylesheet

questions.explanation: The stylesheet blocks rendering, so its download sits on the path to the first paint.

questions.prompt: Round trip is 150 ms. HTML links one stylesheet, which @imports a second. Ignoring connection setup and download size, how many milliseconds of round trips before the first paint?
assumptions: Three sequential fetches: HTML, CSS, imported CSS
questions.explanation: Design implication: each nested import adds a full round trip, so on slow mobile links the import chain alone can delay first paint by about half a second. Flatten imports or inline the critical rules.

flashcards.back: CSS blocks rendering (painting); classic scripts block HTML parsing.
defer runs in document order after parsing; async runs as soon as each script arrives, in any order.
Deferred.

mechanism.title: How the browser decides it can paint
steps: The critical rendering path is the sequence of steps from receiving HTML to the first pixels: DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout and paint. Anything that must finish before those steps can run sits on the path.

Critical resources are files that block the first render. By default these are the stylesheets in the head and classic scripts that appear before the content. Images do not block the first paint; they paint when they arrive.
A stylesheet with a media query that does not match (for example media="print") is still downloaded but does not block rendering. This is one way to keep non-critical CSS off the path.

Classic scripts block the parser because they may call document-writing functions or read styles. A classic script that comes after a stylesheet still loading waits for it, whatever the script reads (the HTML standard calls this a script-blocking style sheet), so CSS can indirectly delay scripts too.

The preload scanner reads ahead in the raw HTML and starts fetching resources it can see while the parser is blocked. Resources hidden inside CSS imports or injected by scripts are invisible to it and are discovered late.
Three numbers describe the path: how many critical resources there are, how many bytes they total, and how many round trips are needed to fetch them in sequence. Reduce any of them to paint sooner.

useWhen: Inline a small amount of critical CSS for above-the-fold content when the full stylesheet is large and the page is visited once.
Use defer for application scripts and async for independent third-party scripts.
avoidWhen: Avoid inlining large CSS on pages people visit repeatedly: inlined CSS cannot be cached separately and is re-downloaded with every HTML response.
Avoid async for scripts that rely on another script or on the full document being parsed.

rows: As soon as it is downloaded

numbers.title: Counting round trips on a slow connection
assumptions: Round trip 200 ms (an example slow mobile connection)
New connection to the origin: DNS, TCP and TLS add about 3 round trips once (example assumption)
HTML links two stylesheets directly; one script uses defer
steps: Connection setup: about 3 × 200 = 600 ms before the first byte of HTML can be requested.
HTML: one more round trip, about 200 ms.
Both stylesheets are found by the preload scanner and fetched in parallel: one round trip, about 200 ms.
The deferred script downloads in parallel but does not block the first paint.
numbers.result: Roughly 1 second before first paint under these assumptions, of which 600 ms is connection setup. Each extra sequential critical file would add another 200 ms.

india.title: Lighthouse “Eliminate render-blocking resources”
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Lighthouse, the auditing tool built into Chromium DevTools and documented on developer.chrome.com, has an audit that lists the stylesheets and scripts that delayed the first paint and estimates how much time each one cost. The usual fixes it suggests match this lesson: inline the critical styles, defer non-critical scripts, and mark stylesheets that only apply to print or large screens with a media attribute so they no longer block.

pitfalls.trap: “Put all scripts at the bottom and you are done.”
pitfalls.say: “Bottom-of-body scripts help, but defer lets the download start early without blocking, and I’d still count the critical CSS round trips.”

pitfalls.trap: “Async is always faster than defer.”
pitfalls.say: “async can run earlier, but it gives up ordering; for scripts that depend on each other defer is the safe choice.”

takeaways: CSS blocks rendering; classic scripts block parsing.
defer keeps order and runs after parsing; async runs on arrival.
Fewer critical resources, bytes and round trips mean an earlier first paint.
Resources hidden in CSS imports or scripts are discovered late.

interactive.title: Which script loading order is safe?
interactive.prompt: A page loads utils.js and app.js, and app.js calls functions defined in utils.js. Both are in the head with the async attribute. What happens?

choices.label: It works sometimes and breaks sometimes
choices.feedback: Right: async runs each file as soon as it arrives, so app.js can run first when it downloads faster.

choices.label: It always works because async keeps document order
choices.feedback: That is what defer does; async gives no ordering guarantee.

choices.label: It always fails because async scripts cannot share functions
choices.feedback: They share the global scope; the problem is only the order they run in.

interactive.reveal: async scripts execute in arrival order, not document order. Use defer for both (document order, after parsing), or load utils.js as a module that app.js imports.

seeAlso.why: Connection and TLS setup add round trips before the first byte

title: The Browser Event Loop
objectives: Explain tasks, microtasks and rendering in one loop
Predict the order of callbacks
Keep long work from freezing the page

cards.title: One thread, one queue at a time
cards.body: The page’s scripts, event handlers and rendering share one main thread. The event loop takes one task (a click handler, a timer callback, a network response), runs it to completion, runs every queued microtask, then the browser may render a frame.

cards.title: Misconception: a zero-delay timer runs immediately
cards.body: A timer with a 0 ms delay only queues a task. It runs after the current script finishes and after all microtasks, such as resolved promise callbacks. So a script that logs a line, schedules a zero-delay timer and then resolves a promise prints: the log line, then the promise callback, then the timer.

cards.title: A single turn of the loop
cards.body: Rendering happens between tasks, never in the middle of one. A task that runs for 300 ms blocks clicks, typing and painting for all of that time.
steps: Take the oldest task from a task queue and run it
Run every microtask, including ones queued by microtasks
If a frame is due: run animation-frame callbacks, style, layout, paint
Repeat

cards.title: Breaking up long work
cards.body: A task longer than 50 ms counts as a long task. Split big loops into chunks and yield back to the loop between them, or move pure computation to a worker thread that has no access to the DOM.

cards.title: Trap: endless microtasks
cards.body: The loop drains the microtask queue completely before rendering. A promise callback that keeps queuing another promise callback never lets the browser paint or handle input, even though no single callback is long.

cards.title: Edge case: timers in background tabs
cards.body: Browsers throttle timers in hidden tabs to save battery, typically to at most about one run per second. Chromium goes further for pages hidden for around five minutes, batching chained timers to about once a minute. A countdown or clock that adds one second per timer tick therefore drifts badly in a background tab. Compute elapsed time from the clock on each tick instead of counting ticks, and refresh the display when the page becomes visible again.

questions.prompt: A script logs A, then schedules a 0 ms timer whose callback logs B and queues a microtask that logs C. Next it resolves a promise whose callback logs D, and finally logs E. Output order?

choices.label: A, E, D, B, C
A, E, D, C, B
A, D, E, B, C
A, E, B, C, D

questions.explanation: The script runs to the end (A, E), then its microtask (D). The timer is the next task (B), and the microtask it queued runs straight after that task, before any later task (C).

questions.prompt: What counts as a long task in browser performance tooling?

choices.label: A task longer than one second
Any task that makes a network request
A task that runs longer than 50 ms
Any task that touches the DOM

questions.explanation: The Long Tasks definition uses 50 ms.

questions.prompt: When can the browser paint a new frame?

choices.label: Whenever a promise resolves, even mid-task
In the middle of any long-running function
Only after all pending timers have fired
Between tasks, once microtasks are done

questions.explanation: Rendering is a step of the loop that runs between tasks.

questions.prompt: Parsing a 20 MB file freezes the page for 2 seconds. What fixes the freeze without changing the result?

choices.label: Wrap the parsing in a promise so it runs later
Split it across many promise callbacks in a row
Run it in a 0 ms timer instead of the click handler
Parse in a worker thread and post the result back

questions.explanation: Promises and timers still run on the main thread; a worker runs in parallel.

questions.prompt: Order one turn of the event loop.
questions.explanation: Rendering steps come after the task and its microtasks.

questions.prompt: A search box filters 50,000 items on every keystroke and typing feels laggy.
constraints: Results must match the full list
The DOM shows at most 50 results
Must stay responsive on mid-range phones

approaches.label: Filter synchronously on each keystroke
Filter in a worker and render only the top results
Wrap the filter in a resolved promise

rationaleOptions.label: A worker can run the CPU-heavy filter in parallel
Microtasks run off the main thread
The main thread stays free to handle input and paint

rationaleConflicts.r3: Microtasks run on the main thread before rendering, so the lag remains.

questions.explanation: Heavy work on the main thread blocks input; workers move it off. Debouncing keystrokes also helps.

flashcards.back: Current synchronous code, then all microtasks, then the next task.
50 ms.

flashcards.front: Can a worker touch the DOM?
flashcards.back: No. It exchanges messages with the main thread.

mechanism.title: How the main thread schedules work
steps: A task is a unit of work the browser queues: parsing a chunk of HTML, dispatching a click, a timer firing, a message from a worker. The loop picks one task at a time and runs it to completion; nothing interrupts it.

Microtasks are smaller jobs queued during a task, mainly promise reactions and mutation observer callbacks. After each task, the loop runs every microtask, and any microtasks they queue, until the queue is empty.

Rendering is an opportunity, not a guarantee, in each turn. When the browser decides a frame is due (often about every 16.7 ms on a 60 Hz screen), it runs animation-frame callbacks, recalculates style, lays out and paints.

Timers are minimums, not exact times. A 0 ms timer waits for the current task and microtasks to finish, and browsers clamp nested timers to at least 4 ms after several levels of nesting, as the HTML standard specifies.

Input responsiveness depends on how long the main thread is busy. If a click arrives during a 400 ms task, its handler cannot start until that task finishes, and the screen cannot update until after that.
Workers run scripts on separate threads with their own event loops. They cannot touch the DOM; they post messages, which arrive on the main thread as tasks.

useWhen: Use workers for CPU-heavy work such as parsing, compression or large sorts.
Split long loops into chunks and yield between them so input and rendering can run.
avoidWhen: Avoid wrapping heavy synchronous work in a promise expecting it to run in the background; it still runs on the main thread.
Avoid chains of microtasks that requeue themselves; they starve rendering.

rows: Yes, if the queue never empties

numbers.title: How long a task can run before input feels slow
assumptions: web.dev’s responsiveness guidance treats about 100 ms as the point where a delay feels sluggish (the RAIL model)
A list of 10,000 items takes 0.03 ms each to process on a mid-range phone (an example assumption)
steps: Total work: 10,000 × 0.03 ms = 300 ms in one task.
A tap during that task waits up to 300 ms before its handler can even start.
Split into chunks of 1,000 items: each chunk takes 30 ms, under the 50 ms long-task threshold.
Yielding between chunks lets the tap run within one chunk, about 30 ms.
numbers.result: The same 300 ms of work, split into 30 ms chunks, keeps input delay near 30 ms instead of 300 ms.

india.title: Long tasks in DevTools
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Chromium DevTools marks every task longer than 50 ms with a red triangle in the Performance panel, and the Long Animation Frames API exposes similar information to monitoring scripts in the field. Teams use these markers to find which click handler or third-party script is blocking the main thread before reaching for a fix such as chunking the work or moving it to a worker.

pitfalls.trap: “Promises make code run in the background.”
pitfalls.say: “Promises schedule callbacks as microtasks on the same thread; CPU-heavy work still needs chunking or a worker.”

pitfalls.trap: “A 0 ms timer runs its callback right away.”
pitfalls.say: “It queues a task that runs after the current task and all microtasks, and possibly after a render.”

takeaways: One task runs to completion, then all microtasks, then maybe a render.
A 0 ms timer runs after promise callbacks.
Tasks over 50 ms are long tasks; split them or use a worker.
Workers run in parallel but cannot touch the DOM.

interactive.title: Predict the log order
interactive.prompt: In pseudocode: print A; schedule a 0 ms timer that prints B; resolve a promise whose callback prints C; print D. What is printed?

choices.label: A D C B
choices.feedback: Right: synchronous logs first, then the microtask (C), then the timer task (B).

choices.label: A B C D
choices.feedback: The timer callback cannot interrupt the running script.

choices.label: A D B C
choices.feedback: Microtasks run before the next task, so C comes before B.

choices.label: A C D B
choices.feedback: The promise callback waits until the current script finishes.

interactive.reveal: The current script runs to the end (A, D). The microtask queue empties next (C). Only then does the loop take the next task, the timer (B).

seeAlso.why: Long-lived connections deliver messages that arrive as tasks
The same event-loop idea, on the server side
How the operating system tells an event loop which sockets are ready

title: Rendering Models: CSR, SSR, SSG and Hydration
objectives: Say where HTML is produced in each model
Explain what hydration does and what it costs
Pick a model for a page’s freshness and interactivity

cards.title: Where the HTML comes from
cards.body: Client-side rendering (CSR) sends a near-empty page and builds the content in the browser with script. Server-side rendering (SSR) builds the HTML on the server for each request. Static site generation (SSG) builds the HTML once at build time and serves the same file to everyone.

cards.title: Misconception: server-rendered means interactive
cards.body: A server-rendered page can be visible before it responds to clicks. The script that attaches event handlers still has to download and run, so there is a gap between “looks ready” and “is ready”.

cards.title: What hydration does
cards.body: Hydration makes server-rendered HTML interactive by running the same components in the browser and attaching their behaviour to the existing markup instead of rebuilding it.
steps: Server sends full HTML and the state it used
Browser paints the HTML: content is visible
Script downloads and runs the components again
Event handlers attach: the page responds to input

cards.title: Choosing by freshness and audience
cards.body: Content the same for everyone and rarely changed (docs, marketing) suits static generation. Content per user or per request (a dashboard, search results) needs server rendering or client rendering. Highly interactive tools behind a login often accept client rendering because search engines do not need them.

cards.title: Trap: hydration mismatch
cards.body: If the browser’s first render differs from the server’s HTML, for example because it prints the local time or a random id, the framework must patch or discard that part of the page, and the user may see content flicker.

cards.title: Edge case: the hidden cost of hydration
cards.body: Server rendering with hydration sends the content twice: once as HTML, and again as serialised data the script needs to rebuild the same state. The page also looks ready before it can respond. A click in the gap between first paint and hydration may do nothing, or be replayed later, depending on the framework. Measure that gap on a mid-range phone, keep the serialised state small, and make key links and forms work as plain HTML so early clicks still go somewhere.

questions.prompt: Which model builds HTML once and serves the same file to every visitor?

choices.label: Server-side rendering
Client-side rendering
Static site generation
Hydration

questions.explanation: Static generation renders at build time.

questions.prompt: A server-rendered page is visible but buttons do nothing for two seconds. Why?

choices.label: The browser does not paint server-rendered HTML until idle
The server sent the HTML without any of the page styles yet
Its script has not yet loaded and attached the handlers
Static pages cannot contain buttons with event handlers

questions.explanation: Visible is not the same as interactive; hydration is still running.

questions.prompt: A personalised account dashboard behind a login, updated every few seconds. Best starting point?

choices.label: Static generation with pages rebuilt each hour
Static generation at build time
A single static file regenerated weekly
Per-request server or client rendering

questions.explanation: Per-user data that changes every few seconds cannot be built once for everyone, so it needs rendering at request time, on the server or in the browser. Build-time generation, hourly rebuilds and a weekly file all serve the same stale page to every visitor.

questions.prompt: Which detail in a component is most likely to cause a hydration mismatch?

choices.label: A CSS class that is the same on both sides
Rendering a list from the props the server used
Printing the current local time during render
Rendering a heading from a fixed string

questions.explanation: The server and browser render at different moments, so the time differs.

questions.prompt: Order what happens for a server-rendered, hydrated page.

items.label: Server renders HTML for the request
Browser receives and paints the HTML
Components run again and attach handlers

questions.explanation: Content is visible before the handlers attach.

questions.prompt: A documentation site with 2,000 pages that change a few times a week.
constraints: Must be indexable by search engines

approaches.label: Client-side rendering only
approaches.description: One shell page, content fetched in the browser

approaches.label: Static generation, rebuilt when content changes
Server rendering on every request

rationaleOptions.label: Every visitor gets the same content, so it can be built once
Static pages cannot be indexed by search engines
Prebuilt files are cheap to serve from a CDN close to readers

rationaleConflicts.r3: Static HTML is the easiest content for crawlers to read.

questions.explanation: Same-for-everyone content that changes rarely is what static generation is for.

flashcards.front: CSR, SSR, SSG: where is HTML built?
flashcards.back: Browser, server per request, build time.
Running the components in the browser to attach behaviour to server-rendered HTML.
Rendering values that differ between server and browser, such as time or random ids.

mechanism.title: What each rendering model does on each request
steps: Client-side rendering: the server returns a small HTML shell and one or more script bundles. The browser downloads and runs the script, which fetches data and builds the DOM. Nothing meaningful appears until that script has run.

Server-side rendering: for each request the server fetches data, renders the HTML and sends it. The browser can paint the content as soon as HTML and CSS arrive. To make it interactive the page usually also ships the script and hydrates.

Static site generation: the same rendering happens once at build time, producing HTML files that a CDN can serve directly. Changing content means rebuilding the affected pages (some tools rebuild individual pages on a schedule).

Hydration: the browser re-runs the components against the existing HTML so their state and handlers attach to it. It costs downloading and executing roughly the same script as client rendering, so it improves when content appears but not necessarily when it becomes interactive.
Streaming and partial approaches reduce that cost: the server can stream HTML in chunks, and some approaches hydrate only the interactive “islands” of a page, leaving static parts as plain HTML.
The choice is per page, not per site: a marketing page can be static, a product page server-rendered and a logged-in editor client-rendered.

useWhen: Static generation for content that is the same for everyone and changes rarely.
Server rendering when content is per request but must be visible fast and indexable.
avoidWhen: Avoid client-only rendering for pages whose first visit and search ranking matter, such as landing pages.
Avoid shipping a large hydration bundle for a mostly static page; plain HTML with small scripts is cheaper.

numbers.title: Where the time goes on a slow phone
assumptions: Download at 1.6 Mbit/s (an example slow mobile connection)
Parse and run the bundle: 1.5 s on a mid-range phone (example assumption)
steps: Download: 300 KB × 8 = 2,400 kbit; 2,400 ÷ 1,600 kbit/s ≈ 1.5 s.
CSR: content appears only after download and execution, about 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 s plus HTML and data fetches.
SSR: content is visible once HTML arrives, before the 3 s of script work.
With hydration, the page still becomes interactive only after roughly the same 3 s.
numbers.result: Server rendering moves when content appears much earlier; when it becomes interactive still depends on the script size.

india.title: web.dev’s rendering guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The web.dev article “Rendering on the Web”, written by Chrome engineers, compares these models on the metrics in this course: time to first byte, first contentful paint and interaction responsiveness. Its central point matches this lesson: server rendering and static rendering show content sooner, but hydration can leave a page that looks ready while it still ignores input, so the size of the script shipped to the browser still matters.

pitfalls.trap: “SSR makes the page interactive sooner.”
pitfalls.say: “SSR makes content visible sooner; interactivity still waits for the script and hydration.”

pitfalls.trap: “Pick one rendering model for the whole site.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d choose per page: static for docs, server-rendered for search results, client-rendered for the logged-in editor.”

takeaways: CSR builds HTML in the browser, SSR on the server per request, SSG at build time.
Hydration attaches behaviour to server-rendered HTML and costs the script download and run.
Visible and interactive are different moments.
Choose per page by freshness, personalisation and search needs.

interactive.title: Which model for this page?
interactive.prompt: A news article page: the same for every reader, edited a few times in its first hour, then never again. It must appear fast and rank in search.

choices.label: Static generation, rebuilding the page when it is edited
choices.feedback: Right: same for everyone and rarely changed, so build once and serve from a CDN.

choices.label: Client-side rendering
choices.feedback: Content would wait for the script, which hurts first view and indexing.

choices.label: Server rendering on every request forever
choices.feedback: It works, but it re-renders identical HTML for every reader.

interactive.reveal: Content that is identical for every visitor and changes rarely is the textbook case for static generation; rebuild the page on edit.

seeAlso.why: CDNs serve statically generated pages close to readers
Client-side routing for the pages rendered here

title: Browser HTTP Caching
objectives: Read Cache-Control, ETag and Last-Modified
Tell no-cache from no-store
Design a caching policy for HTML and versioned assets

cards.title: Fresh, stale and revalidated
cards.body: A cached response is fresh until its max-age runs out. While fresh, the browser uses it without asking the server. Once stale, the browser revalidates: it asks “has this changed?” and gets either a new copy or a short 304 Not Modified.

cards.title: Misconception: no-cache means do not cache
cards.body: no-cache allows storing the response but requires revalidation before every use. The directive that forbids storing it at all is no-store.

cards.title: A conditional request with an ETag
cards.body: The ETag is a version label for the response. Revalidation sends it back so the server can answer with headers only.
steps: First response: 200, Cache-Control: max-age=60, ETag: "v7"
After 60 s the copy is stale
Browser sends If-None-Match: "v7"
Unchanged: server replies 304 with no body; the browser reuses its copy

cards.title: Versioned file names
cards.body: Put a content hash in asset file names (app.3f9a1c.js) and serve them with a long max-age and immutable. When the file changes, its name changes, so browsers fetch the new one. Keep the HTML that references them short-lived or revalidated.

cards.title: Trap: long-lived HTML
cards.body: Caching the HTML for a day while assets change names means returning visitors keep loading yesterday’s HTML, which points at yesterday’s asset names. Short or no-cache HTML plus long-lived hashed assets avoids this.

cards.title: Edge case: caching without any Cache-Control
cards.body: A response with a Last-Modified date but no explicit freshness can still be cached: RFC 9111 lets caches assign a heuristic lifetime, and suggests a typical value of 10% of the time since the resource was last modified. A file unchanged for 30 days might then be reused for about 3 days without asking. Always send explicit Cache-Control on responses whose freshness matters.

questions.prompt: Which directive forbids storing a response in any cache?

choices.label: max-age=0
no-store
private
no-cache

questions.explanation: no-cache stores but always revalidates; no-store does not store.

questions.prompt: A stale response had ETag "a1". What does the browser send to check it?

choices.label: If-None-Match: "a1"
ETag: "a1" in the request body
If-Modified-Since: "a1"
Cache-Control: "a1"

questions.explanation: If-None-Match carries the ETag; If-Modified-Since carries a date.

questions.prompt: What does a 304 Not Modified response contain?

choices.label: A redirect to the cached URL
Headers only; the stored body is reused
The full body again, with an unchanged ETag
An error the browser must retry

questions.explanation: The point of 304 is to skip re-sending the body.

questions.prompt: Which policy fits app.3f9a1c.js, whose name changes whenever its content changes?

choices.label: Cache-Control: no-store
Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
Cache-Control: max-age=3600, must-revalidate
Cache-Control: no-cache

questions.explanation: The URL changes with the content, so the old URL can be cached for a year.

questions.prompt: Order what happens on a repeat visit after max-age has expired.

items.label: Use the stored body and refresh its freshness
Send a conditional request with the validator

questions.explanation: Revalidation turns a full download into a header-only exchange.

questions.prompt: Caching policy for a site’s HTML entry page that references hashed assets.
constraints: Users must see a new deploy on the next visit

approaches.label: HTML and assets both cached for one day
HTML: no-cache with an ETag; assets: one year, immutable
Everything no-store

rationaleOptions.label: Revalidating HTML is a cheap 304 when nothing changed
no-store everywhere is fastest for repeat visits
Hashed assets never change at the same URL, so they can be cached for a long time

rationaleConflicts.r3: no-store forces a full download every time.

questions.explanation: Short-lived or revalidated HTML plus long-lived hashed assets gives both freshness and speed.

flashcards.back: no-cache: store but revalidate before use. no-store: do not store.
ETag with If-None-Match; Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since.
So a long max-age is safe: new content gets a new URL.

sources.title: web.dev: Prevent unnecessary network requests with the HTTP Cache

mechanism.title: How the browser decides to reuse a response
steps: When a response is stored, the browser computes its freshness lifetime: from max-age in Cache-Control if present, otherwise from Expires. With neither, RFC 9111 lets caches use a heuristic, commonly a fraction (such as 10%) of the time since Last-Modified, which is why unlabelled responses are sometimes cached unexpectedly.
While the response is fresh, the browser serves it from cache with no network request at all. That is the fastest case and the one long max-age values on hashed files aim for.

When it is stale, the browser makes a conditional request using the stored validators: If-None-Match with the ETag, or If-Modified-Since with the Last-Modified date. The server compares and replies 304 Not Modified with headers only, or 200 with the new body.

Directives refine this: no-cache requires revalidation before every use; no-store forbids storing; private allows the browser but not shared caches (CDNs, proxies) to store it; public allows shared caches; immutable tells the browser not to revalidate while fresh, even on reload.
The cache key is mainly the URL (with the method). Vary lists request headers, such as Accept-Encoding, that also select a stored copy, so different variants do not overwrite each other.
A practical policy for web apps: HTML with no-cache (or a short max-age) and an ETag; versioned assets with max-age=31536000, immutable; personal API responses with private or no-store.

useWhen: Long max-age with immutable for any file whose URL contains a content hash.
no-cache plus an ETag for HTML and other files that keep the same URL but change.
avoidWhen: Avoid long max-age on URLs whose content changes without the URL changing; users keep the old version until it expires.
Avoid no-store on static assets; it throws away the cheapest performance win.

numbers.title: What revalidation saves
assumptions: A 304 response is about 300 bytes of headers (example)
steps: Full download: 60 KB × 8 = 480 kbit ÷ 10,000 kbit/s ≈ 48 ms of transfer plus 100 ms round trip ≈ 150 ms.
304: one round trip of 100 ms plus negligible transfer.
Fresh cache hit with max-age: no request at all, close to 0 ms of network time.
For a 2 MB script: full download ≈ 1.6 s at 10 Mbit/s, versus 0 ms when served fresh from cache.
numbers.result: Revalidation saves bandwidth but still costs a round trip; a fresh hit costs nothing, which is why hashed assets get long lifetimes.

india.title: MDN’s recommended caching pattern
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The MDN guide to HTTP caching describes the same pattern under “cache busting”: give the main HTML a policy that forces revalidation, and give versioned JavaScript and CSS files a long max-age with immutable so browsers never ask about them again. The pattern is widely used by build tools that append content hashes to file names at build time.

pitfalls.trap: “Set no-cache so users never see stale content.”
pitfalls.say: “no-cache still stores; it revalidates each use. no-store is the one that stops storing.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just cache everything for a day.”
pitfalls.say: “Hashed assets can be cached for a year; HTML should revalidate so a deploy is visible on the next visit.”

takeaways: Fresh responses are reused without a request; stale ones are revalidated.
no-cache revalidates; no-store does not store.
ETag + If-None-Match turns a re-download into a 304.
Hashed assets: long max-age, immutable. HTML: revalidate.

interactive.title: What does the browser do?
interactive.prompt: Yesterday the browser stored style.css with Cache-Control: no-cache and ETag "v3". The file has not changed. The user opens the page again.

choices.label: Sends If-None-Match: "v3", gets 304, uses its stored copy
choices.feedback: Right: no-cache means revalidate before use, and an unchanged file gives a 304.

choices.label: Downloads the whole file again
choices.feedback: It has a validator, so it asks first and gets a short 304.

choices.label: Uses the stored copy without asking
choices.feedback: That would happen with a max-age that had not expired, not with no-cache.

interactive.reveal: no-cache permits storing but forbids using the copy without checking. The ETag makes that check cheap: a 304 with headers only.
