title: Database Replication Basics
objectives: Compare physical and logical replication
Explain synchronous vs asynchronous replication and lag
Handle reads from replicas correctly

cards.title: Copies kept up to date
cards.body: Replication keeps one or more standby databases in step with a primary by shipping the primary’s changes to them. Standbys can take over if the primary fails and can serve read-only queries, but in the common asynchronous setup they are slightly behind.

cards.title: Worked example: what an asynchronous failover can lose
cards.body: Replication lag turns into lost writes if the primary dies.
steps: Assume: asynchronous replication with 2 s of lag at peak (illustrative)
The primary commits 300 transactions a second
It fails and the standby is promoted
Commits in the last 2 s never reached the standby: up to 300 × 2 = 600 transactions
cards.note: Result. Up to about 600 acknowledged transactions are missing after failover under these assumptions. Synchronous replication to at least one standby closes that window, at the cost of a network round trip on every commit.

cards.title: Read your own write from a replica
cards.body: A user saves a profile and the next page reads from a lagging replica.
steps: User updates their name on the primary
The next request reads from a replica 500 ms behind
The page shows the old name, as if the save failed
Fix: read from the primary for a short time after that user writes
Or wait until the replica has replayed past the write’s log position

cards.title: Physical vs logical
cards.body: Physical (streaming) replication ships the write-ahead log, producing an exact byte-level copy of the whole cluster, same major version. Logical replication sends row changes for chosen tables, so subscribers can be a different version or have other tables and indexes, which suits upgrades and selective copies.

cards.title: Trap: treating a replica as a backup
cards.body: A replica copies every change, including mistakes: a dropped table or a bad UPDATE reaches the standby within seconds. Backups with point-in-time recovery (a base backup plus archived WAL) let you restore to the moment before the mistake.

cards.title: Failure story: one command on the wrong server
cards.body: Publicly reported by GitLab in its January 2017 post-mortem: while fixing replication lag, an engineer deleted the data directory on the primary database instead of the replica. Several backup methods turned out not to be working, and about six hours of database changes were lost. The lesson they drew: a replica is not a backup, and a backup is only real once a restore has been tested.

questions.prompt: What does synchronous replication add to each commit?

choices.label: A second write-ahead log on the primary
A full copy of the table to the standby
A lock on the replicas’ tables
A standby must confirm it has the change

questions.explanation: The commit returns only once a standby has it, so a failover loses nothing.

questions.prompt: Users sometimes see stale data right after saving. Reads go to async replicas. What is the cause?

choices.label: The write went to the wrong table on the primary
Replication lag: the replica is behind
The primary rolled back the write afterwards
Replicas cache query results for a day

questions.explanation: Async replicas trail the primary.

questions.prompt: You need to upgrade to a new major version with minimal downtime. Which replication fits?

choices.label: Synchronous physical replication
Physical streaming replication
Restoring last night’s backup on the new version
Logical replication to the new version

questions.explanation: Physical replicas must run the same major version.

questions.prompt: Someone runs DELETE without a WHERE clause on the primary. What protects you?

choices.label: A read replica
Increasing replication lag
Backups with point-in-time recovery
A synchronous standby in another zone

questions.explanation: Replicas faithfully copy the delete.

questions.prompt: Order a synchronous commit with one synchronous standby.

items.label: Standby confirms it has flushed it
Primary reports success to the client
Primary streams the WAL to the standby

questions.explanation: The client hears “committed” only after the standby confirms.

questions.prompt: Async lag is 3 s and the primary commits 200 transactions a second. Up to how many committed transactions could a sudden failover lose?
questions.explanation: Design implication: if losing that many confirmed writes is unacceptable, use a synchronous standby for those commits or alert on lag well before it reaches seconds.

flashcards.back: WAL bytes for the whole cluster vs row changes for chosen tables.
Commits not yet sent to the standby (the lag window).
No; it copies mistakes too.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication
PostgreSQL: Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery

mechanism.title: How changes reach standbys
steps: Physical streaming replication sends WAL records from the primary to standbys as they are written. Standbys replay them continuously and can serve read-only queries (hot standby). They are byte-for-byte copies, so they must run the same major version and contain every database in the cluster.

Logical replication decodes the WAL into row-level changes for published tables and applies them on subscribers. Subscribers are ordinary writable databases, can have different indexes and versions, and can receive only some tables, but schema changes and sequences need extra handling.

Asynchronous replication returns from COMMIT once the primary has flushed locally. Lag is usually small but grows under heavy writes, long-running queries on the standby, or network trouble. Synchronous replication waits for one or more standbys to confirm, adding at least one network round trip per commit.

Failover promotes a standby to primary. The hard part is making sure the old primary stops accepting writes (fencing); otherwise two primaries accept conflicting writes (split brain). Most teams use a tested failover manager rather than manual steps.

Reads from replicas need a consistency plan: route a user’s reads to the primary briefly after they write, wait for the replica to pass the write’s log position, or accept stale reads where they are harmless (public listings, analytics).
Backups are separate: a base backup plus continuously archived WAL allows point-in-time recovery, which is the only defence against mistakes that replication copies instantly.

useWhen: Use replicas for failover and to offload read-heavy, staleness-tolerant queries.
Use synchronous replication for data where losing acknowledged writes is unacceptable.
avoidWhen: Avoid sending read-after-write paths to async replicas without a consistency rule.
Avoid replacing backups with replicas.

rows: Writes stall if no sync standby is available

numbers.title: The latency cost of synchronous replication
assumptions: Primary and standby in different zones, 1.5 ms round trip (illustrative)
Local WAL flush 1 ms; standby flush 1 ms
steps: Async commit: about 1 ms (local flush).
Sync commit: local flush, then send, standby flush and confirm: about 1 + 1.5 + 1 = 3.5 ms (send and local flush can overlap, so often less).
A single client’s commit rate drops from about 1,000 to about 285 a second; concurrent clients still share flushes.
A standby in another region at 80 ms RTT would add 80 ms to every commit, which is why cross-region standbys are usually asynchronous.
numbers.result: Synchronous replication is cheap within a region and expensive across regions; choose per data set.

india.title: Replication options in the PostgreSQL documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL high-availability chapter compares solutions including shared disk, file-system replication, WAL shipping, logical replication and synchronous multi-server setups, with a table of their trade-offs. The log-shipping chapter describes streaming replication, hot standby and synchronous standbys, and the continuous-archiving chapter describes point-in-time recovery from base backups and archived WAL, the safeguard that replication alone cannot provide.

pitfalls.trap: “We have a replica, so we’re backed up.”
pitfalls.say: “A replica copies a bad DELETE in seconds; I’d keep backups with point-in-time recovery as well.”

pitfalls.trap: “Send all reads to replicas.”
pitfalls.say: “Read-after-write paths would show stale data; I’d route those to the primary briefly or wait for the replica to catch up.”

takeaways: Physical replication copies the whole cluster’s WAL; logical copies row changes.
Async replication can lose the lag window on failover; sync cannot, at a latency cost.
Plan read-your-writes for replica reads.
Replicas are not backups.

interactive.title: Where did the change go?
interactive.prompt: A user changes their email (written to the primary). The redirect loads the profile from an async replica that is 800 ms behind.

choices.label: The page shows the old email for up to about a second
choices.feedback: Right: the replica has not replayed the change yet.

choices.label: The page shows an error
choices.feedback: The replica answers normally, just with older data.

choices.label: The write is lost
choices.feedback: It is committed on the primary and will reach the replica.

interactive.reveal: Read-after-write needs routing to the primary, or waiting until the replica has replayed past the write.

title: The NoSQL Families
objectives: Describe key-value, document, wide-column and graph databases
Model data around access patterns
Recognise when a relational database is still the better fit

cards.title: Different shapes for different questions
cards.body: “NoSQL” covers several data models. Key-value stores fetch a value by key. Document stores keep nested records, often JSON-like. Wide-column stores group rows by a partition key and sort them within it. Graph databases store nodes and relationships and follow links quickly.

cards.title: Worked example: designing a wide-column table from a query
cards.body: In wide-column stores, the table is shaped by the query it must answer.
steps: Assume: query “latest 20 messages in a chat”, run often; chats can have years of messages
Partition key: chat_id, so one chat’s messages live together
Clustering (sort) key: sent_at descending, so the newest come first
Partitions grow without bound, so add a time bucket: (chat_id, month)
cards.note: Result. Reading the latest 20 messages touches one partition and reads in sorted order. A different question, such as “all messages by one user”, needs a second table shaped for it, written alongside the first.

cards.title: Picking a family
cards.body: Start from the questions the application asks.
steps: Lookups by one id, no relationships: key-value
Self-contained records read and written whole: document
Huge write volume, reads by partition and range: wide-column
Many-hop relationship queries: graph
Ad-hoc queries, joins and multi-row transactions: relational

cards.title: Consistency and transactions vary
cards.body: Products differ in what they guarantee: some offer only single-key atomicity, others multi-document transactions; some let you choose per request between faster reads and reading the latest write. Check the guarantees of the product, not of the family.

cards.title: Trap: choosing NoSQL “for scale” before knowing the queries
cards.body: Models built around access patterns are fast for those patterns and awkward for new ones; adding a question can mean a new table and a backfill. If queries are still changing, a relational database (which also stores JSON and scales a long way) is often the safer start.

cards.title: Edge case: the partition key decides the hot spot
cards.body: Key-value and wide-column stores spread data by partition key. If many writes share one key, such as today’s date or a single popular tenant, they land on one partition and its limit becomes the whole system’s limit, however many nodes there are. Pick keys with many distinct, evenly used values, or add a suffix to spread a hot key.

questions.prompt: A session store needs “get session by id” and “delete session”, nothing else. Which family fits best?

choices.label: Graph
Key-value
Document with secondary indexes
Wide-column with many clustering keys

questions.explanation: Single-key access is exactly what key-value stores do.

questions.prompt: In a wide-column store, how should you serve “messages by user” as well as “messages by chat”?

choices.label: Scan the chat table filtering by user
Store users and chats in one partition
A second table partitioned by user
Add a join between the two tables

questions.explanation: Query-first modelling duplicates data per access pattern.

questions.prompt: Which query is a graph database’s strength?

choices.label: “Latest 20 log lines for a host”
“Get user by id”
“Total sales per month”
“Friends of friends who like this band”

questions.explanation: Multi-hop relationship traversal.

questions.prompt: A team’s queries change every sprint and include ad-hoc reports. Which is usually the safer start?

choices.label: A key-value store
A relational database
A graph database
A wide-column store

questions.explanation: Relational models handle new questions without redesign.

questions.prompt: Order query-first modelling for a wide-column store.

items.label: Choose clustering columns for the order it needs
For each, choose the partition key that groups its data
List the queries the application must serve
Write each item to every table that serves a query

questions.explanation: Queries first, then keys, sizes and duplication.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce catalogue: products with varied attributes, frequent new filters from the business, and orders that must update stock atomically.

approaches.label: Document store for everything
Key-value store keyed by product id
Relational database with a JSON column for varied attributes

rationaleOptions.label: Key-value is fastest so it fits everything
Transactions and ad-hoc queries are native
Documents are always better for varied attributes
JSON handles the varied attributes

rationaleConflicts.r3: Many relational databases store and index JSON too, and keep transactions and joins.
rationaleConflicts.r4: It cannot filter or report by attributes without building your own indexes.

questions.explanation: Pick the model that serves the queries and guarantees you need; varied fields alone do not require leaving relational.

flashcards.back: Key-value, document, wide-column, graph.
Design tables from queries: partition key groups, clustering key sorts.
Changing or ad-hoc queries, joins, multi-row transactions.

sources.title: MongoDB Manual: Data Model Design (embedding vs references)
Apache Cassandra: Dynamo architecture and tunable consistency

mechanism.title: How each family stores and queries data
steps: Key-value stores treat the value as opaque (or as a small data structure) and do only what the key allows: get, set, delete, often with expiry. In-memory ones are used for caches, sessions and counters; persistent ones for simple, very high-volume lookups.

Document stores hold nested records with flexible fields. You read and write a document as a unit, and can index fields inside it. The modelling question is what to embed (data read together) and what to reference (data shared or growing without bound).

Wide-column stores (in the style of Cassandra and Bigtable) distribute rows by partition key across nodes and sort them within a partition by clustering columns. Reads are efficient for one partition and a range within it; queries that cross partitions are expensive or not allowed, so tables are designed per query.
Graph databases store nodes and edges with properties and traverse relationships without join costs that grow with table size, which suits recommendations, fraud rings and network topologies.

Guarantees differ by product: atomicity per key, per document or across documents; tunable consistency levels; secondary-index support. Many systems favour availability and partition tolerance with eventual consistency, but several offer strong consistency options.

Relational databases now overlap heavily: JSON columns with indexes, partitioning, and distributed SQL systems. The choice is less “SQL vs NoSQL” and more which access patterns, guarantees and operational model you need.

useWhen: Use a NoSQL family when your access patterns are known and match its model.
Use more than one store when needs differ: a relational system of record plus a key-value cache, for example.
avoidWhen: Avoid choosing a store before you can list its queries.
Avoid unbounded partitions or documents that grow forever.

rows: High write volume, partition range reads
Very high write scale on one node

numbers.title: Sizing a wide-column partition
assumptions: A busy chat sends 2,000 messages a day of about 500 bytes each
steps: Per month: 2,000 × 30 = 60,000 messages.
Size: 60,000 × 500 bytes = 30 MB per partition, which is manageable.
Without the month bucket, five years would be 3.6 million messages and about 1.8 GB in one partition, too large to handle comfortably on one node.
Bucketing by time bounds partition size and spreads a busy chat across nodes over time.
numbers.result: Partition keys must group what you read together and also keep partitions bounded; time buckets do both for time-ordered data.

india.title: Modelling guidance from official documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: MongoDB’s data-modelling guide explains when to embed related data and when to reference it, based on how the application reads it. Cassandra’s data-modelling documentation teaches query-first design with partition and clustering keys and warns about large partitions. Redis documents its value types (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams), and PostgreSQL documents JSON and JSONB columns with indexing, showing how far relational systems now overlap.

pitfalls.trap: “We need NoSQL to scale.”
pitfalls.say: “First I’d list our queries and guarantees; a relational database with JSON may scale far enough and keep transactions.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just add another query to the Cassandra table.”
pitfalls.say: “Queries across partitions are costly; I’d add a table shaped for that query and write to both.”

takeaways: NoSQL is several models: key-value, document, wide-column, graph.
Design around access patterns; new questions can mean new tables.
Guarantees vary by product; check them.
Relational is still the safer default when queries are changing.

interactive.title: Which store fits?
interactive.prompt: A fraud team needs to find accounts linked through shared devices, cards and addresses, up to four hops away, in under a second.

choices.label: A graph database
choices.feedback: Right: many-hop relationship traversal is its core strength.

choices.label: A key-value store
choices.feedback: It can fetch one account by id but cannot follow links efficiently.

choices.label: A wide-column store
choices.feedback: It serves partition range reads, not arbitrary multi-hop traversal.

interactive.reveal: Choose the model that matches the question. Relationship-heavy, multi-hop queries are where graphs shine; a relational database with recursive queries can work at smaller scale.

title: Schema Changes Without Downtime
objectives: Run schema changes as versioned, repeatable migrations
Use expand and contract to change a live schema safely
Avoid long locks and table rewrites on large tables

cards.title: Schema changes are deployments
cards.body: A migration is a versioned script that moves the schema from one version to the next, kept in source control and applied the same way in every environment. On a live system, old and new application versions run side by side during a deploy, so every step must work with both.

cards.title: Worked example: backfilling a new column in batches
cards.body: Updating every row in one statement locks and bloats; batches keep each transaction short.
steps: Assume: 50 million rows; batches of 10,000 rows; each batch takes about 200 ms
Time: 5,000 × 0.2 s = 1,000 s ≈ 17 minutes, plus pauses
Each batch commits on its own, so locks are brief and replicas keep up
cards.note: Result. About 17 minutes of short transactions instead of one huge transaction holding locks on 50 million rows. Pausing between batches lets autovacuum and replicas keep pace.

cards.title: Expand and contract: renaming a column
cards.body: Never rename in place under a running app; move in compatible steps.
steps: Expand: add the new column
Deploy code that writes both columns and reads the old one
Backfill the new column in batches
Deploy code that reads the new column
Contract: stop writing the old column, then drop it

cards.title: Changes that lock or rewrite
cards.body: In PostgreSQL, adding a column with a constant default is fast (since version 11), but changing a column’s type usually rewrites the table under an exclusive lock. Plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does not, though it takes longer and cannot run inside a transaction block. New constraints can be added as NOT VALID and validated later with a weaker lock.

cards.title: Trap: dropping a column the old code still reads
cards.body: During a rolling deploy some servers still run the previous version. If a migration drops or renames a column they use, those servers fail until the deploy finishes. Contract steps go in a later release, after no running code references the old column.

cards.title: Edge case: a quick ALTER that waits in line
cards.body: Even a fast schema change needs a brief exclusive lock. If a long-running query holds a conflicting lock, the ALTER waits, and every new query on that table queues behind the ALTER, so an “instant” migration takes the table offline. Set a short lock timeout on migrations (for example lock_timeout in PostgreSQL) and retry, instead of waiting indefinitely.

questions.prompt: You need to rename users.fullname to users.display_name on a live system. What is the first step?

choices.label: Stop all servers, then rename
Drop fullname and recreate it
Rename the column in one statement
Add display_name next to fullname

questions.explanation: Expand first, so old and new code both work.

questions.prompt: How do you add an index to a busy PostgreSQL table without blocking writes?

choices.label: ALTER TABLE … ADD INDEX with a lock
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
CREATE INDEX inside a long transaction
VACUUM FULL, then CREATE INDEX

questions.explanation: It builds the index without the write-blocking lock, at the cost of time.

questions.prompt: Why backfill a new column in batches instead of one UPDATE?

choices.label: One UPDATE cannot change more than a million rows
Short batches keep locks and lag small
A single UPDATE is not atomic
Batches skip the write-ahead log

questions.explanation: A single huge update holds locks and creates a large burst of dead rows and WAL.

questions.prompt: Which property should a migration tool give you?

choices.label: Each runs once, in order, and is recorded
Migrations run in random order for speed
Each environment uses different scripts
Migrations are edited in place after running

questions.explanation: A version table records what has been applied.

questions.prompt: Order a safe column rename.

items.label: Stop writing the old column and drop it

questions.explanation: Expand, migrate data, switch reads, contract.

questions.prompt: A backfill updates 20 million rows in batches of 5,000, each taking 250 ms. About how many seconds does it take, ignoring pauses?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: roughly 17 minutes is fine for a background job, but too long to run inside a deploy step that blocks releases; run it as a separate job.

flashcards.back: Add new, migrate and switch, then remove old, each step compatible with running code.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
Short transactions: brief locks, steady replication and cleanup.

mechanism.title: How to change a schema under live traffic
steps: Migrations are numbered scripts applied in order, with a table in the database recording which have run. They are reviewed like code and are forward-only in production; undoing a change is a new migration, because data written after the change must be considered.

Rolling deploys mean old and new application versions overlap. Every migration step must be compatible with both: additive changes (new tables, nullable columns, new indexes) are safe; removals and renames are not, until no running code uses the old shape.

Expand and contract (also called parallel change) splits a breaking change into compatible steps: expand the schema, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then contract. Each step can be deployed and rolled back on its own.

Lock-sensitive operations: DDL takes table locks, and many ALTER TABLE forms take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Set lock_timeout so a migration gives up quickly instead of queueing every query behind it. Prefer operations that avoid rewrites: constant defaults, NOT VALID constraints followed by VALIDATE, concurrent index builds.

Some changes need a full rewrite (changing a column’s type in incompatible ways). Doing these online means building a new column or table, copying data in batches, keeping it in sync, then switching, which is expand and contract again.
Large data changes are run as background jobs, in batches by primary key range, with progress tracking and the ability to pause. Monitor replication lag and autovacuum while they run.

useWhen: Use additive migrations and expand and contract for anything that removes or renames.
Use lock timeouts and concurrent index builds on large, busy tables.
avoidWhen: Avoid editing migrations that have already run anywhere.
Avoid mixing large data backfills into the same transaction as schema changes.

rows: Add NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT

numbers.title: How long a write-blocking index build would stall
assumptions: Table of 200 million rows; plain CREATE INDEX takes about 20 minutes (illustrative)
The table receives 300 writes a second
steps: A plain build blocks writes for the whole 20 minutes: 300 × 1,200 s = 360,000 writes waiting or failing.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY might take about twice as long, around 40 minutes, but writes continue throughout.
If a concurrent build fails, it leaves an invalid index that must be dropped and rebuilt.
Running it outside peak hours reduces its extra load on the table.
numbers.result: A longer, non-blocking change is almost always better than a short, blocking one on a live table.

india.title: Online schema changes in the PostgreSQL documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL ALTER TABLE page lists the lock level for each subcommand and notes that adding a column with a non-volatile default does not rewrite the table, and that NOT VALID constraints can be validated later with a lighter lock. The CREATE INDEX page describes building indexes concurrently, its extra cost, and that it cannot run inside a transaction block.

pitfalls.trap: “Just rename the column in this release.”
pitfalls.say: “Old servers still read the old name during the deploy; I’d expand and contract over two releases.”

pitfalls.trap: “Run the backfill as one UPDATE in the migration.”
pitfalls.say: “That holds locks and floods replicas; I’d batch it in a background job.”

takeaways: Migrations are versioned, ordered and forward-only.
Expand, migrate, switch, contract: every step works with old and new code.
Use lock timeouts, NOT VALID constraints and concurrent index builds.
Backfill in short batches as a separate job.

interactive.title: What breaks?
interactive.prompt: A release renames orders.addr to orders.shipping_address in a migration that runs before the rolling deploy. Half the servers still run the old code for ten minutes.

choices.label: Old servers fail on every query that uses addr
choices.feedback: Right: the column they reference no longer exists until they are replaced.

choices.label: Nothing; the database maps the old name
choices.feedback: A rename does not leave an alias behind.

choices.label: New servers fail until all old ones stop
choices.feedback: New code uses the new name, which exists.

interactive.reveal: Renames and drops break code that is still running. Expand and contract spreads them over releases so every running version works.

title: The N+1 Query Problem
objectives: Recognise the N+1 pattern from query logs
Rewrite it as a join or a batched query
Estimate its cost from round-trip time

cards.title: One query becomes many
cards.body: A page lists 50 posts, then for each post runs another query for its author. That is 1 query for the list plus N queries, one per row: N+1. Each is fast alone, but every one is a separate round trip, and the total grows with the page size.

cards.title: Worked example: 50 posts, 1 ms per round trip
cards.body: Round trips add up even when the database is quick.
steps: Assume: 50 posts, each query takes about 1 ms including the network round trip
N+1: 1 + 50 = 51 queries ≈ 51 ms
Batched: list query, then one query for all 50 authors by id ≈ 2 ms
Joined: one query returning posts with authors ≈ 1–2 ms
cards.note: Result. About 51 ms against about 2 ms under these assumptions. If the database is 5 ms away (another zone or region), N+1 becomes about 255 ms while the batched version stays near 10 ms.

cards.title: Fixing it with a batched query
cards.body: Collect the ids first, then fetch the related rows in one go.
steps: Query 1: SELECT the 50 posts
Collect their distinct author_ids
Query 2: SELECT authors WHERE id IN (… the ids …)
Match authors to posts in memory by id
Two round trips regardless of page size

cards.title: Where it hides
cards.body: Data-access layers that load related records lazily make N+1 easy to write by accident: the loop looks like it touches an object field, but each access runs a query. Templates and serialisers that read related fields per row are common culprits. Counting queries per request in logs or tests catches it.

cards.title: Trap: fixing N+1 with one huge join
cards.body: Joining several one-to-many relations at once (posts → comments → likes) multiplies rows and can return far more data than needed. Prefer a separate batched query per relation, which keeps results small and the number of queries constant.

cards.title: Edge case: batching with a huge IN list
cards.body: Fixing N+1 by loading related rows with WHERE id IN (...) works until the list holds tens of thousands of ids: statements get large, some drivers cap the number of bind parameters (PostgreSQL’s protocol allows at most 65,535), and plans change. Batch in chunks of a few hundred to a few thousand, or join against the parent query instead.

questions.prompt: A request log shows SELECT … FROM authors WHERE id = ? run 100 times after one SELECT … FROM posts. What is this?

choices.label: Normal connection pooling
An N+1 query pattern
A deadlock retry loop
Replication lag

questions.explanation: One list query followed by one query per row.

questions.prompt: What is the usual fix?

choices.label: Load the authors in one query (IN or a join)
Increase the database connection pool size
Cache each separate author query for a second
Add an index on the posts.title column

questions.explanation: Batching makes the query count constant.

questions.prompt: How can a test catch N+1 regressions?

choices.label: Assert the page returns status 200
Assert the response time on a laptop
Count the queries a request makes
Assert the database CPU stays low

questions.explanation: Query counts are stable and machine-independent.

questions.prompt: The database moves to another zone, adding 2 ms per round trip. Which page slows most?

choices.label: The page that makes 2 batched queries
The page that makes 201 queries
All pages slow down equally
The page that makes one join

questions.explanation: Added latency is multiplied by the number of round trips.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a batched load.

items.label: Run one query for all related rows
Index the results by id in memory
Attach each related row to its parent

questions.explanation: Two queries, then an in-memory match.

questions.prompt: A page shows 80 rows with the N+1 pattern; each query costs 3 ms. About how many milliseconds go on queries?
assumptions: One list query plus one per row
questions.explanation: Design implication: a batched version takes about 2 × 3 ms whatever the row count, so the fix matters more as pages and distances grow.

flashcards.back: One query for a list plus one query per row.
A join or a second batched query with IN (…).
Count queries per request.

sources.title: PostgreSQL: Row and Array Comparisons (IN, ANY)

mechanism.title: Why N+1 hurts and how to remove it
steps: Every query pays a fixed cost: a network round trip, parsing or plan lookup, and scheduling on the server, before any rows are read. For tiny queries the fixed cost dominates, so many small queries are much slower than one query returning the same rows.
The N+1 pattern appears when code loops over a result and queries inside the loop. Its cost is (N + 1) × per-query cost, so it grows with page size and with network distance to the database.

Batching collects the ids from the first result and fetches all related rows at once with IN (…) or = ANY(array). The number of queries becomes constant: one per relation, independent of N. Very long id lists can be split into chunks of a few thousand.

Joins return parent and child data in one query. They are ideal for one-to-one and many-to-one relations (posts with their author). For one-to-many relations, a join repeats parent columns per child, so a separate batched query is often leaner.

Detection: log the number of queries per request, flag requests above a threshold, and add tests that assert query counts for key pages. Database statistics views that show the most frequently executed statements also reveal suspiciously high call counts.

When fetching in one query is impractical, pipelining (sending several queries without waiting for each result) or running independent queries in parallel reduces the round-trip cost, but batching usually removes the problem more simply.

useWhen: Use batched loads or joins whenever code fetches related data for a list.
Use query-count assertions in tests for important pages.
avoidWhen: Avoid queries inside loops over result sets.
Avoid joining several one-to-many relations at once, which multiplies rows.

rows: Grows with page size and distance
Still N + 1 worth of server work

numbers.title: The same page in the same region and across regions
assumptions: A page lists 100 orders and loads each customer (N+1)
Same-zone database: 0.5 ms per query; cross-region database: 40 ms per query (illustrative)
steps: Same zone, N+1: 101 × 0.5 = 50.5 ms; batched: 2 × 0.5 = 1 ms.
Cross region, N+1: 101 × 40 = 4,040 ms; batched: 2 × 40 = 80 ms.
The N+1 page goes from acceptable to unusable purely because of distance.
This is why moving an app or its database to another region often exposes hidden N+1 patterns.
numbers.result: N+1 multiplies network latency by the row count; batching makes the cost independent of it.

india.title: Round trips in the PostgreSQL documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL client library documentation describes pipeline mode as a way to send multiple queries without waiting for each result, explicitly to reduce the cost of network round trips between client and server, which is the same cost that makes N+1 patterns slow. The documentation on row and array comparisons describes IN and = ANY, which batched loads rely on.

pitfalls.trap: “Each query takes 1 ms, so the page is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “There are 200 of them; I’d batch them into two queries.”

pitfalls.trap: “The new region made the database slow.”
pitfalls.say: “The database is the same; the page makes hundreds of round trips that now each cost 40 ms.”

takeaways: N+1: a query per row after a list query.
Cost grows with rows and with round-trip time.
Batch with IN (…) or join; keep query count constant.
Assert query counts in tests.

interactive.title: Count the round trips
interactive.prompt: Each query costs 2 ms of round trip. Change how many rows the page lists and compare N+1 with two batched queries.
interactive.takeaway: N+1 grows by 2 ms for every row and passes a 100 ms budget at about 50 rows, while the batched version stays at 4 ms. The fix pays off more as pages grow and the database gets further away.

seeAlso.why: Paginating lists efficiently

title: Connection Pooling
objectives: Explain why opening a database connection is expensive
Size a pool with Little’s law
Keep the total across many app instances under the server limit

cards.title: Connections are not free
cards.body: Opening a database connection means a TCP handshake, often TLS, authentication and, in PostgreSQL, starting a server process for that connection. A pool keeps a set of open connections and lends one to each request for the duration of its queries, so that cost is paid once.

cards.title: Worked example: how many connections does the app need?
cards.body: Little’s law: connections in use = query rate × time each query holds a connection.
steps: Assume: 500 queries a second across the app, each holding a connection for 20 ms
In use on average: 500 × 0.020 = 10 connections
Allow headroom for bursts: a pool of 20
If queries slow to 60 ms under load: 500 × 0.060 = 30 in use, more than the pool
cards.note: Result. About 10 connections are busy on average, and a pool of 20 copes. If query time triples, requests start queueing for connections, so slow queries show up as pool waits in the application.

cards.title: Many instances, one database
cards.body: Every app instance has its own pool, and they all count against the server limit.
steps: The server allows 200 connections, with some reserved for admin
The app runs 30 instances with a pool of 10 each: 300
That exceeds the limit: new connections are refused
Shrink each pool, or put a shared pooler between the app and the database
Recheck whenever autoscaling adds instances

cards.title: Bigger is not faster
cards.body: A database has a fixed number of CPU cores and disks. Beyond a point, more concurrent queries just compete for them and for locks, and each gets slower. A smaller pool with a short queue in the app often gives better throughput and latency than hundreds of connections.

cards.title: Trap: session state with a transaction pooler
cards.body: A shared pooler in transaction mode gives each transaction whichever server connection is free. Session-level state (temporary tables, session settings, advisory locks, some prepared statement setups) does not follow you to the next transaction. Use session mode for code that needs it, or avoid session state.

cards.title: Edge case: pools multiplied by instances
cards.body: Each application instance has its own pool. Twenty instances with a pool of 20 each can open 400 connections, and autoscaling to 50 instances makes it 1,000, past the database’s max_connections. Size pools from the database’s limit divided by the maximum instance count, or put a shared pooler such as PgBouncer in front.

questions.prompt: Why is opening a new PostgreSQL connection per request slow?

choices.label: It needs TCP, often TLS, auth and a new process
Each connection copies the database into memory
PostgreSQL limits each client to one query per connection
Connections must wait for a checkpoint

questions.explanation: Pooling pays these costs once and reuses the connection.

questions.prompt: 1,000 queries a second, each holding a connection 15 ms. About how many connections are busy on average?
Autoscaling grows the app from 10 to 40 instances, each with a pool of 10. The database allows 200 connections. What happens?

choices.label: Each instance shares one connection
The database raises its limit to fit
Connections past 200 are refused
Pools shrink to share the 200

questions.explanation: 40 × 10 = 400 wanted, against 200 allowed.

questions.prompt: Doubling the pool from 50 to 100 made latency worse. Why is that plausible?

choices.label: More queries contend for CPU, disk and locks
Connections in a pool cannot run in parallel
Larger pools disable query caching
Pools above 64 are not supported

questions.explanation: Past the database’s capacity, concurrency adds contention, not throughput.

questions.prompt: Order how a request uses a pool.

items.label: Request returns the connection to the pool
Pool hands over an idle connection, or the request waits
Request asks the pool for a connection
Pool keeps it open for the next request

questions.explanation: Borrow, use briefly, return.

questions.prompt: 20 app instances share a database that allows 220 connections, with 20 reserved for administration. What is the largest pool per instance?
assumptions: Reserved connections not usable by the app
questions.explanation: Design implication: autoscaling to 40 instances would halve that to 5 each, so plan for a shared pooler or cap instance counts before scaling out.

flashcards.back: Connections busy = query rate × hold time.
More concurrency than the database can run just adds contention.
Pool size × instances must stay under the server limit.

mechanism.title: How pools work and how to size them
steps: In PostgreSQL each client connection is served by its own backend process, started when the client connects. Setup includes the network handshake, TLS if used, authentication, and process start, which together cost far more than a typical indexed query.

A pool keeps connections open and lends them out. Requests borrow a connection, run their queries or transaction, and return it. Pools usually have a maximum size, a minimum idle count, a wait timeout for borrowers, and a maximum lifetime so connections are recycled.

Little’s law gives the average number in use: arrival rate × hold time. Hold time includes everything done while holding the connection, so code that does network calls or heavy computation in the middle of a transaction inflates it.

The server has a hard limit (max_connections, 100 by default in PostgreSQL, with a few slots reserved for superusers), and each connection uses memory. The sum of all pools across instances, jobs, migrations and admin tools must fit under it.

External poolers sit between many app instances and the database, multiplexing thousands of client connections onto a small set of server connections. In transaction mode a server connection is assigned per transaction, which is efficient but breaks session-level state.

Throughput peaks at a modest number of active connections, related to the database’s cores and storage; beyond that, contention for CPU, locks and I/O raises latency. Measure with realistic load to find the point, rather than raising pool sizes when things are slow.

useWhen: Use a pool in every long-running service that talks to a database.
Size pools from Little’s law plus headroom, and budget totals across all instances.
avoidWhen: Avoid opening a connection per request.
Avoid holding a connection while waiting on slow external calls.

numbers.title: What happens when queries slow down
assumptions: Normal hold time 25 ms; during an incident it rises to 80 ms
steps: Normal: 400 × 0.025 = 10 busy, half the pool.
Incident: 400 × 0.080 = 32 needed, more than the 20 available.
Requests queue for connections; if the pool wait timeout is 1 s, some start failing even though the database is up.
Raising the pool to 40 only adds load to a database that is already slow; fixing the slow query (or shedding load) restores the margin.
numbers.result: Pool exhaustion is usually a symptom of slower queries; Little’s law shows how quickly a small slowdown uses up the headroom.

india.title: Connections in the PostgreSQL documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: PostgreSQL’s documentation explains that the server starts a separate backend process for each connection (“process per user”), and the max_connections setting defaults to 100 connections, with some reserved for superusers. The kernel-resources chapter shows how connection counts drive memory and semaphore needs, which is why large numbers of idle connections are costly even when they do nothing.

pitfalls.trap: “The pool is exhausted, so let’s double it.”
pitfalls.say: “Hold times probably rose; I’d find the slow queries first, since a bigger pool adds load to a struggling database.”

pitfalls.trap: “Each instance has a small pool, so we’re fine.”
pitfalls.say: “Instances times pool size must fit under max_connections; autoscaling can blow through it.”

takeaways: Opening connections is expensive; pools reuse them.
Busy connections = query rate × hold time.
Sum of pools across instances must fit the server limit.
Bigger pools past the database’s capacity add contention.

interactive.title: Size the pool
interactive.prompt: Your app sends 500 queries a second through a pool of 20 connections. Slide how long each query holds its connection.
interactive.takeaway: At 20 ms about 10 connections are busy. Once queries hold a connection for 40 ms or more, all 20 are busy and requests queue. Slower queries, not more traffic, are the usual reason pools run dry.

seeAlso.why: Scaling app servers horizontally
Ports and sockets are what a connection pool holds open

title: Processes and Threads
objectives: Say what a process owns and what its threads share
Explain what fork and exec each do
Choose processes or threads for isolation versus cheap sharing

cards.title: A process is a container for a running program
cards.body: A process owns an address space (its memory), open file descriptors, credentials and at least one thread of execution. The kernel keeps these apart, so one process cannot read another’s memory unless both deliberately share it. A crash in one process normally leaves the others running.

cards.title: Threads share almost everything
cards.body: Threads are separate paths of execution inside one process. Each has its own stack, registers and program counter, but all share the heap, global data and open files. That makes passing data between threads cheap and also makes it easy for one thread to corrupt data another is using.

cards.title: Worked example: starting a program with fork and exec
cards.body: Unix-like systems create processes in two steps.
steps: The shell calls fork: the kernel creates a child process that is a copy of the parent, sharing memory pages copy-on-write
fork returns twice: the child’s process id to the parent and 0 to the child
The child calls exec with the program path: its memory is replaced by the new program, while open file descriptors (unless marked close-on-exec) stay
The parent calls wait to collect the child’s exit status
If the parent never waits, the finished child stays as a “zombie” entry in the process table

cards.title: Misconception: threads are always lighter, so always better
cards.body: Threads avoid copying address spaces and switch a little faster, but sharing memory means a bug in any thread can corrupt the whole process and a crash takes every thread down. Processes cost more memory but isolate failures and can run with different permissions, which is why browsers and many servers use several processes.

cards.title: Trap: forking a process that has many threads
cards.body: fork copies only the calling thread into the child. If another thread held a lock at that moment, the child inherits the locked lock with no thread to release it. POSIX therefore allows only async-signal-safe calls in the child of a multi-threaded process until it calls exec.

cards.title: Edge case: fork in a multithreaded program
cards.body: fork copies the whole address space but only the thread that called it. If another thread held a lock at that moment, such as the memory allocator’s, the child inherits the lock in its held state with no thread to release it, and can hang on its next allocation. POSIX allows only async-signal-safe calls in the child of a multithreaded fork until it calls exec; prefer posix_spawn or spawning before starting threads.

questions.prompt: Two threads in one process both read a global variable. What does each see?

choices.label: The same memory location
Nothing until the kernel syncs them
A copy-on-write page per thread
A private copy made at thread start

questions.explanation: Threads share the address space; only stacks and registers are per thread.

questions.prompt: What does exec do to the calling process?

choices.label: Replaces its program image
Starts a thread in the same process
Creates a new child process
Closes all open file descriptors

questions.explanation: exec keeps the process id but loads a new program; fork is what creates the process.

questions.prompt: A plugin with a history of crashes must not take the main app down. What is the safer home for it?

choices.label: A separate thread in the app
A larger thread stack
A higher scheduling priority
A separate process

questions.explanation: Process boundaries contain crashes and memory corruption; threads do not.

questions.prompt: A parent never calls wait on its finished children. What accumulates?

choices.label: Orphaned memory pages
Leaked threads in the parent
Open sockets in the child
Zombie process table entries

questions.explanation: A zombie keeps its exit status until the parent collects it.

questions.prompt: Order how a shell runs a command.

items.label: The parent waits and collects the exit status
exec the program in the child

questions.explanation: Create, replace, run, reap.

questions.prompt: An image-conversion service runs third-party decoders that occasionally crash on malformed files.
constraints: A crash must not drop other users’ requests

approaches.label: Run decoders inside the request handler
One process with a thread per conversion
A pool of worker processes the main server hands jobs to

rationaleOptions.label: Each worker can run with fewer permissions
Threads isolate crashes just as well
Processes cannot use several CPU cores
A decoder crash kills only one worker, which is restarted

rationaleConflicts.r3: A segmentation fault in one thread terminates the whole process.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Separate processes run on separate cores like threads do.

questions.explanation: Use processes when isolation matters more than the small cost of copying data between them.

flashcards.back: An address space, file descriptors, credentials and one or more threads.

flashcards.front: What do threads in one process share?
flashcards.back: Heap, globals and open files; each has its own stack and registers.
fork copies the process; exec replaces the program in it.

mechanism.title: How the kernel represents processes and threads
steps: The kernel keeps a record for each process: its memory map, open file table, current directory, user and group ids, signal handlers and resource limits. Each process gets a process id (PID), and every process except the first has a parent.

A thread is the unit the scheduler runs. On Linux both processes and threads are created with clone; flags decide what the new task shares with its creator (memory, file table, signal handlers). A “process” is a group of tasks sharing one address space.

fork creates a child whose memory is a copy of the parent’s, but the copy is lazy: pages are shared read-only and copied only when one side writes (copy-on-write). That is why forking a large process is fast until both sides start writing.

exec loads a new program into the current process: new code, data, heap and stack, same PID. File descriptors stay open across exec unless they carry the close-on-exec flag, which is a common source of leaked descriptors in child programs.

When a process exits, the kernel keeps a small entry with its exit status until the parent reads it with wait. If the parent exits first, the child is re-parented to an init-like process that reaps it.

Choosing between them: threads suit work that shares large data structures and needs fast communication; processes suit isolation, different privileges and crash containment. Many servers combine both: a few processes, each with a pool of threads or an event loop.

useWhen: Use processes to isolate untrusted or crash-prone code and to drop privileges.
Use threads when tasks share large in-memory data and need cheap communication.
avoidWhen: Avoid forking a multi-threaded process and doing real work in the child before exec.
Avoid assuming a crash in one thread leaves the others running.

numbers.title: What copy-on-write saves when forking a large process
assumptions: A parent process uses 2 GB of memory in 4 KB pages (illustrative)
The child calls exec almost immediately
steps: 2 GB ÷ 4 KB ≈ 524,000 pages would need copying with an eager fork.
With copy-on-write, fork copies only page tables and marks pages read-only; almost no data is copied.
The child execs at once, so its shared mappings are dropped before either side writes much.
If instead both keep running and the parent rewrites 25% of its pages, about 131,000 pages (≈ 512 MB) are copied over time.
numbers.result: Copy-on-write makes fork-then-exec cheap, but a long-lived forked child that shares a write-heavy parent slowly duplicates its memory.

india.title: Copy-on-write snapshots in an in-memory store
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Redis documents that its RDB persistence forks the server process and lets the child write a snapshot while the parent keeps serving. Because of copy-on-write the child initially shares all memory, but every page the parent modifies during the snapshot is duplicated, so a write-heavy instance can need noticeably more memory while saving. The same effect appears whenever a long-running process forks a helper.

pitfalls.trap: “Threads are faster, so we run every plugin in a thread.”
pitfalls.say: “Threads are cheaper, but a crashing plugin would take the whole process down; I’d isolate it in a worker process.”

pitfalls.trap: “fork copies all memory, so it is too slow.”
pitfalls.say: “fork is copy-on-write; the cost appears only as pages are written afterwards.”

takeaways: A process owns memory, files and credentials; threads share them.
fork copies lazily (copy-on-write); exec replaces the program.
Processes isolate crashes and privileges; threads share data cheaply.
Parents must wait on children or zombies accumulate.

interactive.title: What happens to the other threads?
interactive.prompt: A web server process runs 16 worker threads. One thread dereferences an invalid pointer and the kernel sends a segmentation fault.

choices.label: The whole process, all 16 threads, is terminated
choices.feedback: Right: the default action for SIGSEGV terminates the process, and threads share it.

choices.label: Only the faulting thread stops
choices.feedback: Signals like SIGSEGV act on the process unless handled; there is no per-thread crash by default.

choices.label: The kernel restarts the faulting thread
choices.feedback: Nothing restarts threads automatically; a supervisor would restart the process.

interactive.reveal: Threads share fate. Isolation from crashes needs separate processes plus a supervisor that restarts them.

seeAlso.why: Process boundaries scaled up: monolith vs services
Containers build on process isolation
What a process and a thread actually are underneath

title: CPU Scheduling and Context Switching
objectives: Explain what a context switch saves and costs
Describe how a fair scheduler shares a CPU
Reason about time slices, run queues and latency

cards.title: More runnable threads than cores
cards.body: A core runs one thread at a time. The scheduler decides which runnable thread runs next and for how long, and switches between them many times a second so each makes progress. Threads waiting for I/O or a lock are not runnable and use no CPU.

cards.title: What a context switch does
cards.body: To switch, the kernel saves the running thread’s registers and program counter, picks the next thread, and restores its state. Switching to a thread in another process also switches the memory mappings, which can flush cached address translations. The direct cost is commonly a few microseconds; the indirect cost of colder caches can be larger.

cards.title: Worked example: the time-slice trade-off
cards.body: Round-robin scheduling gives each runnable thread a slice of time in turn.
steps: Assume a context switch costs 5 µs and 11 threads are runnable on one core (illustrative)
With 1 ms slices: 5 ÷ (1,000 + 5) ≈ 0.5% of the CPU goes on switching; a thread waits up to 10 × 1 = 10 ms to run again
With 10 ms slices: overhead ≈ 0.05%; waiting can reach 100 ms
Shorter slices mean responsiveness, longer slices mean throughput

cards.title: Misconception: more threads means more throughput
cards.body: Once every core is busy, extra CPU-bound threads add no capacity. They only add switching, cache misses and memory for stacks. For CPU-heavy work, a thread count close to the number of cores is usually best; extra threads help only when threads spend time waiting on I/O.

cards.title: Trap: a busy-waiting thread
cards.body: A thread that spins in a loop checking a flag stays runnable and burns its whole slice, slowing every other thread on that core. Waiting should block (on a lock, condition variable or I/O readiness) so the scheduler can run something useful.

cards.title: Edge case: the container sees every host core
cards.body: A container limited to 2 CPUs by a CFS quota may still report the host’s 64 cores. A runtime that sizes its thread pool or garbage collector from that number starts dozens of busy threads, uses up the quota early in each 100 ms period and is throttled for the rest, which shows up as latency spikes. Size pools from the cgroup limit; many modern runtimes now read it.

questions.prompt: What must the kernel save when it switches threads?

choices.label: Each open file’s contents
The process’s source code
The thread’s heap memory
Registers and program counter

questions.explanation: Execution state lives in registers; memory stays where it is.

questions.prompt: A thread is blocked waiting for a disk read. How much CPU does it use?

choices.label: Half a slice, to keep polling
A fixed 1% reserved for it
Its full time slice each round
None until the read completes

questions.explanation: Blocked threads leave the run queue until woken.

questions.prompt: Shrinking the time slice mostly trades what for what?

choices.label: Fewer threads for more cores
Less memory for more CPU
Larger stacks for less I/O
Overhead for responsiveness

questions.explanation: More frequent switches cost overhead but let waiting threads run sooner.

questions.prompt: A 4-core machine runs a CPU-bound job. Which thread count is a sensible start?

choices.label: 1, to avoid switching
About 4
One per request in flight
About 400

questions.explanation: More CPU-bound threads than cores only add switching.

questions.prompt: One core, 21 runnable CPU-bound threads, round robin with 5 ms slices. Worst-case milliseconds before a thread runs again?
assumptions: Each other thread uses its full slice
questions.explanation: Design implication: interactive work stuck behind 20 CPU-bound threads waits about 100 ms, so latency-sensitive work needs fewer competitors or a higher priority.

questions.prompt: A request handler waits for a lock held by another thread for about 2 ms.

approaches.label: Sleep a fixed 10 ms, then try again
Spin in a loop checking the lock
Block on the lock so the thread sleeps until it is released

rationaleOptions.label: A fixed sleep wakes exactly on time
Spinning is faster for any wait
Sleeping threads give their CPU to others
The kernel wakes the thread when the lock is free

rationaleConflicts.r3: Spinning helps only for very short waits; 2 ms of spinning wastes a whole slice.
rationaleConflicts.r4: It adds up to 10 ms of extra latency after the lock is free.

questions.explanation: Block for waits longer than a context switch; spin only for waits of a few microseconds.

flashcards.back: Saving one thread’s CPU state and restoring another’s.
Lower latency, more switching overhead.
No, they leave the run queue until woken.

sources.title: Linux kernel docs: CFS scheduler design

mechanism.title: How a general-purpose scheduler shares cores
steps: Each core has a run queue of runnable threads. A thread leaves it when it blocks (I/O, lock, sleep) and rejoins when woken. Preemption happens on a timer tick or when a higher-priority thread wakes, so one thread cannot hold a core forever.

Linux’s CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) tracked each thread’s weighted run time and always ran the one that had received the least; since kernel 6.6 the default policy uses EEVDF, which also accounts for how late each thread is. Both aim to share CPU in proportion to weights set by nice values.

Real-time policies (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR) sit above normal threads: a runnable real-time thread always runs before normal ones. That is useful for audio or control loops and dangerous for anything that might spin.

A context switch saves registers, switches the kernel stack and, across processes, switches page tables. The CPU’s caches and translation buffers then hold the previous thread’s data, so the new thread runs slower until they warm up.

Waking a thread on another core and moving threads between cores to balance load both cost cache warmth. Schedulers prefer to keep a thread on the core it last ran on, and you can pin threads (CPU affinity) for latency-critical work.

Measure, do not guess: per-thread run time, voluntary versus involuntary context switches (reported per process by the kernel) and run-queue length show whether threads are starved of CPU or simply waiting on I/O.

useWhen: Use a CPU-bound thread count near the core count.
Use blocking waits (locks, condition variables, readiness APIs) instead of spinning.
avoidWhen: Avoid thousands of runnable threads per core; switching and cache misses dominate.
Avoid real-time priorities for code that might loop or block on others.

rows: Pinning a thread to a core

numbers.title: How many context switches a busy server does
assumptions: A server handles 20,000 requests a second (illustrative)
Each request blocks twice (database call, then network write), causing a switch each time it blocks and each time it wakes
steps: Switches ≈ 20,000 × 2 blocks × 2 (out and back in) = 80,000 per second.
At about 5 µs each, that is 0.4 CPU-seconds per second: 40% of one core.
Spread across 8 cores, about 5% of total CPU goes to switching.
An event loop that handles many sockets per thread avoids most of these switches, which is part of why it scales to many connections.
numbers.result: Context switches are cheap one at a time but add up to a measurable share of CPU at tens of thousands of requests a second.

india.title: The Linux scheduler moved from CFS to EEVDF
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux kernel documentation describes CFS as modelling an “ideal, precise multi-tasking CPU” by tracking virtual run time, and documents EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First), which replaced it as the default in Linux 6.6. EEVDF keeps proportional fairness but also gives each task a virtual deadline, which improves latency for tasks that run in short bursts.

pitfalls.trap: “Add more threads, the server will go faster.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if threads are waiting on I/O; for CPU-bound work beyond the core count they just add switching.”

pitfalls.trap: “Context switches are free.”
pitfalls.say: “A few microseconds each plus cache effects; at 80,000 a second that is a noticeable share of a core.”

takeaways: The scheduler shares cores among runnable threads; blocked threads use no CPU.
A context switch saves and restores CPU state and cools caches.
Short slices favour latency; long slices favour throughput.
Match CPU-bound threads to cores; block rather than spin.

interactive.title: Pick a time slice
interactive.prompt: A core has 11 runnable threads and each context switch costs 5 µs. Slide the time slice and watch overhead against how long a thread waits to run again.
interactive.takeaway: Below about 0.5 ms the CPU spends over 1% just switching; above 10 ms a thread can wait over 100 ms for its turn. Schedulers pick slices in the low milliseconds, and the real fix for long waits is fewer runnable threads.

title: Virtual Memory and Paging
objectives: Explain how virtual addresses map to physical memory
Distinguish minor and major page faults
Predict what happens when memory runs out

cards.title: Every process sees its own address space
cards.body: Programs use virtual addresses. The memory management unit translates them to physical addresses using page tables the kernel maintains, in fixed-size pages (commonly 4 KB). Two processes can use the same virtual address for different physical memory, which is how isolation works.

cards.title: Pages are loaded on demand
cards.body: The kernel does not load a program’s whole file or allocate all requested memory up front. The first touch of a page causes a page fault, and the kernel then maps a physical page. A minor fault finds the data already in memory (for example in the page cache); a major fault must read it from disk.

cards.title: Worked example: why a translation cache matters
cards.body: Each memory access needs a translation, so CPUs cache recent ones in a translation lookaside buffer (TLB).
steps: Assume 4 KB pages and a TLB with 1,536 entries (illustrative)
Memory covered without a page-table walk: 1,536 × 4 KB = 6 MB
A program touching 1 GB randomly misses the TLB often, and each miss walks several levels of page tables
With 2 MB “huge” pages, the same 1,536 entries cover 3 GB
That is why databases and JVM-style runtimes often offer huge-page settings

cards.title: Misconception: free memory is wasted memory, so the box is full
cards.body: Tools often show little “free” memory because the kernel uses spare RAM as a page cache for files. That memory is reclaimable: it is dropped when programs need it. The useful number is available memory, not free memory.

cards.title: Trap: assuming allocation means memory exists
cards.body: On Linux, allocations are usually overcommitted: asking for memory succeeds, and physical pages are assigned only when touched. If many processes then touch what they asked for, the system runs out and the out-of-memory killer terminates a process, often the largest, rather than the allocation failing cleanly.

cards.title: Edge case: memory that fails later
cards.body: Linux overcommits memory by default: allocating a large block usually succeeds, and physical pages are assigned only when they are first written. If the system then runs out, the allocation does not fail; the out-of-memory killer ends a process, possibly a different one. In containers the cgroup memory limit triggers the same kill, so watch for exit code 137 rather than for allocation errors.

questions.prompt: Two processes print the same pointer value. Do they share that memory?

choices.label: Not necessarily; mappings differ
No, the kernel forbids equal addresses
Yes, addresses are global
Yes, unless one is a thread

questions.explanation: The same virtual address can map to different physical pages per process.

questions.prompt: Which page fault is the expensive one?

choices.label: A major fault that reads from disk
A fault on a page already mapped
A fault on the stack guard page
A minor fault on a cached page

questions.explanation: Major faults wait for storage; minor ones only update mappings.

questions.prompt: A monitoring tool shows 200 MB free on a 16 GB server with 9 GB of page cache. Is it short of memory?

choices.label: Probably not; page cache is reclaimable
Yes, it will start swapping within minutes
Yes, the OOM killer will fire
Only if swap is turned off

questions.explanation: Look at available memory, which counts reclaimable cache.

questions.prompt: Processes touch more memory than RAM plus swap can hold. What usually happens on Linux?

choices.label: The OOM killer ends a process
Processes pause until memory frees up
The kernel compresses all code pages
The allocation call returns an error

questions.explanation: With overcommit the failure shows up at touch time, not at allocation.

questions.prompt: A TLB has 1,024 entries of 2 MB pages. How many MB of memory does it cover?
assumptions: Every entry holds a distinct 2 MB page
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the same TLB with 4 KB pages covers only 4 MB, which is why huge pages help large in-memory data sets.

questions.prompt: Order what happens on the first read of a page from a memory-mapped file that is not cached.

items.label: The kernel finds the file page is not in memory
The kernel maps the page and the instruction is retried
The kernel reads the page from disk into the page cache
The CPU finds no valid translation and raises a page fault

questions.explanation: Fault, look up, read, map, retry.

flashcards.back: An access to a page with no valid mapping, handled by the kernel.
Minor: data already in memory; major: must read from disk.
A CPU cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations.

sources.title: Linux kernel docs: Memory management concepts

mechanism.title: From a virtual address to a physical page
steps: A virtual address is split into a page number and an offset. The page number is looked up in multi-level page tables (four or five levels on 64-bit x86) to find the physical page; the offset selects the byte inside it.

The TLB caches recent translations. A TLB hit costs almost nothing; a miss triggers a page-table walk through memory. Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB) reduce the number of entries needed for large data sets.
Mappings carry permissions (read, write, execute) and flags such as present and dirty. Writing to a read-only shared page (as after fork) causes a fault the kernel resolves by copying the page.

Memory comes in two kinds: anonymous memory (heap, stacks) and file-backed memory (program code, memory-mapped files, the page cache). Under pressure, clean file pages can simply be dropped and re-read later; anonymous pages must go to swap if there is any.

The kernel reclaims memory in the background when free memory falls below watermarks. If reclaim cannot keep up, allocations stall in direct reclaim, which shows up as latency spikes before any process is killed.

When memory is exhausted, the out-of-memory killer picks a victim using a badness score (mostly memory use, adjustable per process). In containers, a cgroup memory limit triggers the same mechanism for processes inside that group.

useWhen: Use available memory (including reclaimable cache) to judge headroom.
Use huge pages for large, long-lived in-memory data such as database buffers.
avoidWhen: Avoid sizing a heap to almost all of RAM; the page cache and other processes need room.
Avoid treating swap activity as harmless on latency-sensitive servers.

rows: First touch, copy-on-write, cached file page

numbers.title: How major faults turn into latency
assumptions: A service handles a request with 50 page touches, normally all in memory (illustrative)
Under memory pressure, 2% of touches become major faults costing 100 µs each on SSD
steps: Faulting touches per request: 50 × 0.02 = 1.
Added time: 1 × 100 µs = 0.1 ms on average.
But faults cluster: a request that hits 10 faults waits an extra 1 ms, and on spinning disks (about 10 ms per read) 10 faults add 100 ms.
So the tail latency grows long before average latency moves.
numbers.result: Memory pressure hurts tail latency first; watch major faults, not only free memory.

india.title: Kernel documentation on memory management concepts
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux kernel’s admin guide explains virtual memory, huge pages, zones, page cache, anonymous memory, reclaim and the OOM killer in one place. It notes that the kernel uses otherwise unused memory to cache file data and reclaims it under pressure, and that when reclaim fails the OOM killer selects a task to kill to free memory.

pitfalls.trap: “The server has no free memory, we need more RAM.”
pitfalls.say: “Most of it is page cache; I’d check available memory and major fault rates first.”

pitfalls.trap: “If malloc succeeded, the memory is ours.”
pitfalls.say: “With overcommit, pages are assigned on first touch; the failure can come later as an OOM kill.”

takeaways: Virtual addresses map to physical pages through page tables cached in the TLB.
Major page faults read from disk and hurt tail latency.
Page cache is reclaimable; judge headroom by available memory.
Overcommit moves out-of-memory failures to touch time and the OOM killer.

interactive.title: Which process is killed?
interactive.prompt: A container has a 1 GB memory limit. Its app grows to 1.1 GB of touched heap. The host has 64 GB free.

choices.label: A process inside the container, by the OOM killer
choices.feedback: Right: the cgroup limit applies regardless of host memory.

choices.label: Nothing: the host has plenty of memory
choices.feedback: The limit is per cgroup, so host free memory does not help.

choices.label: The allocation call fails and the app handles it
choices.feedback: With overcommit, the failure comes at touch time as a kill.

interactive.reveal: Container memory limits are enforced by the same OOM mechanism, scoped to the container’s cgroup.
